A Shocking Double Murder in Los Angeles County.

A Shocking Double Murder in Los Angeles County.

SANTA ANA, January 26th.—A mysterious disappearance and probably a double murder case was developed here this morning. A Mr. Hitchcock, a prominent farmer of the Garden Grove, five miles from Santa Ana, came to town on last Monday morning with his wife and acknowledged a deed to his property to a German named Anschlag, who lived on the ranch, and has not since been heard of.

Suspicious were aroused last night and investigation proves that Hitchcock and his wife returned home Monday afternoon and delivered the deed to Anschlag, who claims that he paid them the balance in cash, viz., $8,000, and brought them to Santa Ana before daylight Tuesday morning to take the early train. They were not seen here and no such parties are known to have taken the train on that date.

Search at the house proves all their clothing, including three overcoats of Mr. Hitchcock and his wife's clothing, trunks and jewelry, including her gold watch, are all unmolested, or not even packed up and put away.

Every indication leads to the guilt of Anschlag, who has been placed under arrest, and detectives have been detailed to work up the case at once.

LATER—Anschlag's wagon was found this afternoon covered with blood. The excitement is very high. A strong guard will be necessary to prevent lynching.

LATER—THE MURDERER LYNCHED.

SANTA ANA, January 26th.—P. M.—The murderer, Fritz Anschlag, was captured today and summarily lynched. Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock were beloved by the entire community, and their terrible fate has cast a gloom over the place. The murderer confessed his crime.

FINDING OF THE BODIES.

The bodies of the two victims were found buried in a shallow grave. The husband's throat was cut, and both had their heads beaten almost to a jelly by a club. The people became frantic when the discovery was made, and a party set off at once for the house determined to wreak vengeance on the fendish author of the terrible crime.

They returned home, but not having been seen thereafter, neighbors grew suspicious of foul play and instituted a search. Their dead bodies were found yesterday a long distance from the house. antoine-dyker-santa-ana-1888-01-26.A4:
MURDER MOST FOUL.
Terrible Tragedy Enacted Near Santa Ana.
A MAN AND HIS WIFE KILLED.
The Assassin Lynched by a Posse of Infuriated Citizens.
[Associated Press dispatches to the HERALD]
SANTA ANA, January 26.—Mr. Hitchcock, a prominent farmer of Garden Grove, five miles from Santa Ana, came to town last Monday evening with his wife, and acknowledged his property to a German named Anschlag, who had bought his ranch, and after that was not heard of. Suspicion was aroused last night, and investigation proves that Hitchcock and his wife returned home on Monday afternoon and delivered the deed to Anschlag who claimed that he paid them the balance in cash, viz: $8000, and brought them to Santa Ana before daylight on Tuesday morning to take the early train. They were not seen here and no such parties are known to have taken the train on that date. Search at the house proves that all their clothing, including three overcoats of Mr. Hitchcock and his wife's clothing, trunks and jewelry, including her gold watch, are all unmolested, or not even packed up and put away.

A GHASTLY DISCOVERY.

At 4:45 this afternoon one of the numerous parties of searchers, riding three miles southeast of the Hitchcock house, discovered fresh straw on the prarie. They commenced digging and soon discovered bodies. They soon unearthed them, and after taking the names of witnesses, lifted out the bodies of Chas. B. Hitchcock and his wife.

HOW THE DEED WAS DONE.

Hitchcock while attending to his team between 9 and 10 p. m. as usual, was waylaid in the barn by Anschlag with an axe, who followed this up by killing Mrs. Hitchcock, loading both bodies in the wagon, drawing them to this forsaken spot, burying them and starting to Santa Ana by daylight. Out of the horrible hole came several cans, probably of blood, gathered from the ground where the victims were killed. Next came two ropes which had been on the legs of the bodies to haul them around with. A party of lynchers quickly organized and started at once for Anschlag, but Marshal Insley had foreseen the trouble and started the prisoner for Anaheim.

IDENTITY OF THE DECEASED.

Mr. Hitchcock, was a handsome man, tall, broad, shouldered, and commanding of appearance; Mrs. Hitchcock, was likewise a handsome, refined lady highly accomplished. Both were leaders of social societies. He was one of the main leaders in the advancements of the Santa Ana valley and first in railroad movements, hotels, etc. Both were loved and honored by all who knew them. Mr. Hitchcock's father and mother are now tottering on the edge of their graves. Mrs. Hitchcock's father and mother are living at Compton, Illinois, with another son, Frank.

Anschlag is a middle sized man, dark brown eyes, smooth face, well dressed, speaks very little English. He has been here one year. He has a brother in Manchester, England. His mother lives in Germany.

LATEST—ANSCHLAG LYNCHED.

Information reached here at 8:30 P. M. that the lynching party overtook the officers a few miles south of Anaheim, near a bunch of trees, and finished by hanging the murderer. The courts will be petitioned to set aside the deed and allow the property to go to the heirs of the murdered instead of to those of the murderer.

The Santa Ana Avengers Fall to Catch Murderer Anschlag.

[Copyright, 1888, by the California Associated Press.]

SANTA ANA, January 27th.—As your reporter left the lynchers last night, at the residence of the deceased, they started in pursuit of the officers. The crowd arrived shortly at Anaheim and broke open the jail, not overtaking the officers, but found no prisoner. The half-frightened populace of Anaheim, believing they had succeeded in catching the murderers, telephoned the officers here to that effect.

The night was dark, and a very thick fog had arisen before 6 o'clock. It was impossible to see 100 yards ahead, and the officers, by turning at the first cross-road, easily evaded the mob, and, by lying out all night, reached Anaheim in safety and took the Southern Pacific train to Los Angeles and delivered the prisoners at the County Jail.

Constable Farley, in the discharge of his duty, is deserving of the greatest praise, as not only did he do his duty, but he was no doubt the means of saving the life of Antonio Decker, who as yet stands clear of all evidence of guilt, circumstantially or otherwise.

The bodies of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock were washed this forereon, and multitudes of people, reaching thousands in number, viewed the ghastly sight.

Mr. Hitchcock had been chopped in the back of the head by the stroke of the ax, and then chopped a second time as he turned around, this time over the right car and just below the crown of the head. His throat was then cut with a knife.

Mrs. Hitchcock had been chopped first in the right temple by one blow of the sharp ax, as she was, no doubt, approaching the murderer face to face, her every expression on her once beautiful, but now firm, countenance, showing she had evidently been coming to the protection of her beloved husband, thinking naught of herself and caring less for the dangers before her, her mind and her soul intently bent on the defense of her husband. No more touching picture of pure womanhood ever blessed the countenance of humanity than the firm and determined look on the corpse of Mrs. Louise Hitchcock to-day.

New and startling developments were made this morning at the residence of the murdered couple. The bloody ax which had done the fatal deed was a common ax well sharpened, and was found under the barn thoroughly besmeared with the blood of its victims, and a few moments later J. C. Gormley, reporter of the Los Angeles Tribune, discovered the connecting link of the tragedy in the form of Anschlag's well-known overalls thoroughly saturated and besmeared with the blood of the victims and the mud from their grave.

The Double California Murder.
SANTA ANNA, CAL., Jan. 28.—The coroner's jury summoned yesterday to investigate the cause of the deaths of Hitchcock and his wife returned a verdict that they met their deaths at the hands of persons unknown, but they believe Anschlag, who was lynched, to be one of the persons.
antoine-dyker-santa-ana-1888-01-26.A10:
No doubt now remained in the minds of the populace but that Anschlag was the murderer, and the enraged citizens started out to lynch him. Constable Finley had removed him and the German who was arrested with him to Anaheim, whence he was followed by the infuriated mob, who broke into the jail, but did not find Anschlag to vent their rage upon, as he had been removed from the jail shortly before, and, it is stated, was hidden in a corn-bin. Yesterday both men were brought to the county jail in this city, where they will be safe for a time.

Drs. Kelly and Ball made a thorough post-mortem examination of the bodies, but had not sent in their report when our reporter left.

THE INQUEST.

Mr. O. Witham testified at the inquest as follows: I am a farmer and blacksmith residing at Garden Grove. On Thursday morning I went to Dr. John Chaffee, brother-in-law of the deceased, and had a conversation with him concerning the disappearance of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock, and from the facts I had learned I thought that perhaps a murder had been committed. I told him my suspicions and he stated that he thought that probably the two Germans had done the deed. Mrs. Chaffee told me that she had gone down to Mrs. Hitchcock's house and searched it. All the clothes were there except the dress that Mrs. Hitchcock had on. She asked Anschlag what sort of clothes Mrs. Hitchcock had on when he drove her and her husband up town. His statement did not compare with any clothes that the two deceased had. Anschlag also told Mrs. Chaffee that he drove them to Santa Ana, but he did not know whether they were going to Los Angeles or not when he left them. I then suggested that we commence the search for the bodies at once. I went to the barn of Mr. Hitchcock and took measurements of the horses' feet, also the width of the wheels apart and the breadth of the tiers. I examined the wagon and found blood on the floor of the wagon and on the cross-bar; this showed us that there had been foul play, and we started out for the store near Garden Grove and went westwards, examining the tracks of horses' feet and the wagon tracks. When we got near Dr. Head's residence we saw three men digging. We drove down and they told us that they had found Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock. They had dug as far as the corpses when we got there. Mr. Robinson was with me. They had thrown out the dirt and also a canvass frock, a pair of overalls and a hat Both bodies were severely bruised and cut about the head and neck. We took the bodies out, put them into a wagon and brought them to the undertaker's rooms at Santa Ana. The search for the bodies commenced on Thursday, after 1 'oclock P. M. We found no instruments, that had been used to commit the deed, in the barn. The hired German that was arrested with Anschlag came to his place on Tuesday, and the murder probably occurred on Monday night between 8 and 10 o'clock p. m. A social had been arranged on Sunday to take place on Wednesday evening at the house of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock."

Several papers, a bank bill, a powder or two, two pair of bloody overalls, and a half-burned letter were found in a clump of cane trees a short distance from where the murderer had buried his victims. The letter was in Mrs. Hitchcock's hand-writing, and had evidently been written on Sunday or Monday. The inquest was still in progress when the reporter left for this city.

THE PRISONER.

Upon learning that Fred Anschlag had been brought to this city, a representative of THE HERALD. visited the County Jail, and through the kindness of Jailer Russell was permitted to see and talk to the prisoner. He is a tall, slender, black-haired, smooth-faced, youngish-looking man, with high cheek bones, and was rather fashionably than otherwise attired. He could speak very little English, but said that he was not guilty of the murder of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock, and that the last he had seen of them was on Tuesday morning last, when he had left them in front of Mr. Taylor's house in Santa Aua. The first time he met Mr. Hitchcock was when he went to the office of W. A. Beckett in Santa Ana for the purpose of buying a ranch. Mr. Beckett had shown him property in several places, and among others that of Mr. Hitchcock, for which he was to pay $8000. In making preliminary arrangements for the purchase, the prisoner had engaged Mr. Taylor, a lawyer, who could speak German. On Wednesday, last week he agreed to buy the place and paid Mr. Hitchcock $95 on account, at the same time signing an agreement to purchase the same. After the agreement had been made he had gone to Anaheim and engaged Antone Decker to work for him and then went back to Santa Ana and stopped at the Taylor House until Saturday, when he went to the residence of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock and stayed until Tuesday. Mr. Hitchcock had obtained a deed and had taken it home with him. On Monday, Mr. and Mrs Hitchcock said they were coming to Los Angeles on the morning train. So on Tuesday morning he and the murdered people rose at 5 o'clock. Shortly afterward he paid Mr. Hitchcock the remainder of the $8,000 and received the deed in return. He then hitched the team to the wagon and all three started for Santa Ana, where Mr. Hitchcock expected to take the train for this city. A Farmer and His Wife Brutally Murdered.

The Horticulturists—Bad Man Bagged—What the Committees are Doing—Russian Rackets.

SAN FRANCISCO, January 27.—A special from Santa Ana says, C. B. Hitchcock, a prominent farmer, came to Santa Ana last Monday with his wife, and acknowledged a deed to his property to a German named Anschlag. They returned home, but not being seen thereafter the neighbors grew suspicious of foul play, instituted a search to-day, and found the dead bodies a long distance from the house. Hitchcock and wife were found side by side in a hole in the ground which had been covered over with earth and straw. Hitchcock's throat was cut from ear to ear, and his wife's head split open with a hatchet. It seemed evident that Anschlag had murdered them to retain the money he had paid them for the land. A lynching party at once started to find Anschlag. Before the officers could interfere Anschlag had been hung by the hands of the lynchers.

Charles B. Hitchcock came to this State in 1876 from Elgin, Illinois. His father and mother are now living at Compton, Illinois. The malden name of Mrs. Hitchcock, who was found murdered with her husband, was Rose Bradley. She also lived with her parents at Elgin, and was a daughter of W. S. Bradley. Fritz Anschlag, who is supposed to have murdered the couple is a German, 25 years old, and came to this State about one year ago, living at San Francisco for some time. He had a supposed partner named Antone Dyker. Two weeks ago Anschlag appeared at Santa Ana, ostensibly to buy a farm, and arranged to buy the Hitchcock place for $8,000, paying a small advance. Last Saturday the abstract was completed, and the deed to the farm was executed at Santa Ana. Anschlag desired to postpone paying over the money until Monday, and accompanied Hitchcock to their home. It is supposed that he murdered Hitchcock and his wife some time on Monday or Monday night, secreting their bodies as telegraphed. A telegram was received this morning that both Anschlag and Dyke were lynched seven miles from Santa Ana last night, and their bodies left hanging to a tree. Hitchcock was a man very highly respected and was one of the most prominent men in the county.

LOS ANGELES, Cala., January 27. — Accounts published this morning about the lynching of the murderers of the Hitchcocks near Santa Ana were incorrect. The murderers were hidden in Anaheim over night to escape the mob and brought to jail here this morning.
antoine-dyker-santa-ana-1888-01-26.A19:
SUNDAY, JANUARY 29, 1888.
The murderer of Mr. and Mrs. Hitchcock has confessed his crime, and this sets all doubts at rest as to his guilt. His confession comports with the rational theory which everybody had formed about the crime and its guilty author. Indeed, Anschlag had concocted his plan and carried it out in such a manner that the circumstances themselves were an unerring index to the main facts of the entire tragedy. Whilst he thought he was shrewd and cunning, he left a trail that even dullness itself could follow. It was hardly necessary that he should have confessed, for every circumstantial detail that came to light, including his own shallow declarations, were "confirmations strong as proof of holy writ" of his guilt. He was surrounded by a wall of facts, all leading to the door of truth, from which there was no escape. His confession is even yet wanting in verity in some minor and incidental points; but there is no doubt that his declaration exculpating Decker from all connection with the crime is true. This makes us doubly thankful that the lynching threats at Anaheim were not successful. Had they been carried out an innocent man, as well as the murderer, might have fallen a victim to the fury of the exasperated mob.
antoine-dyker-santa-ana-1888-01-26.A20:
THE SANTA ANA BUTCHERY.
The Anschlag-Hitchcock murder in Southern California was one of the most horrible in its bloody details that has been put upon criminal records. Anschlag deliberately chopped to pieces Hitchcock and his wife, and cut their throats, in order to secure the deed to their farm which had been made out for delivery to him when he should have paid over the purchase price he led them to believe he possessed. It was therefore a premeditated and cold-blooded murder, without a solitary feature to suggest merciful doubts, provocation or charitable suspension of judgment. Let us note now how long it will be before the slow processes of our laws visit punishment upon this murderer. In some countries he would be legally hanged or beheaded within a week; with us it takes from one to three years to accomplish the cause of justice in the plainest of cases, so that though Anschlag confesses his horrible crime, and the strongest of circumstantial evidence confirms his story, it is not probable that he will swing for his infamy for a year or two yet, and he may, even lawfully, escape the gallows altogether.

Weak juries, weak Courts, and weaker prosecuting officers, save the necks of many wretches. In the hot indignation of the present, it would seem that nothing could save Anschlag's neck except death before the noose is oiled for him, but it is not safe to count upon the positiveness of his conviction. In jail Anschlag occasionally throws up his hands, and cries out: "I killed Hitchcock and his wife! Oh, my God! my God! what will become of me?" Is there not here a keynote for ingenious lawyers to frame a theory of insanity for this murderer? Will not this class of shrewd and learned men be able to raise doubts of the man's even balance of mind when he so barbarously slew the old man and his wife? Will it not be argued that the horrid character of the butchery is inconsistent with the presumption of sanity? Perhaps Anschlag, under careful instruction, will be able to make his behavior in jail for the next few weeks relate to his past actions in such a manner as to move a weak juryman or two to be more than merciful to him? Certainly it will not do to count confidently upon the conviction of this human butcher, who brained his victims with a hatchet, cut their throats from ear to ear, carried the mutilated bodies some miles and buried them in a shallow grave of his own digging.

While the public mind awaits the solution of the problem whether the murderer will receive his just deserts, and which is ever present until the trap is sprung, the opportunity is open for the sentimental sisterhood to again make their presence manifest. There has never been a case fatter with food for their sickly tears. They can shower this Santa Ana savage with flowers, and mingle their piteous tears with his repentant moans to fine advantage. The case affords them a splendid opportunity to pour out upon a red-handed ruffian the wealth of their sympathies and their purses. He is a fit subject for their pitiful sighing, and is bloody enough to appease the most ardent demands of their natures for objects upon which to exercise their sympathetic souls.
antoine-dyker-santa-ana-1888-01-26.A28:
Anschlag Convicted.
Los ANGELES, Cala., Feb. 19. — The trial of Frederick Anschlag, who murdered Charles B. Hitchcock and wife near Santa Ana, Jan. 24, closed here to-day and the jury, after fifteen minutes deliberation, rendered a verdict of guilty of murder in the first degree. The court fixed Feb. 24, as the day of passing the death sentence.

Anchlag's motives for murdering the Hitchcocks was to obtain possession of a deed to a ranch owned by them. According to his own confession made afterwards, the three were riding along a road in an open wagon on the morning of the tragedy and without giving his victims any warning he attacked them with a hatchet, which he had previously concealed, killing both in a few minutes. He then tied a rope to the bodies and dragged them a short distance and buried them in a hole, which he dug for the purpose. When the bodies were discovered the wildest excitement prevailed among the citizens and Anschlag and another man who was also suspected, but afterwards proved to have had nothing to do with the crime, narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of a mob.

During Anschlag's trial the plea of insanity was advanced by the defense, but the commission appointed by the court, decided that he was a perfectly sane person.

FARMVILLE, Va., Sept. 1.--Archer Cook, a negro about 22 years of age, who had been confined in the Prince Edward county jail for some months awaiting trial for a fiendish assault upon a young lady, named Lizzie Frank, daughter of respectable German parents, and whose trial has been postponed from term to term on account of the continued illness of the unfortunate girl who could not appear in court to testify, was taken from his cell early yesterday morning by a body of armed and masked men and hanged. The jail was badly damaged, though the affair was managed as if by men drilled to this work. Entrance was made through the brick walls, which readily gave way to the force of fearless and furious men. The prisoner screamed piteously, but was hushed by the infuriated and determined lynchers. When taken out he was hurried to the nearest woods, where he was swung to the limb of an oaktree, his feet being allowed to touch the ground. At least twenty five shots were heard. Soon afterwards the men galloped off, leaving a terribly mangled corpse.

J. F. Miller (colored) fell from the New York express train on the Cumberland Valley Railroad on the night of Aug. 29, near Chambersburg, Pa. He was sitting on the platform of one of the cars and thinks he must have fallen asleep and been jolted from the car as the train rushed along at top speed. His left hip and collar bone were broken, his head badly cut, and he sustained other injuries. — An extra freight train on the Burlington Railroad, carrying a coach loaded with passengers for the Creston (Iowa) fair, was ditched by a bad rail near Creston Saturday, and a flagman went back to stop a following extra. The flagman failed to reach the train, which was running down grade, in time to prevent a collision. The passengers had barely time to get out when the engine crashed into the first train. — Crowley, the chimpanzee of the New York Central Park menagerie, was thoroughly dissected Saturday at the Museum of Natural History. The immediate cause of death was found to be congestion of the right lung. By the ravages of consumption it was a putrid mass, caked over with pleuric matter, which fastened on the chest walls and closed the lung cavity. The liver was degenerated and the heart unsound. Peritonitis had diseased the kidneys and covered them with tubercles. Tubercles were found on all the organs, and the walls of the chest and abdomen. The climate and the diet to which the monkey was subjected were undoubtedly the cause of his complete decay. — Dr. Joseph Moore, a prominent politician, was struck by a train at a crossing on the New Jersey Central Railroad in West Bridgeton, N. J., Saturday, and died in three hours. — Dr. Joseph Parker, a wealthy resident of Raleigh, N. C., died in his carriage at the depot in that city Saturday, where he had gone to meet his wife. Asthma is supposed to have caused his death. — Arthur White, a youth of 19, who several weeks ago absconded with $10,000 belonging to the banking-house of Kittredge & Co., Denver, Colo., has been apprehended at Victoria, B. C., and $8,500 of the money has been recovered.——Sunday morning fire destroyed in Baltimore about $1,000,000 worth of property in the block bounded by Sharp, Lombard, Hanover and Pratt streets, and seven firemen were crushed to death by a falling wall.——The freight steamer City of Lawrence, of the Norwich (Conn.) Transportation Co., caught fire Friday night while off New Haven, en route to Norwich. The fire originated in 200 bales of cotton in the hold. The crew succeeded in checking the flames sufficiently for the steamer to reach Norwich. There were between 35 and 40 passengers aboard, and for a time panic reigned.——Friday night a locomotive-boiler exploded at Sewell Station, W. Va., killing John Williams, fireman, and fatally wounding Henry Shooman, engineer. Henry Gunther, Joe Jackson and Wm. Bush were seriously injured.——Friday night Maggie Oxsture, of Campbell's Creek, W. Va., drank a half ounce of laudanum with suicidal intent. A love affair was the cause of attempt at self-destruction. Her recovery is doubtful.——A free-for-all fight occurred at a miners' dance near Hawk's Nest (W. Va.) coal mines Friday night. Constable Eads, who attempted to quell the riot, was shot; it is thought to be fatal. George Jones and Mike O'Hara, miners, were shot. Their wounds are not of a serious nature. Joe Briggs, James Callahan, Conrad Jones, Jerry Kenney and Wm. Studds were arrested for doing the shooting.——The progress of yellow fever in Florida continues without interruption. Every day's telegrams from Jacksonville show from 20 to 30 new cases, with an increasing death rate. The type of the fever is not considered as malignant as usual, however. The people are frightened and are fleeing from the city in large numbers, the quarantine being raised to permit them to escape.——A party of 40 armed men broke down the doors of the jail at Farmville, Va., on Saturday morning and dragged out a negro named Archer Cook. They carved him to the outskirts of the town, hung him to a tree and riddled his body with bullets. He was accused of a brutal assault upon the person of a young white woman.

The last span in the great bridge across the Hudson river at Poughkeepsie, N. Y., was completed on the 30th ult.

JOHN FILLHART, aged ninety-three years, hanged himself in his son's barn at Depauville, N. Y., on the 31st ult. No cause was known.

It was announced on the 31st ult. that a banana "trust" had been formed at New Orleans with a capital of $19,000,000.

Owing to ill-treatment by her husband Mrs. Thompson drowned herself and her one week's old babe on the 31st ult. at New Lisbon, O.

CHARLES I DE BAUM, the absconding assistant cashier of the Park National Bank of New York, who stole $110,000, was arrested on the 31st ult.

ELIAS KOHN, of New York, aged sixty two years, cut his wife's throat on the 31st ult. and then shot himself through the head. Domestic trouble was the cause.

During the seven days ended on the 31st ult. there were 136 business failures in the United States, against 157 the previous seven days. The total of failures in the United States since January 1 to date is 6,721, against 6,412 in 1887.

An explosion of mine gas occurred on the 31st ult. in the colliery of the Mount Pleasant Coal Company, near Scranton, Pa., and it was believed that many miners were killed.

A WATER-SPOUT early on the morning of the 31st ult. did great damage in the Hot Springs (Ark.) district. A raging flood swept through that city, destroying many structures and partly submerging others. It was said that thirteen persons were drowned, and that nine bodies had been recovered. The financial loss was placed at $100,000.

DURING the twenty-four hours ended at six p.m. on the 31st ult. there were twenty-six new cases of yellow fever and three deaths at Jacksonville, Fla. People were quitting the city in thousands.

REPORTS from the Northwest on the 31st ult. showed an average yield of eighteen bushels of wheat to the acre in Northern Minnesota and fifteen bushel to the acre in Dakota.

The Woman's Christian Temperance Union will hold its annual meeting in New York October 19.

DURING the last fiscal year the total number of applications received at the Patent Office in Washington was 40,177; the total number granted, 22,101, against 23,217 the previous year; total receipts, $1,192,944, a decrease of $27,102; total expenditures, $953,730, a decrease of $27,914. There were 7,227 cases on hand awaiting action.

GEORGE W. Cox was hanged on the 31st ult. at San Andreas, Cal., for the murder of his son-in-law, Henry G. Cook, last November.

HEAVY wind and rain-storms had on the 31st ult. injured the cotton crop in Western Tennessee and the northern portions of Mississippi, Arkansas and Alabama about ten per cent.

ARCHER COOK (colored) was hanged on the 31st ult. by a mob at Farmville, Va., for assaulting a white girl.

FIVE cowboys were drowned on the 31st ult. near Pike's Peak, Col., by a cloud burst which flooded the place where they were sleeping.

BURKE MITCHELL, a negro wife-murderer, was hanged on the 31st ult. at Houston, Tex.

Forest fires had on the 31st ult. done great damage to fencing, corn fields and small buildings in the vicinity of Montpelier, Ind.

The American House at West Superior, Wis., was burned early on the morning of the 2d, and three guests lost their lives. The fire was started by a lamp explosion.

A freight train jumped the track on the 1st near Booneville, Mo., killing a x laborers who had stepped aside to let the train pass.

THE Fields Biscuit and Cracker Company at San Francisco failed on the 1st for $100,000.

JOHN BAKER, a farm hand, threw a boy into a threshing machine near Guile Rock, Neb., on the 1st, and his enraged companions lynched him on the spot.

The public-debt statement issued on the 1st showed the total debt to be $1,723,008,805; cash in Treasury, $107,673,320; debt less cash in Treasury, $154,122,683. Decrease during August, $7,324,675. Decrease since June 30, 1888, $11,461,974.

A fire started in a toy warehouse at Baltimore, Md., on the 2d, and an explosion of fire-works wrecked the building, the falling walls burying seven firemen, who were all killed. The fire destroyed every thing in the block, entailing a property loss of $1,500,000.

At twenty-six leading clearing-houses in the United States the exchanges during the week ended on the 1st aggregated $806,578,149, against $807,802,087 the previous week. As compared with the corresponding week of 1887 the decrease amounted to 16.4 per cent.

Advices of the 1st from Paladora, in the public land strip in Colorado, say that a party of vigilantes surrounded a band of seventeen horse-thieves, and in the fight which occurred all of the thieves were killed and the vigilantes had three men killed and nine wounded.

SAMUEL BLISS, a Chicago wholesale sirup dealer, failed on the 1st for $150,000.

MR. AND MRS. ROBERT McClintock were struck by a train on the 1st while crossing the track near Delphi, Ind., and both were killed.

Most of the glass bottle factories in the country resumed operations on the 1st after an eight weeks' shutdown. A slight advance in wages was conceded the workmen.

An oil tank exploded on the 1st near Oil Center. O., killing James P. East, Rembrandt Ransen and Charles Howard. All were young men.

JULE LIST, secretary of the Duckworth Building Association of Cincinnati, was on the 1st found to be a defaulter to the extent of $10,000.

The percentage of the base-ball clubs in the National League for the week ended on the 1st was as follows: New York, .643; Chicago, .558; Detroit, .535; Philadelphia, .515; Boston, .524; Pittsburgh, .471; Washington, .380; Indianapolis, .359. American Association: St. Louis, .681; Philadelphia, .624; Cincinnati, .622; Brooklyn, .604; Cleveland, .409; Baltimore, .398; Louisville, .380; Kansas City, .311. Western Association: Des Moines, .658; St. Paul, .640; Omaha, .581; Kansas City, .530; Milwaukee, .456; Sioux City, .413; Chicago, .400; Davenport, 314.

WILLIAM A. SWART, a private banker at Roseland, a Chicago suburb, disappeared on the 1st, taking with him nearly $50,000 belonging to depositors.

The crop reports for the week ended on the 1st indicated damage to corn by frost in Michigan and Minnesota.

WILLIAM WALL (white), a prominent citizen of Clarendon, Ark., and John Stayton, a negro, were killed on the 1st by John Dillard (colored).

DISPATCHES received on the 1st at Denver, Col., stated that a fight had occurred between the Piute and Ute Indians, during which over one hundred were killed.

During the twenty-four hours ended on the 2d there were 24 new cases of yellow fever at Jacksonville, Fla., and 2 deaths. Total number of cases to date, 258; total deaths to date, 34.

The wife of a Mr. Steinlee, at Delhi, O., on the 1st drowned her two little children and herself. She had been demented for years.

By the explosion of a boiler on the 3d in the Perry stove works at South Pittsburg, Tenn., five men were killed and much damage was done to property.

Labor Day was generally observed throughout the country on the 3d.

Three unknown laboring men were struck by a train at Hammond, Ind., on the 3d, and all were killed.

Nine members of a gang of thieves and burglars who had been operating for months in Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Utica, N. Y., were arrested on the 3d by Rochester officials.

The prairie fires which had been raging on the northern Montana ranges were subdued on the 3d after burning over a large tract of country.

A circular was issued at Detroit on the 3d to all the G. A. R. posts of the country soliciting ten cents each from all veterans for the fund to be used to erect an equestrian statue in Washington to General John A. Logan.

Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith, all colored, were taken from the jail at Oxford, N. C., on the 3d, and hanged by a crowd of masked men for murder.

The Richmond Exposition which opens next month, is to have the Wild West Show of Buffalo Bill, with its Indian village and all the trimmings. There is also to be a large menagerie at the Exposition.

Some weeks ago, Archer Cook (negro) assaulted a young white girl on a Prince Edward county, Va., road. He was lodged in jail in Farmville. His trial was postponed last Thursday on account of the illness of the girl. On Friday at dawn, a mob of men broke into the jail, carried him to the edge of the town, hung him and filled his body with bullets.

D. A. Pence, aged twenty, son of Emanuel Pence, a respected and well-to-do farmer near Mt. Crawford, stole a horse from a farm near Harrisonburg, and took him to McDowell, Highland, where, assuming the name of "D. N. Brooken," he sold him to Geo. W. Rogers, taking R.'s note for $110. A reward of $60 was offered for the recovery of horse and thief, and Magistrate D. N. Wilson and Deputy Sheriff J. N. Wilson, of Augusta county, got on the track of Pence and arrested him with the note in his pocket. He is in jail at Harrisonburg.

A pickpocket was arrested in the waiting room of the Charlottesville junction, for attempting to steal the watch of Mr. Will, of Staunton, who was lying asleep in the room. The thief was arrested and lodged in the station house, but broke out and escaped.

Dr. John W. Bruffey, of Salem, a native of Rockingham, died at the Roanoke Red Sulphur Springs a few days ago.

The famous Washington Artillery of New Orleans has been disbanded.

Giles C. Huffman, member of the House of Delegates from Roanoke and Craig counties, died at Newcastle on Saturday.

The continued rain broke up the West Virginia State Fair at Wheeling, and the fair association is a heavy loser.

Two boys drank soda-water at a drug store in New Haven, Ct., Friday, and died in a half hour. The clerk had given them tincture of aconite instead of syrup, by mistake. Wm. Charles Ludwig, theological student, in charge of Grace church at Lexington, in the absence of Dr. McBryde, died there Friday. He was a son of the lithographer who printed all the bank notes for the Confederate States.

Brutal Murder in Arizona.
Nogales, Jan. 4.—Particulars of the brutal murder of Dr. Brady, an Englishman, by an American named Baggott, near Durango City, have been received. The former had bought a ranch near Baggott, which Baggott claimed and demanded the deed. On the doctor's refusal to give the document, up, Baggott shot him and then escaped to the mountains. A posse followed and had a sharp fight, resulting in the killing of one policeman and the wounding of others. The murderer was captured.
baggott-durango-1888-01-04.A2:
Brutal Murder.
NOGALES, A. T., January 4.—Particulars of the brutal murder of Dr. Eady, an Englishman, by an American named Baggott, near Durango City, have just been received: The former, who had bought a ranch near the ranch of Baggott, which Baggott also claimed, was paying a visit to the place, when Baggott demanded the deed to the place. On the doctor's refusal to give the document up, Baggott shot him several times, one shot breaking the spine. The murderer went to Durango, where he was arrested. He was given permission to take care of his horse, and mounted, firing several shots at the policemen. He made his escape to the mountains. A posse followed and had a sharp fight in a cave, resulting in the killing of one of the policemen and the wounding of another. The murderer was captured after being nearly beaten to death. The victim was a man of considerable wealth, and well known in the United States. The murderer will be shot early to day.

The former had bought a ranch near the ranch of Baggett, which Baggett also claimed. He was paying a visit to the place when Baggett said he wanted a deed to the place. On the Doctor's refusal to give the document up, Baggett shot him several times, one shot - breaking the spine. The murderer went to Durango where he was arrested. He was given permission to take care of his horse, and while doing so mounted, at the same time firing several shots at a policeman. He made his escape to the mountains. A posse followed and had a sharp fight in a cave, resulting in the killing of one policeman and the wounding of others. The murderer was captured, after being nearly beaten to death. The victim was a man of considerable wealth and was well known in the United States. The murderer was shot early to-day.

DOMESTIC.

The public-debt statement on the 3d shows the total debt to be $1,691,360,705; cash in treasury, $69,842,879; debt less cash in treasury, $1,225,598,402. Decrease during December, $14,584,650. Decrease since June 30, 1887, $53,830,335.

Oscar Coger (colored) was lynched on the 3d at Cherokee, Ala., for setting a house on fire.

In a drunken row on the 3d between thirty Poles at Wilkesbarre, Pa., three men were fatally injured and all were more or less seriously wounded.

The list of veterans of the war of 1812 has decreased to 1,069, while widows of veterans survive to the number of 11,831.

James Tutt died at Brazil, Ind., on the 3d of glanders caught from a horse.

Charles Selp, aged thirty years, of Columbus, Ind., died suddenly on the 3d from the effects of excessive cigarette smoking.

Jacob H. Delaplane, a book-keeper at the Portage straw-board works in Circleville, O., disappeared on the 3d, leaving his accounts $12,000 short.

A Madison (Wis.) marble-cutter, Robert M. Bibbs, thirty-five years old and married, froze to death near there on the 3d while intoxicated.

Henry Hoopes, employed by R. J. Allen & Co., of Philadelphia, was arrested on the 3d for embezzling $20,000.

It was discovered on the 3d that ex-Mayor Cramer, of Hackettstown, N. J., who recently fled after defrauding several business men, was betrothed to no less than fifteen women, every one of whom he swindled out of money.

G. C. MILLER, a leading politician of Starke, Fla., was assassinated on the 3d by some unknown person.

SENATOR PALMER, of Michigan, on the 3d gave $10,000 for the erection of a building at Detroit, to be used by the G. A. R. of the State.

The coinage of the mints during December last was $5,762,675, of which $2,785,-200 were standard silver dollars.

The visible supply of wheat in the country on the 3d was 44,421,130 bushels; an increase of 173,490 bushels. The corn supply was 6,025,258 bushels; an increase of 265,851 bushels.

There are sixty-eight collieries controlled by the Reading Company in the Schuylkill (Pa.) region, and sixty-two of these were deserted on the 3d, the twenty-five thousand miners going on a strike. Nearly thirty thousand men have already been on a strike in the Lehigh region for over three months. General Master-Workman Powderly advised that no strike take place, and telegraphed to Reading that he considered it inadvisable.

Advices of the 4th from Madisonville, Tex., say that a body of armed citizens calling themselves reformers had shot and hanged several men who favored maintaining saloons, and a state of terror prevailed.

Physicians are puzzled by the peculiar formation which, starting at the spinal column and growing forward until it pressed against the windpipe, and finally closing it, caused the death by strangulation on the 3d of the little daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Fred Palmer, of Algona, Ia. It is the first case of the kind on record.

There are 36,081 pensioners of the late war in Indiana, and during December last $1,850,000.
THERE are 36,081 pensioners of the late war in Indiana, and during December last $1,250,000 in pensions were disbursed.

All the Reading (Pa.) Company's mines were stopped on the 4th, and twenty thousand miners were idle. Some placed the number of idle men as high as fifty thousand in the Schuylkill basin alone, which with twenty thousand in the Lehigh, make the strike a great one.

The Shoe-makers' Trades Union of Newark, N. J., decided on the 4th to withdraw from the Knights of Labor.

On a farm near Zollarsville, Pa., a subterranean fire was raging on the 4th. Parties making an investigation to discover the cause found the ground so hot that they were obliged to abandon the work.

The December fire losses were $10,308,-000, against $11,200,000 for the same month in 1886. The total fire waste for 1887 was $129,264,000, about $13,000,000 greater than in 1886.

The Haddock murder indictments against all the defendants, except the three who have never been arrested, were dismissed at Stoux City, Ia., on the 4th.

The business portion of Beaufort, N. C., was destroyed by fire on the 4th.

Charles S. Moore, one of the most noted young lawyers in Washington, dropped dead in the streets in that city on the 4th.

A murderer named Baggott was lynched on the 4th near Durango, A. T.

The State of Alabama on the 4th let out all its convicts on ten-year contracts to work in the coal mines near Birmingham. They number six hundred.

The Los Angeles (Cal.) furniture factory was burned on the 4th. Loss, $200,000; insurance, $100,000.

James Smith, his wife and four children, the eldest a sixteen-year-old daughter, were arrested at St. Joseph, Mo., on the 5th for counterfeiting.

JUDGE SHIRAS decided at Dubuque, Ia., on the 5th that the patent of Washburn & Moen, wire manufacturers, was invalid.

By the fall of a viaduct on the 5th in Cleveland, O., eighty-five feet above the ground, two workmen were killed and four wounded.

San Francisco, January 5th, per Barkentine Planter.
Healdsburg with a capacity of 25,000 cases per year.

The California railroad tax case was to be argued before the Supreme Court last week.

Representative Holman believes that the Pacific railroads will pay their debts to the Government.

Washouts were reported at Los Angeles from every direction, delaying trains on nearly all the roads.

San Francisco dried fruits are very quiet in Chicago, the market being well supplied, while nobody is buying.

Representative McKinley of Ohio has introduced a bill in Congress to restore the rate of duty on imported wool.

Two express trains collided on the Dutch State railroad near Meppel, and twenty six persons were killed and many injured.

The Czar, in his congratulatory letter to the Pope, said he was desirous of protecting the interests of his Catholic subjects.

Foreign news was meagre in San Francisco for some days previous to the last advices, owing to a blockade on the telegraph lines.

It is said Lamar will be confirmed on the Supreme Court bench, as the Republicans cannot secure a caucus to agree on opposing him.

The Mexican Government is giving special encouragement to all mining enterprises which may aid in augmenting the gold production of the country.

Representative Felton of California has introduced a bill in Congress to prohibit Chinese immigration; also, one to extend the United States laws over Alaska.

The establishment of the beet sugary at Watsonville, Cal., has caused a boom in real estate. Prices are becoming steeper, especially for good farming land.

A riot occurred, at Jefferson barracks, St. Louis, between white and colored United States soldiers, which resulted in the injury of many men and will probably cost three men their lives.

The Santa Rosa, Cal., city council misdemeanor for boys under 16 to smoke cigarettes, and the same offense for dealers who sell cigarettes to boys under that age.

Pacific Coast lumbermen are sending strong protests to Washington against putting lumber and coal on the free list. The wool-growers of California are sending petitions of a similar kind regarding wool.

A violent gale has been raging on the Irish coast, doing great damage to shipping. A portion of Fastnet Rock has been tumbled into the sea, and the lightkeepers are terrified lest the sea undermine the rock.

The Board of Trustees of San Bernardino, Cal., has accepted plans for a sewerage system for the entire city, to cost nearly $132,000. Waste land will be secured for a sewerage farm, in which the sewer system will empty, and the material will be used as a fertilizer.

The bark Eureka, that sailed from San Francisco with wheat on August 8th, has been wrecked at the entrance to Waterford, Ireland, and her crew, consisting of twenty-five persons, were all drowned. She was built at Bath, Maine, in 1876, and commanded by Captain Southard.

The San Francisco Examiner of the 5th says: Of the 206 Chinese passengers who arrived by the Oceanic, only 100—or less than half—had certificates. Seven of these were rejected by the customs officials. The 106 without certificates will doubtless attempt to squeeze through on the familiar "prior residence" dodge.

A general mortgage and investment company, with capital of $15,-000,000 in gold, has been organized in London to operate in Mexico. This makes the fourth company with a heavy capital organized in England within the last two months to develop property there, evidencing the interest and influence English capital is acquiring in that country. This mortgage company will combat local money lenders by making loans on first mortgages on real estate at half the present rates.

On Saturday morning John H. McAdams, living in the neighborhood of Caritther's store, near Monroe, went out on the river before daylight for a still hunt. Taking a position, he waited patiently for a squirrel to make its appearance. About daylight he heard a stir in some bushes near him, and without a word peered in that direction until he saw, as he thought, a squirrel, when he took deliberate aim and fired, the load taking effect in the side of the face and neck of his father, Jacob McAdams, whom it seems he did not know was in the woods. Mr. McAdams was very low when last heard from, but hopes are entertained for his recovery.

The Gentlemen's Driving club of Atlanta held a meeting Wednesday. After some discussion a resolution was adopted to appoint a committee of five to hold a conference with the general council looking to the sale of 100 acres of the grounds at Piedmont park to the city of Atlanta. President King-berry R. Gramamol, George W. Parrott, L. J. Hill, Hoke Smith and John A. Fitten. The idea is to sell 100 acres on the northern and northeastern side of the park, partly within and partly without the regular grounds, the city to make the selection. The ground which will be offered to the city does not include the club house and its immediate surroundings.

At Gainesville, Wednesday, Mrs. Amanda J. Tuggle swore out a wrist of habea corpus for two of her minor girl children, Elmina and Zeelpha A., aged respectively 15 and 11 years. She charged that they were in the hands of James E. Ethridge, who hold them without warrant or authority of law. Mr. Ethridge answered that he did not hold the children by force, but that they came to his house and told him that their mother had run them away from home, and that he consented for them to stay with him. The evidence developed the fact that they were a fighting crowd at home and could not live in peace. Mrs. Tuggle had at one time been insane, and was a woman of ungovernable temper. After the evidence was in and argument had thereon, Judge Rudolph dismissed the writ and left the parties in the same condition that he found them. The case will be carried to the superior court.

From information just received from Oak Grove district, in Fulton county, a young rebellion has sprung up against the enforcement of the stock law, which was passed by an act of the last legislature. The antistock law men claim it to be unjust, having been passed over the heads of a majority of the voters of that district. It seems that the officers are powerless to maintain the law, from a demonstration made a few days ago. The court, with its bailiffs and other deputized officers, failed to maintain even the dignity of the court in a trial, and it was dismissed. It is further stated that obstructions in the way of a gate have been placed across the public road, within the limits of DeKalb county. The obstructions were removed by the citizens of DeKalb, but were immediately replaced by Oak Grove citizens. DeKalb citizens say they will ask their next grand jury to settle the question. This body meets next Monday.

At Pleasant Hill, in Talbot county, last Saturday night, a negro by the name of Ben Bethel attempted to burglarize the house of Mrs. Sarah Brewster. Mrs. Brewster and her daughter live alone. As the clock was sounding midnight Miss Annie Brewster awoke and saw a man in her room, standing near her trunk. As she made a noise, the negro rushed to the bed, and with a murderer-looking knife raised over her, told her if she made a noise he would murder her right there. Not intimidated by his threat, she uttered a piercing shriek that awoke her mother, who was sleeping in an adjoining room, and who rushed to her daughter's rescue. The negro jumped out of the window and made his escape. Sunday morning Ben Bethel was captured and evidence sufficient was gathered to fix the crime on him. Once before an attempt to burglarize Mrs. Brewster's house was made. The citizens became very indignant at the way these defenseless ladies were being treated, and assembled at Pleasant Hill Sunday evening, determined to lynch the prisoner, but cooler counsel prevailed and he was sent to jail in Talbotton.

At Atlanta, Wednesday morning, Patrolman Collins found a white woman on Calhoun street. She was not drunk, but just wandering about with nowhere to go. A reporter talked to the woman, and she stated that her name was Lou Bell. "I am out of money and broken down in health," she said. "and I want to go to see my child in Texas," Lou Bell was connected with John Robinson's circus, and has had her name printed upon flaming circulars as an intrepid bareback rider and trapeze performer. Her health failed, and she lost her position in the sawdust ring. Lately she has earned a scanty living by clog dancing in 10 cent shows. Her real name is not Lou Bell, but she refuses to give any other. "Never mind about who I am," she said to the reporter. "I have been known as Lou Bell for many years, and as Lou Bell thousands of people have admired my performances in the ring. It makes no difference what my right name is; all I want is to go home to my poor old mother and little boy." The woman will probably be given free transportation to a little town near Galveston, Tex., where she says her mother is living.

Old soldiers began gathering at Madison Wednesday, to attend the reunion of the Third Georgia regiment on that day, and yesterday, when the three trains rolled from Atlanta, Augusta and Macon respectively, fully 1,000 people alighted, which swelled the crowd to about 4,000 people. The scene at the depot was one long to be remembered at Madison. Old soldiers alighted and greeted those who were already there with a cordiality known only to old vets. The Beardon Brothers' brass band of ten pieces arrived from Augusta, and headed the procession of old soldiers on their march to the court house. The enthusiasm ran high when the band struck up "Dixie," and the old vets flung up their hats and cheered loudly. At the court house the old soldiers were assigned places for lodging in private residences, and such other places as could be procured. Every house in the city is thrown open to guests, and the city is virtually in the hands of visitors. Thirty-one members of the old "Panola Guards" assembled at the court house park, and had their photos taken. After this they marched over to Torbett's.

DROWNED IN THE DAM.
Yesterday Mr. Thomas Young, the well known Assessor for the City Water Board, and three other gentlemen of the Island, went out on the Government Dam in the Back river in a skiff to fish. In some way the skiff was upset. The others escaped, but Mr. Young, after getting nearly to the shore, was apparently seized with cramps, and sank. All efforts to rescue him were unavailing.

The body was recovered some time after the accident. County Coroner Schultze held an inquest at 7 o'clock last evening, and gave a certificate of death by accidental drowning.

The sad accident caused general horror. Mr. Young was widely known and much respected. He was a son of Capt. Hiram Young.

A Brutal Murder.

LITCHFIELD, KAN., Oct. 28.—Bill Short, a miner, shot and fatally wounded Mrs. Alma Barnes, a widow nineteen years of age, last night. The shooting occurred at a dance and was caused by the refusal of the woman to allow Short to escort her home. She died at 3 o'clock this afternoon. On account of threats of lynching Short was taken to Girard.

Illegal Registration.

New York, Oct. 28.—Reports of illegal registration are being supplemented by a few arrests. To-day Justice Welde held William E. Coulter, car driver, in $2,000 bail for registering twice. Michael Duane was held on the same charge. He had only lived nine days in the place from which he registered.

Movements of Great Men.

NEWARK, N. J., Oct. 28.—Mr. Blaine passed a quiet night at the residence of George A. Halsey. To-day he left for New York. Congressman Mills spent the night at John McGregor's house. He was indisposed during the day, but was better to-night.

A Well-Known Minister Dead.
PITTSBURGH, PA., Oct. 28.—Rev. Wesley Smith, one of the best known ministers in the M. E. Church in Western Pennsylvania, Eastern Ohio and West Virginia, died at his home at Sharpsburg, near this city, this morning. Rev. Smith was 84 years of age, and one of the pioneers of the church.

An Immigrant Killed.

CLEVELAND, O., Oct., 28.—August Hertel, an immigrant boy, aged 14, who was on his way from Bavaria to join his father, Wm. Hertel, at Shumway, Ill., walked off a Lake Shore train while asleep, last night, near here, and was killed.

Trying to Fix it Up.
LONDON, Oct. 28.—Lord Salisbury had a private conference with Minister Phelps at the Hatfield house to-day in regard to the Sackville affair.

Metals.

NEW YORK, Oct. 27.—Pig iron quiet and firm. Copper dull. Lead quiet. Tin, straits $23 10.

MEMPHIS, October 28th — An east-bound passenger train on the Mountain road was stopped by train robbers this afternoon near Newport, Ark., and the passengers robbed of $2,000. No details are obtainable.

All the passengers were forced to take off their clothing. One man saved a large roll of bills by wrapping them in a soiled handkerchief.

The Terry Contempt Case.

WASHINGTON, October 28th. — It cannot be positively learned whether the Supreme Court will decide Judge Terry's application for a writ of habeas corpus to-morrow or not. The general opinion is, however, that it will not be disposed of this week, and that when the decision is rendered it will be adverse to Terry.

The Sleep of Death.

NEW YORK, October 28th. — Kirwan Stone, a young man, with Ella Lane, registered as man and wife at Williams' Hotel in Hoboken, on Saturday night. They were found dead in their room this morning, with the gas turned on. It is not known whether it was suicide or accident.

Tools, Etc., for Mare Island.

WASHINGTON, October 28th. — The Bureau of Construction and Repairs has completed the specifications for the necessary tools, etc., to equip Mare Island Navy-yard, in accordance with the $100,000 appropriation made for that purpose in the navy appropriation bill.

Clearing-House Exchanges.

BOSTON, October 28th. — Dispatches to the Post from the managers of the leading clearing-houses in the United States report total gross exchanges for the week ending October 28, 1888, to be $1,067,331,673, an increase of 7.2 per cent. over corresponding period last year.

A Hopeless Wreck.

CHICAGO, October 28th. — It has been ascertained that Clifton & Co., whose failure was the heaviest resulting from the Hutchinson wheat corner, have liabilities of $230,000, with assets of only $50,000. The deficit is much larger than was expected.

A Society Event in Kansas.

LITCHFIELD (Kan.), October 28th. — Bill Short, a miner, shot and fatally wounded Mrs. Alma Barnes, a widow, last night. The shooting occurred at a dance, and was caused by a refusal of the woman to allow Short to escort her home.

**Run Down by a Train.**

DUBUQUE (Ia.), October 28th.—Herman Boade, a section foreman, started to town-to-day with his family on a hand-car. The car was struck by a special passenger train and Mrs. Boade and the two boys killed. Boade escaped.

**Three and a Half Millions Short.**

TOPEKA, October 28th.—The annual report of the Atchison road, filed yesterday with the Railroad Commissioners, shows the total earnings for the year ended June 30th as $16,544,392, and the total expenses $20,061,592.

**Death of a Prominent Hebrew.**

NEW YORK, October 28th.—Louis Steifel, a prominent Hebrew, well known in San Francisco, died here to-day in his sixty-fifth year. He was identified with the Hebrew free schools.

**New Ocean Steamer for the Pacific.**

PHILADELPHIA, October 28th.—The new steamship Corona left the Neafie & Levy shipyards to-day bound for Valparaiso and San Francisco. She will be placed on the line running from the latter city.

**Hall McAllister Starts for Home.**

NEW YORK, October 28th.—Hall McAllister, the well-known California lawyer, who has been seriously ill in this city, left for his home in California to-day, in company with his son.

**The Gasoline's Deadly Work.**

CLEVELAND, October 28th.—Mrs. Jackson and Miss Nellie Norris poured gasoline on the kitchen floor to-day to kill roaches. It ignited from a range and an explosion resulted. Both women were fatally burned.

**Noted Clergyman Deceased.**

PITTSBURG, October 28th.—Rev. Wesley Smith, of the Methodist Episcopal Church, died at Sharpsburg, Pennsylvania, to-day, aged 83 years.

The Southern Pacific Railroad Company has filed a deed of trust to the Central Trust Company, of New York, to secure the payment of a $38,000,000 mortgage on all its property. The railroad company has turned over all its property to the trust company and the latter assumes all the former's debts. The mortgage is to provide for the payment of these debts.

Joseph Murphy, a young convict sentenced for five years for larceny, escaped from the Stillwater, (Minn.) prison a few nights ago. He was on the upper tier and dug through the top cell grating and iron roof and descended by means of ladders on the building to the ground.

On the 24th a scaffold on the new soldiers' home building at Minnehaha Falls, Minn., fell, killing Henry Reitzell and dangerously injuring three other workmen.

The Military Prison Commission, consisting of Major General George Crook, Adjutant General R. C. Drum and Lieutenant Colonel Thomas F. Barr, have made their report to the Secretary of War. All the buildings and grounds connected with the prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., were found to be well kept and in good condition. On October 9 there were in the prison 472 prisoners, as against 485 on the date of the last inspection, May 22, 1888.

At the meeting of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers in Richmond, Va., on the 25th, P. M. Arthur was re-elected Chief, and Mr. Ingraham secretary of the insurance order of the Brotherhood. C. R. Doherty, of Massachusetts, was elected Grand Chaplain and W. Hesky, of Bloomington, Ill., Grand Guide.

W. C. Torry, United States Swamp Land Commissioner, was arrested at Iowa Falls, Ia., on the 25th, charged with treating a personal friend to a drink of whisky. He was fined $100 for the offense. It is said to have been a political persecution.

Forty-three suits, the claim in each case being from $1,000 to $6,000, have been entered in the Superior Court at Chicago against the lumber firm of Spooner R. Howell.

The Chief of the Bureau of Statistics reports that the exports for the twelve months ended September 30, 1888, were $679,689,603, as against $718,204,531 in 1887. The value of the imports for nine months ended September 30, was $544,507,908, and in 1887, $535,824,-604.

The third annual convention of the National Boys' and Girls' Home Employment Association, which was to have convened in Indianapolis October 29, has been postponed until the 19th of November next.

The will of the late John Wentworth, of Chicago, was admitted to probate on the 25th. The estate, which aggregates $1,500,000, is to be equally divided between decedent's daughter Roxana and his nephew Moses.

The total number of immigrants arriving at the ports of the United States from the principal foreign countries, except from the Dominion of Canada and Mexico, during the nine months ended September 30, 1888, was 432,802, against 411,282 during the same period last year.

Wolves and coyotes are doing great damage in Northern Montana, having recently killed many hundreds of sheep and colts besides attacking travelers.

Daniel Hand, an aged and wealthy resident of Guilford, Conn., has given to the American Missionary Association of New York City the sum of $1,000,000 to be held in trust by the association and the interest to be devoted to the education of colored people in the old slave States of the South.

Thomas D. Hosey, paymaster in the United States Navy and stationed at the Brooklyn navy yard, suicided at his home in Paterson, N. J., on the 25th, by shooting himself. Despondency caused by the death of his wife some time ago is the only motive assigned for the deed.

Rev. Robert Eckles, a prominent Methodist minister, was struck by a train near Reno, Pa., on the 25th and almost instantly killed.

The board of trustees of Cornell University has appropriated $80,000 from the permanent funds of the university for the erection of a chemical laboratory.

A TRAIN of nine empty passenger coaches and a freight train on the Chicago & Alton road, both running at full speed, collided near San Jose, Ill., on the 25th, totally demolishing the two engines and seventeen coaches and freight cars. Fireman Taum, of the freight, was killed, and both engineers and Conductor Bishop were seriously hurt.

At Danville, Ill., on the 25th Elisha Allen was sentenced to thirty years in the penitentiary for the murder of George B. Smith. Last August Allen had a difficulty with Smith over a woman, swore out a warrant for his arrest, had himself deputized as special constable, and shot Smith down in cold blood while serving it.

During a quarrel over a game of cards at Thompsonville, Ill., a few nights ago, Warren Jordan shot and instantly killed John Davis. Charles Davis, a brother of the murdered man, seized a hatchet and beat and cut Jordan so that he died in a few minutes. Davis then went to Benton and surrendered to the sheriff. All the men were prominent in their neighborhood and have families.

It has been discovered that J. A. Swan, late treasurer of Knox County, Tenn., is some $25,000 short in his accounts. The discovery was made by his successor in office. Swan's present whereabouts is unknown. The authorities have seized his property at Knoxville to the value of $17,000.

The commissioners of the District of Columbia have decided to honor the memory of General Sheridan by naming the circle at the intersection of Massachusetts avenue and Twenty-third street, Washington, "Sheridan Circle." The Loyal Legion, of which Sheridan was president, will erect a statue of the General in the center of the circle.

The boiler of locomotive No. 480 of the Philadelphia & Reading Railroad Company exploded on the 23d at Glen Carbon, Pa. Conductor John Gangloff and Brakeman John Culman, of Cressona, were killed.

Mrs. Julia Herkless and her daughter aged fourteen, were burned to death in a fire which destroyed their residence at Lexington, Mo., on the 23d.

Two freight trains on the Erie railroad collided near Otisville, N. Y., on the 24th. A west-bound train soon afterward ran into the rear of another one waiting for the track to be cleared, and to make the wreck more complete an express train, east-bound, ran into the other end of the smashup. Two engines and twelve cars were completely destroyed. George McMullen, brakeman, was killed and four other trainmen badly hurt. None of the passengers were injured.

The Secretary of the Treasury has directed the collector of customs at New York to admit, free of duty, tablets to the memory of George W. Schuyler, a charter trustee of Cornell University, which have arrived from abroad.

In the suit of Mrs. Myra Beals against Dr. Augustin Thompson, of Lowell, Mass., for $50,000 damages for having alienated her husband's affections, the jury brought in a verdict for the plaintiff on the 26th, awarding her $30,000 damages.

At Keytesville, Mo., on the 26th James

The twelve thousand coke workers in the Connellsville (Pa.) region have been notified of an advance of from five to ten per cent. in their wages, to take effect on November 1, when the price of coke will be advanced twenty-five cents per ton, in accordance with the agreement recently made by the operators.

The Burlington, Cedar Rapids & Northern passenger train struck a buggy in which were three persons, at a crossing near West Liberty, Ia., on the 26th, killing Mrs. James Dilworth of Chester County, Pa., and Harry Pond of West Liberty, and injuring, but not fatally, Mrs. Isaac Larkin, of Centerville, Del.

Near Paris, Ky., on the 26th, a northbound train on the Kentucky Central railroad jumped the track. Engineer Rebort Black and Elmore Bryan, a passenger, were fatally injured. John Ryan, brakeman, and J. J. Allen, engineer on the Chesapeake & Ohio road, who was a passenger, were severely hur

blalock-1888-04.A1:
BROUGHT TO BAY
A Band of Assassins and Robbers in Southern Kansas
Captured Near Columbus and Landed Safety in Jail.
Two More Indicted Bald Knobbers Present Written Confessions.
Kentucky's State Treasurer Suspended for Defalcation.
COLUMBUS, Kas., March 20.—William and John Blalock, the parties who assassinated Constable David Gordon on last Friday night, were captured yesterday and brought to the city. The excitement among the people was so great, and the threats of lynch law so universal, that Mayor Chester and many of the leading citizens addressed the excited crowd, counseling law and order.

Upon a promise from the crowd that they would abstain from violence the assassins were brought before the coroner's court, which has been in continual session since Saturday morning, last, and are making a full confession of their multitudinous crimes. They have been connected for years with a gang of horse thieves which extends from Kansas City to Arkansas, Texas and Colorado. Their crimes include robbing the mails, blowing open safes, sandbagging and murder.

Fifteen arrests have already been made, and information has been telegraphed that will lead to the arrest of as many more.

The reward of $1,000 offered by the citizens for the capture of the murderers will be given to a boy 19 years of age, who resides four miles from this place. In passing a school house near his home, at 2 o'clock in the morning, he accidentally heard the assassins at work in the attic, and knowing it must be the work of persons desiring to conceal themselves, he gave the information and a posse was sent, who made the capture only after a threat to burn the building in which they were concealed. The town is now patrolled by an armed guard to prevent mob violence to the guilty wretches. A company of the Kansas state militia is located here and its arms are used by a posse under charge of the sheriff.
blalock-1888-04.A3:
THEIR CHEF WAS A GIRL.
Extraordinary Confession of a Kansas School-Teacher After a Murder.
A Kansas City (Mo.) telegram says: For some weeks burglaries had been frequent at Columbus and other points in Southern Kansas. Last Friday night the safe in the railway depot at that place was blown open. The next night the sheriff and Constable David Gordon set to work to watch the house of suspected persons. Saturday morning Gordon's dead body, riddled with buckshot, was found near the house of a family named Blalock. The condition of the shrubbery showed that the shots were fired from the Blalock yard, and the father, mother, and daughters were arrested, but the boys had disappeared.

Sunday it was announced that Clara Blalock, the oldest daughter, had confessed everything. The girl, a handsome brunette twenty years of age, had graduated at the head of her class at the Columbus High School last spring and had been appointed a teacher in the First-Ward School last fall. She had the respect of all classes and was regarded as one of the most promising young girls in the town. Therefore the surprise was the greater when she confessed that she saw her brothers John and William get their guns, steal from the house to the shrubbery, where William took careful aim and murdered the constable in cold blood. When the boys returned to the house she and her mother fixed them up for escape, and made arrangements to supply them with food and ammunition until they could safely return.

All this was told in the coolest, matter-of-fact way. Search of the Blalock house was made Sunday and a secret recess under the roof was found, in which were all manner of stolen goods, including a mail sack, chickens salted in a barrel, and jewelry. There was also found a box containing a vast amount of correspondence, showing that Clara Blalock, the teacher, was secretary and treasurer of an extensive gang of burglars, and she received and divided the spoils, as well as arranged many of the details. She was then searched, and letters were found sewed in her dress giving the location of several stolen horses and telling her who to send for them. The same day the boys were arrested while hiding in the garret of a schoolhouse. Other members of the gang are also under arrest.
blalock-1888-04.A6:
Further Particulars of the Deeds of the Blalock Bandits.
Columbus, Kan., March 23.—The mystery of the Gulf house murder. the Hazeltine powder magazine explosion, the Lowell post-office robbery and other deeds of murder, burglary and arson which had given Columbus and the southeastern portion of Kansas a reputation for lawlessness, has finally been cleared up; one of the most desperate and vicious gangs of outlaws which ever operated in the southwest has been broken up; most of the members have been arrested, and the great wonder is, that they have not been lynched.

The excitement, which had somewhat subsided, was stirred up to a fever heat again this morning by the discovery of the charred fragments of a trunk and a heap of bones back of the Fry house. It was hard to tell whether the bones were those of a human being or not, but the general feeling was that they were, and that the body of a man, a trunk and a heap of rubbish had been burned to cover up a great crime. Dan Fry is now under arrest, but Andy and "Red" Fry have so far succeeded in eluding the officers.

The names of the members of the gang made public are John, Bill and Clay Blalock, Clara Blalock, her father and mother, Dan, Ped and Andy Fry and Bill and Grant Alley. The Frys and Alleys are cousins and Ped Fry ran the principal barber shop in the town. All are property owners. Clay Blalock is the proprietor of a second-hand store at Abilene. The Frys own the house back of which the bones were found yesterday morning, and Allen Fry, the uncle of the Fry boys, is the proprietor and manager of the Palace hotel.

Just twenty miles from here and about twelve years ago the sensational Bender disclosures were made. In the criminal annals of Kansas, the history of the Blalock gang with that of the Benders, and in point of startling, thrilling and sensational details yet unpublished in part—may far surpass it. The mystery of a dozen great crimes was dispelled by the gun shot which ended the life of Constable David Gordon, while the letters found in the possession of Miss Clara Blalock, the First ward school teacher, gave valuable clews, so the officials say, to train robberies and murders in Texas.
blalock-1888-04.A8:
The discovery of Gordon's body was proof to the sheriff that the officer had been on the right track. He immediately raided the house with a posse and put the old man and woman and Clara Blalock under arrest. The boys were not at home, but their hiding place was soon discovered.

"John said they shot him; he said they found him prowling about the house," said Mrs. Blalock, when questioned regarding the crime. She went on with the story in a cool and deliberate manner, without a single indication of remorse or emotion. She said that Billy and John had been home a week or ten days previous to the murder. They remained home during the day and went out nights. She did not know where they went on Friday. The remainder of the family went to bed as usual and slept without being disturbed, when she was aroused by a gun-shot in front of the house, and she asked what the shooting meant. Soon after John came in the house, and she asked what the shooting meant. He said they saw some one prowling around in front of the place and killed him. John told her that Bill said he was pretty sure it was Dave Gordon. She then reproved him for the murder, and he said: "Well, he would have killed me, I guess, if I hadn't killed him, for I heard him cock his pistol and called to me to halt."

"Bill then came into the house," continued the woman, "and asked for some money he had left for me to take care of. It was $15 and I gave it to him. The two boys changed their clothing and left the house."

After leaving the house John and Bill mounted their horses and headed for the schoolhouse, six miles east of town, and when they arrived there turned loose their horses and allowed them to go back home. They then converted the garrett of the schoolhouse into a garrison and made a trap door in the roof with a pocket knife. They remained there two days, but were detected by a young man, who informed the sheriff Monday morning. The latter, with a considerable force surrounded the schoolhouse and called upon the men to surrender.

"Well we might as well give in," said John. His brother insisted on firing upon the posse, as the garret was fortified, but Sheriff Babb declared that he would burn the schoolhouse, and the boys opened the improvised trap-door, and
the undaunted leader of the gang
declared: "I guess you have got
us cornered, but unless you promise
on your honor to defend us
against the mob you will have to
take us dead instead of alive."—
The sheriff promised and the men
then came down from the roof.

At the Gordon inquest Ped Fry,
who had also been arrested, substantiated all that Gordon had previously discovered by making a clean breast of the gang's history. Subsequently a blind trap was found in the Blalock house, in a lean-to, near the roof, which upon being opened disposed the garret of the house filled with all manner of goods and plunder, consisting largely of merchandise, harness, clothing, books, encyclopedias, a United States mail sack with the Lowell, Kansas, tag upon it, sacks from the Lowell mills filled with clothing, boots and shoes, extra amount of jewelry and a box containing a vast amount of correspondence which completely proved that this gang was connected with other "societies" in at least three different territories and states south of Kansas. The letters were addressed to Miss Clara Blalock, and were so worded that her connection with the criminals in the capacity of leader could not be denied.

To say that the excitement was intense when it was learned that Clara Blalock, the beautiful and admired schoolteacher, was in league with her unholy relatives would be the exact truth. It deepened when the young woman was put on the stand, and when she finally contessed to being implicated in the many crimes perpetrated by her relatives. Much of her testimony was kept secret, as it implicated several persons who are not under arrest. She told about the horse-stealing expeditions and the various robberies in a calm and unconcerned manner. She admitted that her correspondent was in fact her brother John. She denied a knowledge of anything at all at first, but was finally compelled to admit everything. Her testimony accounted for the blowing open of

THE BLALOCK GANG.
