Commencement of the Trials at Columbus, Kan. — Jonathan Blalock's Evidence.

Columbus, Kan., April 27. — Dan Fry and Grant Alley, members of the Fry-Blalock-Alley gang, were placed on trial yesterday, when their counsel entered a plea of burglary in the second degree and they were remanded for sentence.

Fred Fry and Alexander Fry, upon being brought before the court entered a plea of not guilty, and a jury was impaneled for the trial of Fred Fry, the case of Alexander Fry being continued to another day of the term.

The cases of Jonathan and William Blalock, for the murder of David Gordon, will be the last reached, as their testimony will be necessary to establish the guilt of Fred and Alexander Fry and their father and mother, and Andy and Helen Fry.

When Jonathan Blalock was introduced on the part of the State in the case of Fred Fry the most eager interest was manifest by the crowd anxious to see the famous leader of the gang also to hear if he would confirm his confession made at the coroner's inquest. He stated on the night of the robbery at Crestline the gang, including Fred Fry, met on the railroad without any fixed purpose of where they were going; that their purpose was to go to Smithfield and rob the post-office and store, but, for some cause concluded to stop at Crestline. They broke a hand car loose at the Columbus section house and rode over to Crestline on it, attempted to break into the store, but were fired upon, then broke into the depot and got a box of garden seeds and some apples. stepped up to them and said: "You s— of a b—, I know what you want." He, at the point of his pistol, made them walk down stairs. SAVED BY A SHERIFF.

Special to the Globe.
Spectal to the Globe.
MOORHEAD, Minn., Nov. 21.—Murderer Brown, alias Murphy, was taken to a place of safety last night to avoid being lynched. Rumors were afloat yesterday to the effect that friends of the murdered policeman, Poull, would lead a mob at 3 o'clock this morning and lynch Brown. The sheriff removed the prisoner, and thus foiled the would-be lynchers. His trial will occur at the January term of the district court, Judge Mills presiding.
brown-alias-murphy-moorhead-1888-11-21.A9:
Man's Wicked Doings.
Taylor Smith, a well known sporting character, was killed at Springfield, Mo., by Margaret Miller, his mistress in a trivial dispute. Taylor and the woman were discussing a laundry bill, when she seized an ax and split his head open. He lived long enough to make an ante-mortem statement.

George Faebel, a member of the board o trade committed suicide by shooting himself at Chicago. It is understood that he lost about $40,000 in the September wheat corner, and despondency, growing out of the loss, is supposed to have been the cause of the act.

Judge Black of Fort Benton, Montana, sentenced Charles Gordon to be hanged Jan. 11. Gordon murdered J. A. Lavalle at Choteau July 11 last. No provocation existed save an insult known only to Gordon. The evidence showed that the murder was cold-blooded and deliberate, as it was committed hours after the alleged insult, and not in the heat of passion.

Frank Vernon, aged fourteen, was arraigned on the charge of forgery. A cigar dealer charged that he obtained $5 from him on a forged order. Vernon is a precocious youth who ran away from home at Chicago to follow horse racing. He came to New York, where he developed into a regular sport.

Murderer Brown, alias Murphy, was taken to a place of safety from Moorhead, Minn. to avoid being lynched. Rumors were afloat to the effect that friends of the murdered policeman, Poull, would lead a mob and lynch Brown. The sheriff removed the prisoner, and thus foiled the would-be lynchers. His trial will occur at the January term of the district court Judge Mills presiding.

The government secret service at Buffalo, N. Y. has for the past few days been closing in around a gang of counterfeiters, who have been making dollars and half-dollars of a kind that was almost impossible to detect, and of which large quantities have been circulated in Erie, Warren, Oil City and Jamestown. Some of the gang are under arrest. "Squire" Richardson, one of the men, who, it is alledged, attended to the manufacture of the money, was brought to Buffalo. Richardson is fully sixty years old. It is thought he will squeal on the whole party.

That somebody with the evil intention of committing arson has been at work in St. Peter has been made evident. In one of the vacant basement rooms of the Gustavus Adolphus college it was discovered that a map had been placed in a small closet and set on fire, but the effort failed for lack of air. Next night the room was examined again, and it was found that straw had been set on fire in the closet and the plot had failed as before. A close watch is now being kept for the evil-doer.

A murder occurred near the Montgomery county line of Tennessee. Dr. J. G. Brake heard a noise in the horse lot. He went to the stable, when a man concealed behind a tree fired, and Brake reeled and started to fall. Two more shots were fired into his body and then the assassin beat his head into a jelly. Next day George Tally gave himself up, saying that he was the murderer and that he killed Brake because the latter had seduced his seventeen-year-old daughter. The girl is said to have borne an unsavory reputation, and the doctor stood high in the community.

A burglar went through three safes in adjoining buildings at Owatonna, Minn. Both B. J. Meixner, wagon manufacturer, and C. Zambari, gunsmith, had left their safes unlocked, there being nothing of value in either. No damage was done to either except that the iron money drawer of Meixner's, being locked, was carried away. At Kubat & Slezak's saloon the safe door was drilled and the lock was blown out of the door, but the bolts were not drawn and the money in the safe was not obtained. They took a small amount of change from the till and helped themselves to the fluids.

Pickpockets who had mingled with the immense throng, in one of the large State street dry goods stores at Chicago raised the cry of fire. Immediately a panic ensued. In the rush the weaker ones were knocked down and trampled upon. One of the large windows of the store was broken out, through which the crowd rushed into the street, scattering the goods in all directions. The fire alarm was turned in and the department was soon on hand, but it was discovered that there was no fire in the building. The presence of the engines added to the confusion. Many of the lady clerks in the store fainted
brown-alias-murphy-moorhead-1888-11-21.A10:
RIS, MINN., WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 28, 1888.
MINNESOTA NEWS NOTES
The Manitoba depot at Albany was burned, with all the contents. Loss, $3,000.

The bodies of the city poor buried on the Minneapolis work house farm, numbering some 250, will be transferred to a small piece of ground set aside for the purpose on the farm attached to the quarantine hospital.

Mrs. John Malesch, a widow residing near Freeport, was murdered by John Pfium, a half demented fellow who had been paying some attentions to her for the past six weeks. She had been to a dance, and Pfium became jealous and shot her while she was entering the house.

The board of education of the city of Cleveland filed papers at Duluth in an action to recover $19,219.13 from the estate of Thomas Axworthy, the defaulting city treasurer of Cleveland. Axworthy had invested in mining stock on the Vermillion range, and owned some valuable dock property at Duluth.

Governar McGill has appointed a board of four members which will represent Minnesota at the labor conference of the National Prison association, to be held at Albany, N. Y., next month. Those appointed are A. K. Doe, of Stillwater; John F. Norrish, of Hastings; Edwin Dunn, of Eyota, and H. H. Hart, of St. Paul.

The new Tileston flour mill, St. Cloud, is running.

Easterville and Marcus postoffices have been raised to the presidential class.

Vosburg and Hopka, the Faribault fire bugs, were sentenced to seven years each in the penitentiary.

During the past four months the Austin cheese factory has manufactured 24,000 pounds of fine cheese.

Work has been completed on the Duluth fish hatchery, and it will be put in operation about the 15th of next month.

At the last election women superintendent of schools were elected in Faribault, Fillmore, Kanabec and Mille Lacs counties.

Henry Beaser, clerk of the Indian agencies in the vicinity of Duluth, is investigating the reported starving condition of the Indians there.

Over $2,000 has been contributed in Winona for the fund for Louis Oleson, who lost both hands by the premature explosion of a cannon at the Republican jollification.

Brown, the Moorhead murderer, was taken to a place of safety Tuesday night, the sheriff fearing he would be lynched. His trial will come up at the January term of court.

Tommy Erb, an 8-year-old boy living at Scrambler, while leading a colt to water tied the haker to his waist, and the colt becoming frightened, ran away, dragging the boy to death.

Nine young ladies, mostly from St. Paul, renounced the world and joined the order of the Sisters of St. Joseph at St. Paul. The ceremonies took place in the chapel of the Academy of St. Joseph, and were conducted by Archbishop Ireland.

A general order suspending all ore trains until the opening of navigation in 1889 has gone into effect on the Duluth and Iron Range road. The mines will keep on producing all winter and will stack the ore ready for an early rush in the spring.

Minnesota's Prohibition vote was less than 15,000.

Anoka is moving towards electric lights and an electric street railway.

Work has been begun on a 550 barrel reservoir to help Wadena's water supply.

It is charged that Minneapolis police have to be "squared" to the extent of $300 before a pugilistic contest is permitted to go on.

Burglars went through three safes in as many business houses at Owatonna Thursday night. The amount of plunder secured was small.

R. S. Shepard, C. E. Reynolds and George O. Hawkins were the prize winners of the Pillsbury academy declamation contest at Owatonna.

A special train on the Wisconsin Central road, transporting the Boston Ideals from Milwaukee to Duluth, was wrecked near the latter place by an open switch. No one was injured.

The Mankato city council has appointed a committee to revise the city charter for submission to the coming legislature. A board of public works and two new wards will be asked for.

H. H. Scott, justice of the peace at Hinckley, shot and killed S. K. Irvin at that place. The quarrel arose over some trivial affair, and in the dispute Scott shot his opponent. The murderer immediately gave himself up to the officers.

An insane man named Hill, a passenger on the Omaha train, took possession of the telegraph office at Mankato, and was secured only after a hard struggle with the train men. He was on his way home from the Rochester asylum.

Moorhead wants a public library.

Ed and Willard Kitohell, cousins, were drowned while skating on the river at Montevideo.

Ludwig Mogrin, a farmer residing near Minneiska, had his neck broken by a fall from a straw stack.

The trustees of the state insane hospitals are looking over the building now in construction at Fergus Falls.

Rose, the 13-year-old daughter of John Topinsky, of Lake City, was sent to the reform school for entering the residence of Mrs. Gines and stealing various articles of value.

John Lindquist was killed in Stillwater by a runaway team. His brother Gust was seriously injured. The two men were walking on the street and did not see the team until too late to escape.

At St. Paul Judge Simons has issued a writ of mandamus to compel Insurance Commissioner Shandrew to issue a license to the National Mutual Indemnity association. Mr. Shandrew recently refused to grant them a license.

The Winona and Southwestern railway was formally opened Friday by an excursion over the first twenty miles of the road, tendered by President William Windom and other officials to about 200 business men and representatives of the press.

Two attempts have been made to set fire to the Gustavus Adolphus college at St. Peter. The first was made on Monday night, when a map was found on fire.

General Master Workman Powderly and General Secretary Hayes have prepared for the members of the order of the Knights of Labor a statement as to T. B. Barry's expulsion from the order. The formal resolution of expulsion appears to have been unanimously adopted by the general executive board on Oct. 15 and was based upon charges that he had illegally drawn money from the treasury of the order and had been guilty of other irregularities during his membership.

Thomas Brown, the man who murdered Policeman Paull of Moorehead Mina, has been in and around Fargo for some time. He is known to be a professional crook, and is suspected to have been one of the burglars who robbed the Minnesota house and the Manitoba house a few nights ago. Policeman also think it was he who shot at William Dent, and it is reported that he was sent to the penitentiary four years ago, but for what crime cannot be ascertained. During the day there has been strong talk of lynching Brown, and if he should meet that fate it would surprise no one. A crowd of several hundred went out to the jail, carrying with them a railroad tie to batter down the doors, but the sheriff had anticipated their visit and removed the prisoner to some place of safety before their arrival.
brown-fort-wayne-1888-10-25.A10:
WEST AND SOUTH.
John O'Brien, a tramp, who had just been received at the Wisconsin Insane Hospital, attacked the head attendant, John Castle, Saturday, but was secured by other attendants before doing any injury. He died shortly after, when it was discovered that during the struggle, in which he had been thrown against an iron seat, several ribs had been broken and driven into a lung.

Christ Meyer, of Fort Wayne, Ind., who had been separated from his wife for several months, and had been drinking heavily since, committed suicide recently while insane.

George Milner, a prominent farmer near Columbus, Ind., died recently from injuries received by falling down-stairs.

A rich vein of zinc ore has been found at Gelena, Ill.

Miss Elvide De Plae, a 14-year-old St. Paul girl has announced her intention of marrying Joen Stuart, a burly negro.

The unveiling of the Grant statue in Lucas Market Square, St. Louis, Saturday, was witnessed by an immense throng.

The State Association of the Michigan Young Women's Christian Association is holding its annual convention at Lansing.

Jonathan Grimes and a man named Johnson, both well known citizens of Minneapolis, were recently eucharced out of $5,000 by bunko men.

Dr. John Scott, a well-known dentist of Pittsburg, died on a train Friday morning, while en route home from Chicago. He was so confident that the end was approaching that he had the conductor forward telegrams to relatives informing them of the sad event.

A writ of mandamus has been issued at St. Paul in the case against Charles Shandrew, Insurance Commissioner of Minnesota, to compel him to record the certificate of the National Mutual Indemnity Association, whose object is to provide medical and surgical attendance for members in case of sickness. The Commissioner claims that experience has taught him that such organizations are radically defective.

A mob of 500 men went to the jail at Fargo, D. T., at midnight Thursday, prepared to batter down the walls, if necessary, to get Brown, the slayer of Policeman Poull, and lynch him, but he had been removed to another place by the Sheriff, and the mob, after a committee had searched the jail, dispersed.

The Iowa State Suffrage Association met in annual convention at Ames Friday.

At Adrian, Mich., Friday, Minnie Durass, Clara Rice, and Maude Badgley, inmates of the State Industrial Home, were sentenced to four years each at the Detroit House of Correction for setting fire to Croswell Cottage, where they were lodged. Two others are still to be sentenced.

Dr. O. W. Wight, who served as health officer of Milwaukee, Wis., four years and in a similar capacity in Detroit, Mich., five years, died in Harper Hospital at the latter city Friday of typhoid fever.

Two miners, Charles and William Weller, while dugging their way through the snow from La Junta basin to Tellwride, Col., Thursday, were caught in a snow slide, carried 1,500 feet down the mountain, and buried under twenty feet of snow and rocks. William dug himself out, but Charles was found crushed to a shapeless mass under several hundred tons of snow and rocks.

At Clarion, Ia., Friday, the grand jury returned an indictment against Mrs. P. Bertha Diggle for murder in the first degree, charging her with poisoning her husband with morphine May 24th, during the engagement at Clarion of the Ford Dramatic Company, of which she was leading lady. Diggle, who lived at Sioux Falls, had gone to Clarion to try and persuade his wife to leave the stage and go home with him. A former grand jury had returned no bill against her.

The convention of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, in Session at Richmond, Va., have approved Chief Arthur's action in the C. B. and Q. strike.

Frederick Mason, a prominent farmer living near Marion, Ind., has been insane on the subject of religion, and a day or two since announced that the Lord had commanded him to sacrifice one of his children and that he would do so as soon as he found out which one would be most acceptable. He was placed in jail Friday and will be sent to an asylum.

A COLORED RAPIST
In Danger of His Life at East Liverpool—A
Rewolting Crime.
In Danger of His Life at East Liverpool—A Revolting Crime.

EAST LIVERPOOL, O., May 29.—Late last evening, as Angelica O'Hanlon, a girl 12 years of age, was walking along a lonely spot on the Lisbon road, and accompanied only by her ten-year-old brother, she was suddenly assaulted and knocked down by a colored man named Charles Smith. The brute attempted to put a gag in her mouth, but failed, and so threw a handful of sand down the girl's throat, which stifled her cries. He then attempted to accomplish his desires, but was prevented by the boy, who seized a stone and hammered the man's head. Turning, Smith caught the lad and endeavored to break his back. Meanwhile

THE GIRL ENDEAVORED TO ESCAPE, but Smith caught her again and used her in a terrible manner and then fled.

The little one, crying, ran to her home and told her story. It was far from police headquarters, but the news soon spread, and officers and citizens started after the negro. He was at last caught by a policeman in a wood. Smith drew a razor, but was knocked down and secured. On the way to the jail the officer several times had to face the mob and beat them back. His efforts to save his man would have been in vain, however, had not assistance arrived, and Smith was locked up.

At one o'clock this morning the City Hall was surrounded by a mob of five hundred, the doors were barred and all the officers were inside. The mob lacked a leader, so the cries of "Lynch him" resulted in nothing. This morning everything was kept secret at headquarters and at the noon hour Smith was given a preliminary hearing. In spite of the secrecy two hundred persons marched into the Court-room. The testimony was of a most revolting nature, and intense excitement became manifest. Dave O'Hanlon, the girl's brother, sprang for ward to assault the prisoner, but was prevented. Seeing that trouble would follow the Mayor hastened the proceedings and committed Smith to jail in default of $5,000 bail. He was then hustled down stairs.

EAST LIVERPOOL, May 21.—As Angelica O'Hanlon, a girl twelve years of age, was walking along a lonely spot on the Lisbon road, and accompanied only by her ten-year-old brother, she was suddenly assaulted and knocked down by a colored man, Charles Smith. The brute attempted to put a gag in her mouth, but failed, and threw a handful of sand down the girl's throat, which stifled her cries. He then attempted to accomplish his desires, but way prevented by the boy, who seized a stone and hammered the man's head. Turning, Smith caught the lad and endeavored to break his back. Meanwhile the girl endeavored to escape, but Smith caught her again and used her in a terrible manner and then fled. Smith has been arrested. The feeling is great against him, and it is thought he will be mobbed.

STATE NEWS.
—Lee county produces 7 pound sweet potatoes.

—The Monday morning edition of the Times-Union has been suspended until further notice.

—The Gainesville Board of Health has refused to allow freight from infected districts to pass through the city.

—The headquarters of the Democratic Congressional Executive Committee of the Second District will be located at Ocala.

—W. C. Cramer, of Manatee, has just closed the season with a yield of 2,000 pounds of first-class sealed honey from twenty-tour colonies of bees.

—Chattahoochee Advance: The Asylum is in an excellent sanitary condition, and great praise is due Captain Moseley and Dr. Foreman for their care of the unfortunate inmates.

—While the residence of Hon. W. P. Head, of Plant City, was being fumigated last Thursday, it caught fire and was burned with its contents. The loss is a heavy one, as it was a valuable house and well furnished.

—Live Oak Banner: Major A. L. Woodward has been reappointed agent for the F. R. & N. Co. at this place. Having served the company in that capacity for eleven years in the past, we are glad to see him get back his old position.

—Kissimmee Leader: Governor Mabry was a visitor to Kissimmee last Saturday. As a member of the Congressional Committee he has been looking over the district and brings the cheering report that we are all right if the Democrats do their duty.

—McClenny Herald: Col. J. J. D. Merritt has an excellent quality of wine, two years old, which he manufactured from home raised grapes. It equals the "best California claret. Wine making bids fair to be one of Florida's chief industries in the near future.

—Chattahoochee Advance: Captain Moseley can take a "hint" before he is knocked down with it, and accordingly is putting the roads around here in first-class order. The Advance is a Moseley man, because his ability is displayed in his kindness and public spirit.

—Marianna Times-Courier: Hurrah for Marianna! Last Saturday the County Commissioners gave $1,000 toward the Marianna public high school. Competent teachers are to be employed, and tuition is to be free. Graded public schools, such as those in Mobile, Columbus and other places, are growing in favor every year, and we do not see why this one should not be a success. Marianna gratefully acknowledges the appropriation, and the result will show that it has not been misapplied.

—Bartow Courier-Informant: The fever in Jacksonville to-day will prove no greater detriment to Florida in the end than the measles in Africa. A short time and all will be over and forgotten. Work, then, now. We want to begin to put ourselves on record now as the leading town and foremost county in the State. Begin to let the world know that we are living, active, moving beings, and not mere drones waiting to be hauled off and buried alive unless the "corn is shelled."

—Orlando Herald: It is estimated that 125,000 gallons of water from the water works are used daily in this city. The ever convincing Irish potato introduced himself to some extent into the market the past week. The demand yet exceeds the supply. Mr. George I. Russell is putting in lots of time in the cultivation of pineapples; we took a stroll out to his patch one day this week and we must say that his lay out overtops anything that we have seen in that line. He has a great many varieties and one row of a very choice kind he has been offered $500 for just the plants alone.

—L. C. Washburn, M. D., writes from Fort Myers to the Oviedo Chronicle as follows: "I have growing semi-tropical fruits and nuts that withstand more or less frost: Olive, camphor, pomegranate, grape fruit, orange, cherry, apple (Siberian crab), currant, gooseberry, grape, lemon, fig, pear, plum, peach, apricot, avacado pear, citron, pecan, hickory nut, blackberry, raspberry, strawberry, mulberry, Japan plum, date, chestnut, almond, tea, making 32 varieties. I have the following things growing and doing well that are strictly tropical and cannot stand frost: Cocoanut, melon, pawpaw, tamarind, sapadilla, mango, lime, pineapple, teeser (egg fruit), mammee apple, sea grape, guava, plantain, banana, beetlenut, bamboo, making 17 varieties. I have all the different varieties of garden vegetables and vines, on land cleared two years ago.

—Lakeland Cracker: Hon. J. W. Bryant has brought us a stalk of sugar cane with sixteen joints, which measures 6 feet 8 inches in length. Before topping it would have measured some ten feet. Mr. C. J. Crantz, of Auburndale, brought to town this week some of the largest horse bananas we have seen in a long time. We measured one for curiosity, and found it to be 8½ inches in length and 7½ inches in circumference. They were from plants one year old, which are growing on ordinary pine land that has not been fertilized. A petition was circulating in town Monday for the pardon of W. W. Willingham, who was sentenced to the penitentiary for life a year or two ago, for the murder of Wm. McGlaughlin, at Fort Meade, and who, had it not been for one of the jury (Dan Mann, who was subsequently lynched at Bartow,) who insisted on a recommendation to mercy, would have been hung.

—Titusville Star: Even the Seminole Indians are rapidly "catching on" to the improvements of the age. Only a few days ago a party of Indians while at Melbourne had the good luck to sell some of their stock cattle, and as the delay of waiting until they could return to St. Lucie was too great, they accordingly telegraphed to St. Lucie to have the squaws go out and hunt up the cattle, so they could deliver them with less delay on their return. Major Westcott, of the Coast Canal Company, arrived here with the steamer "Denny" last Friday and stopped over until the following morning. With him were the contractors and surveyors of the Coast Canal Co. They are on their way to Lake Worth to look after the opening of the canal leading from Lake Worth creek to little Lake Worth, which lies at the head of Lake Worth proper. They expect to dredge through the sawgrass leading from Lake Worth rapids to Lake Worth, a distance of about three or four miles, within the next few months.

—Monticello Constitution: The LeConte pear crop of Jefferson county next year will be worth $20,000 at the lowest estimate. Can't the young ladies of Monticello organize a Cleveland and Fleming Glee Club, so that we may have singing at the meetings every Thursday night. It is rumored that in the near future Mr. J. H Perkins will erect a large city hall over his two stores at the corner of Jefferson and Dog wood streets. Mr. W. M. Girardeau informs us that he has already saved about twenty-five thousand pounds of watermelon seed. Mr. G. is the largest and most successful truck farmer in the State. Messrs. John and James Henry have ordered the machinery for an immense saw and planing mill, which will arrive in a few days. The new mill will be located about 41 miles from town on the T. & M. R. R. Being situated on the railroad it will be a great advantage to parties wishing lumber, as the Messrs. Henry will be enabled to deliver the very best lumber in this market and at lower prices than ever before.

—Sumterville Times: No candidate, who is defeated before the Democratic nominating convention can honestly and conscientiously run as an independent. If he imagines that he has been unfairly dealt with, let him blame the individuals who did it, and not the Democratic party. This is the course for all patriots to pursue. DASTARDLY OUTRAGE.
David Bell Attempts Rape--Don't Be Afraid of the Dark David Bell Attempts
On the night of the 5th David Bell, who was employed by Mr. T. J. Tilson, of Ivy, Madison county, attempted a rape upon Mrs. Tilson during the absence of Mr. T. Mrs. T.'s brother and others were notified, and went in pursuit of Bell, who had traveled. He was caught the next morning, and our correspondent adds, "whether he is dead or not I do not know." This is significant.

ALMOST A LYNCHING.
©XVIII. Tenn. April 9. Dari
KNOXVILLE, Tenn., April 9.—David Bell was arrested at Marshall, Madison county, North Carolina, last night, for criminally assaulting Mrs. Tilson, a young married woman, and lodged in jail. A mob of more than 100 desperate men gathered around the jail this morning, bent on lynching the fiend, but by a clever ruse the sheriff got his prisoner away and took him to Ashville, where he was safely caged.
david-bell-marshall-1888-04.A3:
TELEGRAPHIC BREVITIES.
Mart Duggan, known to fame as the first marshal of Leadville, has been killed.

Judge Howell E. Jackson of Louisville is mentioned as the possible successor of the late Chief-Justice Waite.

The State normal school at Terre Haute, Ind., was Monday destroyed by fire.

Lillian Olcott, the actress, died at the Westminster Hotel in New York City Monday.

The remains of Jacob Sharp were buried Monday in Greenwood Cemetery in New York.

In a quarrel over a trifle Charles Ramsey shot and killed Redford Jeter at Campbellsville, Ky.

The residence of Mark Modlin a Sioux City, Io., was totally destroyed by a tornado Friday.

A package of diamonds valued at $10,000 was stolen from the safe of Burt & Hurlburt at Detroit, Michigan.

The murderers of the Grand Vizier of Bokhara, Russia, were executed by being thrown from a tower 180 feet high.

Charles G. Kelly, while working on a railroad bridge near Fort Scott, Kan., was killed by a piece of falling timber.

An adverse report on the Hennepin Canal bill was decided on in the House Committee Tuesday.

3 An incendiary fire at the Seventy-one Ranch in the Indian Nation destroyed about $2,000 worth of property.

A young boy by the name of Rushing was fatally injured by machinery in the Mobile & Ohio shops at Jackson, Tenn.

Three prisoners in the Friars Point (Miss.) jail were burned to death, the jail having been set on fire by a man named Grey, imprisoned for arson.

Hanson Grover Cleveland Willis, who has four murders to his account, was captured on board a steamboat at Wheeling, W. Va.

Two children of Frank Dent, living at Springfield, O., died from drinking water out of a well in which some rats killed with arsenic had been thrown.

Two freight trains on the Missouri Pacific Railroad were completely wrecked in a collision, near Leavenworth, Kan.

Dorsey Lewis, who runs a plantation near Talledega, Ala., killed a man named J. M. Lewis for not paying a small debt.

The town of Amesbury, Mass., was almost totally destroyed by fire Friday night. The loss will reach nearly a million dollars.

Lee Adcock, a brakeman, while trying to board a moving train near Hopkinsville, Ky., fell under the cars receiving injuries from which he will die.

Miss Jasper, a wealthy old spinster living at Somerset, Ky., shot and killed a negro named Abe Clay, who was trying to force an entrance into her house.

A Hungarian murderer who had been released went to the house of the Judge who had tried him, killed him, then killed the Notary's deputy, murdered his wife and children and fled.

Sheriff Reed of Billings, Mont., captured two horse-shelters with fifty-eight head of stollen horses in their possession, thereby gaining rewards aggregating $6,000, which had been offered in Idaho and Nevada.

A mob of about one hundred men attempted to lynch David Bell, who was in jail at Marshall, N. C., for criminal assault, but were prevented by the Sheriff, who smuggled the prisoner out to another town.

Miline, member from the Vasses, and Clemenceau were tied in the French Chamber Thursday for President, but Miline, being the older member, secured the honor. The Chamber will not re-assemble till May 19.

Four workmen in the Delemater Iron Foundry at New York were standing over a mould about twenty feet in diameter when the plank broke dropping the men and a ladle of molten iron into the pit, killing two of them and seriously burning the other two.

Post-offices established: Arkansas—Macedonia, Columbia county, Junius W. Whitlow, postmaster, Texas—Vilas, Bell county, Geo. L. Tilman, postmaster. The name of postoffice Blossom Prairie in Lamar county, Texas, has been changed to Blossom.

A man named Albert Smith committed a murder in Towson County, Indian Territory, killing a man named Thomas Pringle, and was traced and identified by peculiar tacks in the soles of his boots.

Miss Maggie Lepage and Edward Smith of Chandlerville, O., were mysteriously murdered Thursday evening. It is supposed that Smith, who had been rejected by Miss Lepage, killed her and then committed suicide.

J. H. Howe of Fort Collins, Colo., murdered his wife in cold blood, throwing her down and cutting her throat with a pocketknife. The murder occurred at noon Thursday. At 8 o'clock in the evening a mob of 1,000 armed men took him from jail and lynched him.

State News.
THE A. & N. C. RAILROAD.—The election of officers at the recent meeting of the stockholders of the A. & N. C. Railroad resulted as follows: President, Washington Bryan; Secretary and Treasurer, F. C. Roberts; Superintendent, S. L. Dill. The following Directors were elected in addition to those appointed by the Governor: Eugene Morehead, Arnold Borden, J. A. Pridgen and Charles H. Fowler. The latter was elected to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Maj. John Gatling. The following were elected on the finance committee: John W. Hinsdale, John C. Wooten, and W. B. Duncan. The time of meeting was changed to the second Thursday in September.

WILL REMOVE HEADQUARTERS TO RALEIGH.—James S. Battle, Esq., Revenue Agent for Virginia, North and South Carolina, was in the city yesterday arranging for the removal of his headquarters here, which have heretofore been at Greensboro. Mr Battle expects to be permanently established here in a few days and will make his future home here.—Raleigh Observer.

There is a considerable sensation at Oxford caused by the arrest and lodgment in jail of Henry C. Adcock and Jennie C. Adcock. The pair stand charged with poisoning Eliza Ann Adcock, Henry Adcock's wife, to get her out of the way of their guilty love. Henry Adcock and Jennie Adcock, the wife of John W. Adcock, had been living together for months, the woman being completely inflatuated. The men are brothers. The state of affairs had led to many quarrels and rights between them. Henry Adoock's wife threatened to make legal trouble. As a result, her husband and his paramour poisoned her, using arsenic. The coroner's jury brought in a verdict of guilty and both the poisoners were taken to jail without privilege of bail. Henry C. Adcock has eight children and his paramour two. There are many capital cases to be tried at the next term of Granville Superior Court.

It is learned that Bill Thornburg, the noted desperado who in June murdered Lee Adderholt, in Lincoln county, is in his old neighborhood again defiant of the law. It is said that the officers are afraid to attempt his capture. He fired into a private house at which an entertainment was in progress, and killed young Adderholt.

The accident on the Charlotte, Columbia & Augusta Railroad, 22 miles from Charlotte, made a fearful wreck, and it was a wreck deliberately made. The South-bound passenger train, which left Charlotte last Sunday afternoon on the Charlotte, Columbia & Augusta Road, was wrecked at a point 22 miles south of Charlotte. The engine encountered an obstruction that had been placed on the track, and a fearful wreck ensued. No one on board the train was killed outright, but five people were wounded, one of whom has since died. The names of the injured are: James Alexander of Columbia, the engineer in charge of the train, cut on the head, scalded and bruised; J. A. Parks of Columbia, the fireman, flesh terribly mutilated and both legs broken at the thigh; J. A. Cobb of Columbia, baggage master, flesh lacerated and badly bruised; John Ross, colored, car greaser, scalded fatally and died; Madison Broughton, mail agent, left shoulder dislocated. The wreckers fastened a piece of iron to one of the rails and the deadly wreck soon followed. There is no clew whatever to the guilty parties, but no effort is to be spared to hunt them down.

SENTENCED TO BE HUNG.—David Bell, charged with an outrage on Mrs Thomas J. Tilson some time ago in Madison county, was on trial for his crime on Saturday. The case was given to the jury on Saturday afternoon. They deliberated until Monday morning, when they reached a conclusion, bringing in a verdict of "guilty." Judge Boykin sentenced the prisoner to be hanged on the 20th day of September next. A motion for appeal was entered, which will be granted as a matter of course.—Asheville Citizen.

State Librarian Birdsong has just issued a catalogue of the miscellaneous books in the State's collection. There are in all over 50,000 books in the library. They are in better shape than ever before.

LYNCHING IN NEVADA.
A Cold-Blooded Murder Spedily Avenged.
AUSTIN, Nev., November 10.—News has just reached here concerning the particulars of a tragedy at Cortez, ninety miles from here, brought by Deputy Sheriff W. J. Higby and Amos Corbett. Davis Saban, an Italian, shot Richard Holt Wednesday evening in the stomach, inflicting a mortal wound, the latter dying in twenty-four hours. His dying request was that he should get justice, and the court should hang his murderer. Sabani shot Holt because he could not get the loan of money. Parties took the murderer to a mill near Cortez and lynched him by throwing the rope over the limb of a tree and hoisting him by the neck. The Deputy Sheriff found his body tied to a bed-post at the boarding house, life having been extinct about ten hours. The men would say nothing about it, saying he must have committed suicide. The knot was under his left ear and the rope had cut into the flesh of the neck. Coroner Moss left here last night to hold an inquest. Holt had a good reputation and was generally liked. Sabani was only 22 years old and of unsavory reputation, having been in a number of shooting scrapes, and was run off a ranch lately by a rancher with a Winchester rifle.

The Cortez Lynching.
The Italian residents of Cortez, Eureka county, are represented as greatly excited over the lynching of their countryman, Sabini, for the murder of Richard Holt, and vow vengeance against the members of the necktie party, and threaten to shoot them on the spot and burn the stamp mill and hoisting works at the Wenban mine. The mill and mine employees have been armed by the management, and if the Italians attempt to carry out their threats, bloodshed will follow. The question of ordering them to leave the district is being agitated by the miners and mill men.
davis-sabini-cortez-1888-11-16.A24:
TRE VERDICT, SUICIDE.
The Friends of Sabint Making Threats-Inquest Held.
Public Administrator Joseph Moss returned here last night from Cortez after holding an inquest over the remains of David Sabini. We learned from him to-day that he arrived at Cortez Saturday night and found the citizens in a buzz of excitement. The next morning he held an inquest, getting testimony from the following witnesses: Henry Welch, William Christian, John Bollano, Sam Puryer, Barrello and Nelse Hayden.

The Coroner's jurymen were as follows: Maurice Isaac, John Engstrom, Edward Bouton, Thomas Paddock, Richard Smitt and Otis Fulton.

All the witnesses testified that the deceased committed suicide, though they could not give any particulars. Joe says that he could get no one to help him bury the body of Sabini, and that he and his oldest son had to do it alone. The Italians are much exercised over the affair and have made their threats that they would burn down the mine property and mill, and shoot those on sight who had anything to do with the lynching. The men around the mill and store have therefore armed themselves with pistols and keep under cover at night, and do not go around unless business compels them. Joe says that when he left the owner of an old rifle was repairing it so that he could use it in case of need. When he first arrived Sunday night the Italians passed him with their hands on their hip pocket, ready to resist, should he make the first move to serve any papers upon or detain them. Joe went ahead as if he didn't see the scowls and threatening faces on all sides, but he is now glad he is through and the inquest is over. The boys at the mill and boarding-house treated him first class.—Reveille.

e-l-little-conway-1888-04-13.A1:
CONDENSED NEWS.
Business property valued at $50,000 was destroyed by fire in Wheeling, W. Va., Friday morning.

Mrs. Joseph Trancht committed suicide by hanging Friday after a quarrel with her husband, at Lima, Ohio.

A mother and her infant perished in the flames of their burning home at Florida, Orange county, N. Y., Friday morning.

A book-store and seven buildings opposite the Michigan State University, Ann Arbor, were destroyed by fire Friday morning; loss $40,000.

City Marshal Harrell, of Conway, Ark., killed E. M. Little, a colored preacher Friday. The latter had abused him for arrests he had made.

The breaking of a dam near Appleton, Wis., has caused an extensive overflow. About half a mile of the track of the Wisconsin Central railroad was washed away.

Burglars effected an entrance into the First National bank at St. Johnsville, N. Y., and plundered the vault of $10,000 in cash and some jewelry left there for safe keeping. They escaped with their booty.

The Parnellite members of parliament have distributed placards throughout County Claire urging the people to assert their rights and assemble in thousands at the twenty meetings to be held on Sunday.

The Mexican chamber of deputies Friday received a visit from Sir Thomas Grattan Esmonde, a well-known Irish member of parliament. The Mexican legislators gave him a handsome reception, and he made them a little speech.

The legislative, judicial and executive appropriation bill, as agreed upon in the house committee, appropriates $20,472,394, which is $937,606 less than the estimates and $209,-246 less than the current appropriations for the same service.

Circuit Judge Jacob W. Wilkin, of Danville, has been nominated by a delegate convention of the Republican party of the third grand judicial division for justice of the Illinois supreme court, to succeed Hon. John M. Scott, of Bloomington.

The Republican convention for the Eleventh Ohio district has taken 753 ballots for a candidate for congress without selecting a man. Each county in the district has a candidate, and the highest vote cast on the first ballot was 24 for H. S Bundy, father-in-law of Governor Foraker.

New trouble has arisen in the German emperor's throat, indicating that the trachea has been attacked by a local complaint. The air passage having contracted, it became necessary to insert a new cannula. At noon Friday the emperor and empress drove to Berlin in a close carriage and visited the palace, returning to Charlottenburg later in the day.

The right to buy ships in the markets of the world and sail them under the American flag without the payment of duties, is granted in a bill agreed upon by the majority of the house committee on merchant marine and fisheries Friay. It is also contemplated that no duty shall be paid upon materials entering into the construction of vessels built in the United States.

Chicago is to have a grand temperance temple if the ladies of the Women's Christian Temperance union succeed in raising the money necessary to carry the project to a successful completion. The plan contemplates a building twelve stories high, containing a great hall and a big tower, costing $800,000. Of this $250,000 has already been subscribed in Chicago, and Mrs. Carse and Miss Willard are going to try to raise the balance in the eastern cities.
e-l-little-conway-1888-04-13.A2:
Killed a Negro Preacher.
St. Louis, Mo., April 13 — A dispatch from Conway, Ark., says: City Marshal John H. Howard shot and killed E. L. Little, a colored preacher, last night. The preacher had knocked the marshal down with a can of peaches for some unexplained affront.
e-l-little-conway-1888-04-13.A3:
At Waynesburg, Pa., the jury in the George Clark-McCausland murder case found Clark guilty in the first degree.

E. L. Little, colored preacher, was shot and killed by City Marshal John H. Howard at Conway, Ark., last Friday.

Indianapolis presbytery has elected Gen. Ben Harrison commissioner to the general assembly of the presbyterian church.

Seth Coffin, a well known and eccentric man of Hudson, N. Y., aged sixty-three, committed suicide by shooting himself.

The last of the Kansas breweries has been closed under the U. S. supreme court decision in the Ziebold & Hagelin cases.

In the Bald Knobber cases at Ozark, Mo., a verdict of murder in the first degree has been returned against Dave Walker.

Ed Bradshaw and John Goodrich, both colored, fought a duel at Hopkinsville, Ky., and both are dangerously wounded.

William Anson Wood mower and reaper works, Youngstown, O., destroyed by fire. Loss, $250,000; insurance, $75,000.

Edmund Daniels, arrested at Wooster, O., charged with killing his aged wife, has been convicted of assault and battery.

At Oakland, Md., James Woods was shot and killed by Joseph Murphy, his brother-in-law, while practicing with a revolver.

Brick wall in course of erection, New York city, falls and crushes two laborers to death. By a like accident at Pittsburg a woman was killed.

John Gaynor, a Chicago board of trade man, has been awarded $10,000 damages in a suit against Henry Hager et al. for attempted blackmail.

Mrs. M. Austin Jones, a favorite in Boston society, dropped dead of heart disease while singing at a reception to her friends at Hotel Vendome.

Ocean race for £1,000 between Aimes' yawl Atlantis and Buller's ketch Bridesmaid, from Southampton to Madeira, won by the latter by seven miles.

The Leader and Sunday Dispatch offices, Binghamton, N. Y., destroyed by fire. Loss, $75,000, of which A. W. Carl, proprietor of the Leader, loses $50,000.

City Treasurer Weir, of New Albany, Ind., denies the sensational stories published concerning his alleged shortage, and threatens to fight the matter in the courts.

"Happy Bob" Van Brunt hanged at Warsaw, N. Y., and Jerry Smith (colored) lynched near Memphis, Tenn., last Friday. Holong hanged at Fergus Falls, Minn., Saturday.

The Ohio legislature has passed the Sunday saloon-closing bill, which is to have effect in all municipalities. The measure was opposed by the city districts. The vote was 25 to 2.

Henry Wilhelm, a butcher of Clarksville, Ia., placed the muzzle of a shotgun under his chin and sent the heavy charge of the buckshot through his head into the ceiling above.

Dr. Thos. J. Norris, editor of the Macon (Mo.) Democrat, was assaulted and beaten into insensibility by Alexander Hudson, editor of the Macon Times. It is feared his skull is fractured.

The Kootenia Indians in Montana are getting ugly, and threaten to avenge the hanging of three of their number for murder by the white people. The governor has been called on for troops.

Illinois Central railroad gives a mortgage to the Central trust company, of New York, for $16,350,000 as security for $15,000,000 borrowed to complete and equip branches operated by the road.

Miss Helen Forster, a Philadelphia belle, is suffering from a terribly seared back, the result of the slipping under her clothing of a red-hot slate pencil with which she was frizzing her hair.

George Starkweather, a wood-chopper, sixty years of age, under arrest at Grand Valley, Pa., narrowly escaped lynching. He is charged with criminal assault upon his fifteen-year-old daughter.

William Quillen, night watchman, Dennison, O., assaulted by a gang of roughs, shoots and kills two of his assailants—John Gow and Amos Thompson. Quillen exonerated at coroner's inquest.

One of the walls of the former convent of San Fernado, in the city of Mexico, which was in progress of demolition, fell in, burying many workmen in the ruins. Three dead bodies have been recovered.

The most furious rain, hail and wind storm ever known in that latitude, passed over Pine Bluff, Ark., Monday night. There was no loss of life. A two-story frame building and a church toppled over.

While a family named Meyer, consisting of the father, mother and two sons, were crossing a bayou near New Madrid, Mo., in two small boats, the father and mother fell overboard. Both were drowned.

Miss Sarah Chellis, aged forty, teacher in the public school in Watertown, N. Y., sued John B. Chapman, farmer, aged seventy-three, for breach of promise of marriage, and the jury rendered a verdict of $8,000.

The Massachusetts humane society has awarded a handsome gold medal to Editor A. Hill, of the Springfield Union, for the courage and brave efforts he displayed at the recent burning of the Union office.

The business failures during the seven days ending last Saturday, numbered for the United States 200 and for Canada 22, or a total of 222, as compared with 227 last week and 175 for the corresponding week of last year.

Near Wellsville, O., last Friday, the five-year-old daughter of Thomas Baker fell into a brush pile. Mrs. Baker went to her child's assistance and both were fatally burned. Mr. Baker also received serious burns.

Silas Sapp was dangerously wounded, adjacent to Savannah, Ga., by Farmer Coleman, who objected to Mrs. Bird, his daughter, marrying Sapp. Coleman, thinking he had killed Sapp, committed suicide. Sapp will recover.

A Mrs. Smith, who has been living with John and Henry Hill, on the line of Russell and Pulaski counties, Kentucky, has confessed to assisting the Hills in killing two peddlers who were stopping at their house. The Hills were arrested and placed in the Jamestown jail.

Emmons and James G. Blaine, jr., say that letters received from Naples contain only favorable notices of their father's health, and denounce the report of his ill health. S. B. Elkins says the reports show a malicious purpose.

J. W. Wharry, who bought the Minnehaha county (Dak.) Moil printing outfit from Postal Inspector Bath last fall, has been arrested, charged with forging a mortgage on property in Missouri. The mortgage was given to Bath as security in the purchase of the Moil office.

Detective Sergt. Aldrich has returned to Chicago from his fruitless chase after Tascott. He has traveled every inch of ground from St. Paul to Washington territory, invaded the queen's dominions at Winnipeg, and gone through the Northwest territory. Tascott was heard of everywhere, but all the clews amounted to nothing.

Minnie Rose Parsons, a young girl of Pittsburg, was enticed from her home by Lieut. Ryan, of the U. S. navy, who acted under an assumed name. He promised to secure her a stage engagement, but deserted her in New York, where she was found by the police and returned to her home. Ryan and an accomplice, J. H. Meade, are under $1,000 bonds each in Pittsburg.

The suspension of the American exchange in Europe, limited, reported in New York, and William C. Boone, treasurer of the company, appointed receiver by U. S. Circuit Judge Lacombe; liabilities, $1,000,000. E. D. Keplinger, dry goods, Canton, O.; liabilities, $2,000. E. A. Weigler, grain, Sun Prairie, Wis.; liabilities, $17,000; and Walbridge Bros., furniture, Bos-
e-l-little-conway-1888-04-13.A4:
MERE-MENTION.
At Greenville, Ohio, last Thursday, Judge Elliott sentenced J. S. Simon, the defaulting ex-treasurer of Drake county, to six years in the penitentiary, and to pay a fine amounting to about forty-eight thousand dollars and costs, the fine being double the amount of the embezzlement. Speaker Carlisle and Mr. Randall estimate that the present session of Congress may be prolonged into September. Senator Hampton was thrown by his horse on Sunday of last week, and his wooden leg broken. He was only slightly hurt. Gen. Sherman has extended an invitation to Generals Longstreet, Mosby, Gordon, Buckner, Lee, Mahone and Johnston to be present at the Delmonico banquet, on the 27th instant, to celebrate Gen. Grant's birthday. The appropriation asked for taking the next national census is $6,000,000. This is about ten cents a head for every man, woman and child in the land. The Atlanta prohibitionists have in convention publicly declared against a third party movement. The business failures throughout the country during last week number, for the United States 200, Canada 22; a total of 222, against 227 the previous week. On Thursday last at Conway, Ark., City Marshal John H. Harol, shot and killed the Rev. E. L. Little, colored pastor of the African M. E. Church. The preacher undertook to remonstrate with the city marshal for having arrested his (Little's) brother for disturbance. Little finally made an assault and was shot. Clement Dowd, of Charlotte, has been appointed receiver of the United National bank at Raleigh, N. C. The president and cashier are in the Raleigh jail. E. P. Duplex, a colored Republican, was elected mayor of Wheatland, California, last Thursday. He is the first colored man honored with such a position on the Pacific coast. A resolution providing for the submission to the people of a prohibition amendment to the State constitution of New York, was adopted by the Assembly last Thursday. According to the Rev. Dr. DeCosta, "the commander of the Pinkerton force can gather in a day's notice a larger number of armed men, either in New York, Pittsburg or Chicago, than the general commanding the army of the United States." Mr. Brooks, the father of Preller's murderer, has addressed a touching appeal for mercy to his son, now under sentence of death at St. Louis. The Oregon Democrats have declared in favor of the election of United States Senators by the people. The Mexican government is seriously considering a proposition for the completion of the railway across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec by an English syndicate. A family near New Richmond, Ind., was poisoned last week by eating diseased pork.

CROP REPORTS.—The South Carolina weather service furnishes the following concerning the effect of the weather on the crops during the

Saturday:
Rainfall about the average, fairly distributed, and has affected the growing crop favorably. But little time has been lost during the past week owing to wet weather.
The temperature was below the average, but the farmers are encouraged by the fine weather of the last seven days.
Of sunshine an average amount has been received.
Oats, wheat, barley and rye look well. Cotton is being planted. In some sections corn is up, and cotton high enough to side. On the whole, the past week has been good both for the crops and for farming operations.
The Washington department of agriculture has issued the following crop bulletin for the week ending Saturday:
It has been warmer than usual in the Southern States, the Central Valleys and Northwest, and colder in New England and the Middle Atlantic States. The season from January 1 to April 14 has been colder than usual throughout the Northern States, Ohio Valley, New England and Middle Atlantic States, while throughout the Southern States the temperature for the season has differed but slightly from normal. The rainfall for the week has been slightly in excess in Ohio and Central Mississippi Valley, Missouri, Kansas, Kentucky and Northern Tennessee. There has also been a slight excess of rainfall on the middle and Atlantic coast, and from Northern New England westward to Wisconsin. Well distributed showers are reported from New England, New York, Virginia, the upper Missouri Valley and the West Gulf States, while very little rain is reported from the South Atlantic States. The weather for the week has been favorable and fair for growing crops. All agricultural district reports from the Southern States show that the week was favorable for cotton and cane, and that small grain crops have been affected favorably. The season is probably ten days late in the Middle Atlantic States, and fifteen to twenty days late in the Northwest, where seeding is progressing slowly.

THE STATE PENSIONS.—The Columbia correspondent of the News and Courier writes: An interesting question has just arisen in regard to the pension appropriation, and it shows that the pension bill is not altogether waterproof.

The attorney general was in the city yesterday, and the pension board submitted to him the question whether after the appropriation of $50,000 is exhausted, the pension board should continue to receive and pass on pension applications.

The attorney general's opinion was that the board should continue to pass upon the pension applications, approving and rejecting as they are doing now, and render their decision to the comptroller general. Now the question which arises is whether after the appropriation is exhausted the comptroller general shall continue to issue his warrants for pension money? The appropriation for pensions is not made in the Pension Act, and this Act does not instruct the comptroller general to draw his warrant for only $50,000. The attorney general has not rendered a decision upon this point.

IT WILL NOT DOWN.—In the South Carolina Presbytery, in session at Anderson last week, the Woodrow question was brought up indirectly in the form of an overture to the Board of Directors of the Columbia Theological Seminary, introduced by Dr. Crosby, of Newberry. The overture was couched in a series of questions addressed to the Board of Directors, the purport of which was: "Do the Board of Directors approve of the action of the Seminary faculty in refusing to allow a certain student in the Seminary to attend the lectures of Dr. Woodrow, a professor in the South Carolina College?"

On the adoption of this resolution, the ayes and noes were demanded, and the resolutions were adopted by a vote of 33 to 13, indicating a positive Woodrow sentiment in the Presbytery. The Moderator was excused from voting.

The municipal election for the town of Chesterfield was held on the 9th instant. The prohibition ticket was elected by a majority of seventeen.
e-l-little-conway-1888-04-13.A9:
Train Robbers Captured. HAMBURG, ARK., April 13—T. A. Ward and A. L. Rogers, Cleveland County, have just returned from the southwest portion of Ashley County with two men known as John Jones and Mark McQuestion, arrested and charged with implication in the recent robbery of a train on the St. Louis Arkansas and Texas railroad, near Kingsland. The officers are satisfied that they have the right men. "Happy Bob" Hanged. WARSAW, N. Y., April 12—Robert Van Beunt was hanged in Warsaw jail-yard this morning. He spent much of the night in prayer and reading his Bible. Eva Roy, his victim's sister, unexpectedly arrived from Albany this morning, and at six o'clock she called at the jail, but was refused admittance. Fatal Can of Peaches. CONWAY, ARK., April 13—City Marshal John H. Howard shot and killed E. L. Little, a colored preacher, last night. The preacher had knocked the marshal down with a can of peaches for some unexplained affront. Petroleum Fuel Prohibited. WASHINGTON, April 13—Supervising Inspector Lubbock, of San Francisco, having reported to the Treasury Department that petroleum is not safe fuel for large boilers, has been instructed by Secretary Fairchild to withdraw all permits heretofore given for its use, except in the case of small steam launches. Texas Furnishes a Hanging. LONDON, TRA, April 13, Chillers Bank
Texas Furnishes a Hanging.
LIBERTY, TEX., April 18—Chillers Banks, colored, was hanged to-day at Wallisville. The execution was public, and was witnessed by hundreds of people. Banks met his doom with stolid indifference.

Mother and Child Perish.
MIDDLETOWN, N. Y., April 18—At Florida, Orange County, two dwellings belonging to John Gillilny were burned last night. The owner occupied one and Joseph Bird the other. When the fire started Bird jumped from the window. Mrs. Bird and her babe perished in the flames.

Disappointed Buckeyes.
WASHINGTON, April 18—Several Ohio

Disappointed Buckeyes.
WASHINGTON, April 13.—Several Ohio men have gone home much disappointed. Had the direct tax refunding bill passed, it is said a nice percentage of over $130,000 would have been divided among about four Ohio men for their valuable persuasive services.

Four Workmen Killed.
BIRMINGHAM, ALA., April 13.—A construction train on the Kansas City, Memphis & Birmingham railroad was wrecked sixty miles west of here at half-past seven last evening. Four workmen were killed, one injured fatally and nine others seriously hurt. The train was backing at a high rate of speed and struck a cow and was ditched.

The body of Mrs. Bergreen was found to the cellar of her house at Evansville, Minn. She had been murdered.
e-l-little-conway-1888-04-13.A11:
South and West.
THE Maryland Republican State Central Committee has fixed May 17 as the date and Easton as the place for holding the convention to nominate delegates to the Chicago convention.

ALBERT DUMKEE, of Columbus, Nebraska, in a drunken frenzy murdered his aged wife with a club and then assaulted his daughter, but he was overpowered before injuring her seriously.

SILAS BANKS killed three brothers named Monroe at Parkersburg, W. Va., as the result of an old feud. He himself was wounded four times.

THE Kootenai Indians, in Montana, are getting ugly and threaten to avenge the hanging of three of their number for murder by the white people. The Governor has been called on for troops.

FIRE destroyed eighteen buildings in Massey, Md., including the principal stores and hotels.

THE Kentucky Prohibitionists, in convention at Louisville indorsed Rev. Green Clay Smith, of Kentucky, for President, and made Clinton J. Fiske, of New Jersey, the second choice.

WILLIAM ANSON's extensive Wood Mower and Reaper Works at Youngestown, Ohio, have been destroyed by fire. The loss is estimated at $250,000. Five hundred employees were thrown out of employment.

J. S. SIMON, defaulting Treasurer of Darke County, Ohio, has been sentenced to six years in the penitentiary and to pay a fine of $48,-000 and costs.

ALL the union maltsters and brewers in Chicago have gone on a strike, and there is a complete shut down of the breweries in that city.

The body of a boy, age six, was found in the woods a short distance from his home in Georgetown County, S. C. An inquest brought to light the fact that the father had beaten him until he was unable to walk. The child had crawled into the woods and died.

The five year-old daughter of Thomas Baker, living near Wellsville, Ohio, fell into a burning brush pile. Mrs. Baker went to the child's assistance, and both were fatally burned. Mr. Baker also received serious burns while extinguishing the flames on his wife and child's clothing.

WILLIE GRADY, six years old, accidentally shot and killed his sister Ella, three years old, at his parents' home in Chicago, while at play with a pistol.

A CHICAGO paper figures up the loss of the Burlington strike to the Brotherhood and switchmen at $601,580. The loss to the company is $2,102,000.

A MAN on the Muerto ranch, near Brownsville, Texas, was bitten by a mad wolf, from the effects of which he became wild and fled to the woods. He entered the Asadore ranch and seizing a six-year-old child of Manuel Cantu, bit and tore it to pieces.

CITY MARSHAL HOWARD shot and killed E. L. Little, a colored preacher, at Conway, Ark., because the preacher had knocked him down with a can of peaches for some unknown reason.

Two white men, J. T. Halsey and J. C. Hulist, were returning home from Fort Smith, Ark., drunk, and as they passed a cabin by the roadside one of them said, "Watch me kill that kid," whereupon he put a bullet through the breast of a four-year-old colored boy, killing him instantly.

MAJOR W. Z. LEITNER, Secretary of State of South Carolina, died suddenly of heart disease in Columbia.

The bakers and brewers of Chicago are on a strike.

MAX MOLLER, of Tribune, Kan., has died of hydrophobia, contracted from a mad dog bite received two weeks ago.

WILLIAM POLK, an insane colored convict in the Tennessee State Penitentiary,at Nash ville, committed suicide by biting his tongue off, thus bleeding to death.

frank-easterling-1888-10-06.A1:
Killed for Being a Democrat-- Carry the News to Chandler and John Sherman.
BRANDON, Miss., Oct. 8. Last Wednesday a negro named Frank Easterling, who was living in this county, declared on the streets of Brandon that he intended to vote the Democratic ticket in November, and on Saturday night a mob took him out and hung him. The same mob on the same night shot Sharper Easterling, a negro Democrat at whose house Frank was found. It is thought Sharper will die.
frank-easterling-1888-10-06.A2: It seems colored Democrats are not safe in Rankin county. One negro was hung and another shot by a mob in that county Saturday night for being Democrats. It is not stated of what race these slayers were, whether white or colored, but they were evidently carpetbaggers, scalawags or negroes, and perhaps some of each, and all ultra Republicans. That little bit of political news would be a nice morsel for James G. Blaine to roll under his tongue.
frank-easterling-1888-10-06.A3:
THE STATE.
NEWS ITEMS GATHERED AND CONDENSED FROM ALL QUARTERS.
Pearl River is quite low. Nother now has electric li

The Aberdeen Fair is booming this week.

The Durant compress is now at work.

West Point is to have another new bank.

Holly Springs has organized a Democratic Club.

The "Old Ship of Zion" is to appear at Corinth.

The farmers of Warren have boycotted jute bagging.

Returned refugees have been rejoicing at Jackson this week.

Bill Arp delivers the opening address at the Macon Fair.

English walnuts are being grown successfully in Benton county.

Natchez will not raise quarantine against Jackson until after frost.

The Y. M. C. A. of Natchez, proposes erecting a $24,000 building.

The Supreme Court met at Jackson Monday and adjourned to Oct. 29th.

The State University opened Monday with 125 students in attendance.

The Farmers Alliance numbers 72,000 in this State, and still on the increase.

Mr. W. Adams, one of Yallobusha's leading farmers, died at Coffeeville last week.

The Farmers' co-operative warehouse will be erected at once at McComb City.

Frank Wilson, col., was shot and killed by Will Harris, at Grenada on the 12th.

The Booneville Pleader has been chosen as the official organ for the Farmer's Wheel.

R. C. Kelly, of Port Gibson, made, an assignment last week, assets, $18-360 liabilities, $18,000.

Mrs. Nancy Barrow, aged 78, died at Greenville on the 13th, from the simple lack of vitality.

Geo. Liberman was killed while unloading a heavy boiler from a freight car south of Vickburg on the 15th.

Miss Lulie Hamilton, of Clinton, and Judge Byrne, President of the Senate of Arkansas, were married last week.

A goodly number of farmers over the State are wrapping their cotton with the Lane Mills Cotton Bagging.

Mrs. M. J. Bingham, wife of the Rev. S. J. Bingham, of the Presbyterian church, died at Moss Point on the 14th.

Hamburg is called an old "Sleepy Hollow," by an exchance, because there is no public manifestations of enterprise.

A. D. Smith's gin was burned last week near Shubata. 20 bales of cotton and 1000 bushels of cotton seed were a total loss.

Durant's new bank has a capital stock of $25,000, H. P. Davis, President, S. W. Weems, vice-president, W. D. Lawson, chashier.

The steamer Ed. Ricardson, one of the finest ever on the Mississippi, and which cost over $100,000, was sold recently in New Orleans for $2,750.

Peyton Harrison, chief engineer of the Vicksburg Wharf and Land company, was killed by a caving bank on the 12th. His body was not recovered.

Alice Ross, of Natchez, widow of a colored United States soldier, has received recently a check for $2,251, being arrears of pension due her husband.

The Lexington Advertiser paid a high tribute last week to that young Presbyterian divine, Rev. John H. Boyd, who closed his ministry at that place.

The Board of Supervisors of Perry county, have an order prohibiting persons from killing and shipping game—deer and turkeys—out of the county.

At Lexington Jeff Gantt blew his brains literally out of his head, leaving his skull empty. He was 28 years of age and no cause assigned for his rash deed.

It cost Natchez, Miss., $2,742 for quarantine restrictions, which includes guards and all expenses pertaining to the preservation of the health of the city.

Mrs. H. F. Kennedy & Son in Clay county own a fine flock of Cotswold sheep, numbering some 200 head, the wool of which brings them 25 cents per pound in its unwashed state, at Enterprise.

A telegram to the Memphis dailies gives the news, that as a result of a protracted meeting, Rolling Fork is now a prohibition town. After this there is no use talking to us about the days of miracles being passed.

The Warren county planters claim that they are not getting full weight at the Vicksburg compresses and threaten to hunt another market, unless they can have a representative there to see that they get justice.

Frank and Sharp Easterling, colored, were mobbed by unknown persons in Rankin county recently. Frank was a notoriously bad character, while Sharp was shot for haboring him. Polites had nothing to do
frank-easterling-1888-10-06.A4: Two negroes Frank and Sharp Easterling were mobbed recently in Rankin county. Frank's offense was stealing cotton, and Sharp was charged with harboring Frank, after the vigilantes had notified him to leave. Up in this section where negroes are much more numerous than in the piney woods, we turn over such cases as Frank Easterling to the Grand Jury and we know no law that would constitute Sharp's conduct a crime. But Gov. Lowry's home is in Rankin; his nephew Rod occupies a part of a public building in the county, and the Brandon Republican is published there. Taking all these facts together the wonder is that more people are not lynched in that locality.

franklin-franklin-1888-11.A1:
POINTED PARAGRAPHS.
Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner.
John O. Kannahan, Anderson Hoosier, paid $150 for the privilege of using second hand two-cent stamps.

Isaac Keenan, colored, convicted of the murder of John Heilly for $1.80 in Baltimore, has been sentenced to death.

The postoffices at Lewis Creek, Letcher county, and at Small House, Ohio county, Kentucky, have been discontinued.

John Williams, on trial at Birmingham, Ala., for the murder of Simon Isaacs, was acquitted on the ground of insanity.

At the funeral of Admiral Baldwin in New York Gen. W. T. Sherman and Levi P. Morton were among the pallbearers.

At Sharpsburg, Ky., Judge Withers shot and killed David Lewis, a negro desperado, who was threatening members of the judge's family.

Daniel Thomas was cut and killed by William Hugely, and John Lewis was shot in the knee, during a row, at Nicholasville, Kentucky.

The British cruiser Hyacinth has taken possession of the Cook's Islands in the name of the British government. The natives are rejoicing.

The select committees appointed by the Ohio legislature to consider the subject of taxation and penitentiary removal met at Columbus.

The family of Samuel Patterson, mayor of Piketon, O., consisting of four persons, were all taken with fits simultaneously. Mysteriously poisoned.

John Armstrong shot and instantly killed Joe Glasrow at Grape Creek, Ii. Armstrong was beating his wife and Glasrow remonstrated with him.

The annual graduating exercises of the Dartmouth medical college occurred Tuesday night, when twenty-six students received the degree of M. D.

Indiana will have a contest in its First district whereby Col. Posey, defeated Republican, will endeavor to make the Parrott come off the congressional perch.

James Seaman, a farmer near West Liberty, O., was thrown from his buggy by his horse taking fright, cutting a long and dangerous gash in Mr. Seaman's head.

Two prominent attorneys of Birmingham, Ala., were swindled by a young man who represented himself as the son of an ex-chief justice of the supreme court of Texas.

The passenger agent of the Kansas City, Memphis & Birmingham road, at Birmingham, Ala., ticketed two Mormon elders and five converts to Ogden and Salt Lake City, Utah.

Springfield, O., is rejoicing over the wonderful supply of water from the new artesian well. They hope to utilize it some way after they find out what the stuff really is.

Two masked men entered the Louisville & Nashville depot at London, Ky., and forced the night operator to give them what money was in the cash-drawer—$29.90—and $5 of his own.

Near Mackville, Ky., a little girl four years old, daughter of Richard Cavanaugh, fell into a large kettle of boiling water setting on the kitchen hearth, and died almost instantly.

James Mills, colored, who assaulted and tried to murder Bertie Howard, the eleven-year-old adopted daughter of a farmer living near Paoli, Pa., was captured at Cranberry, New Jersey.

Mrs. Dr. Weaver, aged seventy, died at Fort Wayne, Ind., from injuries sustained in falling down stairs a few days ago and breaking a leg and arm, and receiving internal injuries.

At Tiffin, O., Alfred Edwards' belladonna plaster came very near drawing him up the golden stairs. He was dying of mysterious poisoning when the plaster accidentally dropped off and he recovered.

Gen. Raum is one of the incorporators of the Illinois and Indiana Phonograph company, of Chicago, with a capital stock of $2,000,000, whose certificate of incorporation was filed with the Illinois secretary of state.

Representatives of the American Dairymen's and Breeders' association met at Chicago, Tuesday, and made arrangements for holding an exhibition of butter, cheese and eggs annually in that city at the same time that the fat stock snow is held.

John W. Keely, of motor fame, who was sent to jail on Saturday last for contempt of court in refusing to give experts appointed by the court information regarding his mysterious motor, was released on bail. The case will be heard in the supreme court January 12.

James Van Sant, of Zanesville, O., evidently believes the lately advanced theory that the more a woman cries the healthier she is. In her petition for divorce she asserts that he refused her tue service of a physician, and pulled her hair viciously whenever she asked for one.

Dan Epps, of Steubenville, O., stole a barrel of cider, which is about the amount required to make a Steubenville man drunk, wrapped the drapery of O. G. Russell's buggy around him and laid down to pleasant dreams, from which he awoke to sixty days in the workhouse.

The annual meeting of the National Cattle Growers' association met in Chicago. The session was devoted to papers demonstrating the contagion of Texas fever, and recommendations to congress for laws restricting the shipment of such cattle indiscriminately from one state to the other.

Mrs. Anthony Newell, widow of the well known restauranteur, who died suddenly a few weeks ago, committed suicide at Pittsburg by shooting herself through the heart. Despondency over the death of her husband and fear that the estate was heavily involved are the causes assigned for the deed.

Near Franklin, Tenn., as Miss Mary Nichol and Miss Leela Vaughn were driving in a buggy, a colored man attempted to stop their horse. The whipping of the horse made the wheel of the buggy tarrow the negro down and the girls escaped. The negro will be lynched if caught and indicted.
