On the day for the sale of delinquent lands in Jackson County, there was but one small tract left on the list, the taxes having been paid on the rest.

Editor Eugene Moore of the Atkine Mail, was the only member of the Western District Press Association who responded to the recent call for a meeting at Clarksville. More hospitality had been prepared for the occasion than he could dispose of.

There is considerable excitement and much rejoicing at Little Rock over the reported discovery of natural gas in the city. Prof. Reuben Carroll, of Louisville, Ky., recently said he would stake his reputation as a gas and oil expert upon there being natural gas in inexhaustible quantities in the vicinity. Prof. O. F. Mitchell, of the oil regions of Pennsylvania, and Mr. Hiram Robbins, a mineral expert, of Little Rock, have made the investigations and found the place where the gas comes forth from a hole two feet in diameter, and burned brightly until extinguished by heavy rainfall. The opening is about two miles from the city in a dense wood.

The sheriffs of Izard, Sevier, Jackson Poinsett and Clay counties have settled with the State Treasurer for taxes collected for 1887.

In a row at Corning, a few nights ago, Jim Inman was seriously wounded. Carl Wall and Tom Kuykendall are in jail charged with the shooting.

While in bathing in Sutton Lake, near Texarkana, a few evenings since, Jeff Robinson, a colored youth, eighteen years old, was seized with cramp, drowning before assistance could reach him.

Miss Alaska Dunn is the name of a recent addition to the household of Congressman Dunn, of this State. The little daughter weighs eight pounds, and she and her mother "are doing quite well."

News from Paris, Logan County, reports the killing of Ed Jarard and Alois Zeller, German boys, by lightning. They were aged respectively eighteen and sixteen years, and were engaged in shocking bats at the time they were killed.

Twenty years ago David Ashley, of Grant County, killed a rabid dog and got some of the saliva on one of his hands, which a few years later began to affect him. A few days since he died in the greatest of agony, a victim of hydrophobia.
Some very important moves on the railroad checker-board in Arkansas, in the way of new lines to be constructed, may be looked for soon.

Little Rock is suffering from an epidemic of petit burgiaries.

The people of Carlisle are projecting a fine school building, upon which they propose to expend some $3,000, and which they hope to build in the near future.

Colonel H. E. Kelley, of Kansas, who is interested in the properties known as the Highlands, about a mile up the river from Little Rock, is arranging for the construction of a dummy line opening up that section of country.

Arkansas has added not less than one hundred factories to her industrial wealth within the last year.

The recent Sunday-school convention at Bentonville showed that Benton County had last year 2,942 pupils enroled, requiring the services of 290 teachers. The total amount of contributions for Sundav-school purposes was $1,026.51.

Sheriff J. S. Reagan of Nevada County arrived in Little Rock a few nights ago, and lodged in the penitentiary for safe-keeping Grant Holly, colored, who attempted an assault upon a white woman near Bowden, Nevada County, and to mob whom several attempts were made. When the train passed Bowden six armed men tried to enter it and secure their man, but were stopped by the conductor, who stood them off until he could start the train.

A desperate encounter occurred between revenue officers and moonshiners near Black Springs, Montgomery County, a few days ago. Internal Revenue Collector Fry and a posse raided the moonshiners' camp in the vicinity, destroying three distilleries. Shortly afterward the posse was attacked from ambush by an armed band of moonshiners. A regular battle ensued, in which Deputy United States Marshal Trammel was killed. Collector Fry at once telegraphed to Fort Smith for reinforcements, and more bloodshed was expected.

The Board of Public Affairs of Little Rock has closed a contract with the Fort Wayne Jenny Electric Light Company to furnish the city an electric light plant for $27,000, with Corliss engine and all necessary equipment to run 100 arc lights, which are to be hung at the intersections of the streets. The company will enter into a bond of $25,000 to the city that the plant shall be in running order by the 1st of September, 1888. The $27,000 are to be paid by the city in four annual pay-
The case of the Eureka Vinegar Company vs. the Daily Arkansas Gazette, for libel, came up in the United States Circuit Court at Little Rock, a few days since. The suit was brought on account of the paper publishing a communication to the effect that Old Orchard cider, manufactured by the company and sold extensively throughout the prohibition districts of the State, was intoxicating. Upon the judge intimating that he would hold that hard-cider was a vinous and spirituous liquor and an intoxicant, the plaintiff had a nonsuit entered. The judge then delivered an able and lengthy opinion, holding that it was contrary to the State laws to sell hard cider without license. This is expected to create a wonderful uproar in the State, as nine-tenths of the towns have local-option laws and hard cider is the only beverage sold.

Rain is entirely too frequent.

Governor Hughes has pardoned E. L. Corn and remitted the fine imposed for disturbing the peace in Lonoke, May 10. Corn was fined and sentenced to thirty days' imprisonment by the mayor, but a large number of the prominent citizens of Lonoke asked for the remission of the fine and the pardon, which was granted. To Stand His Trial—Great Fears of Lynching.

Special Dispatch to The Appeal.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Nov. 7.—This morning J. B. Crossland, Deputy Sheriff of Nevada County, this State, came up from Prescott, and returned this afternoon with Grant Holly, a negro, who was placed in the penitentiary here last June to prevent his being lynched. He is charged with having attempted to outrage a respectable white lady at a small town on the Iron Mountain Railroad. At the time of the attempt a large number of citizens gathered, and frequent threats of lynching caused the Sheriff to bring the prisoner to Little Rock for safe keeping. His trial comes up this week in the Nevada County Circuit Court.

James McCoy and John Murphy, who escaped from the county jail at Palmyra, Mo., were recaptured at Kansas City.

In a duel on the road in Washington county, Kentucky, Peter H. Head, a wealthy farmer, was shot dead by his son-in-law, Sam Milton.

The third burglary in two weeks, at Peru, Ind., was committed Monday night, $200 worth of goods being taken from John Bell's tailor shop and dye house.

The rear coach of an east-bound Texas and Pacific train was turned over on its side Monday afternoon at Paris, and was smashed to pieces. The following persons were injured: Vic Bloom, of Paris, leg broken and internal injuries; James Cundy, colored porter, internal injuries; Doctor James Hayes, of Blossom Prairie, head mashed. Five others, whose names could not be learned, were also seriously injured and a number of others slightly hurt.

"Craps" is as dear to the African heart and excites his blood as much as does the facinating game of "draw" his brother in white. Willis Webb and Henry Ellis were engaged in agitating the cubes across the classic San Pedro Sunday afternoon. Willis had thirty-five cents staked on the result of one throw against Henry's quarter. Both claimed to win and both started to rake in the tempting pot. Of course they both couldn't win. In the scramble for the money Ellis whacked Webb two or three times in the back with a small pocket-knife, and finally broke off the blade in his head, while Webb was trying to gouge out Ellis' left eye. The antagonists were arrested and plunged into the bowels of the bat cave where the rattle of dice disturb not their sleep. Recorder Adams got hold of them yesterday morning and fined Ellis $25. Webb was allowed to go and get a doctor to pick the knife blade out of his skull. — San Antonio Express.

A Monday's special from Longview says: Ever since the fight between democrats and republicans and union labor has been instituted in this county it has been very bitter, especially with the republicans, who joined the union labor party, and the straight labor party. Not long since a colored physician, Silas Sherman, who is a democrat and wears a Cleveland hat and carries the campaign flag for all the democratic rallies, was notified through the postoffice by a supposed politician of his color to leave or he would be hurt. This so exasperated the democrats that they made diligent search for the writer, declaring vengeance. This had hardly blown over when it was learned that a very influential negro named Harrison Spencer, living on the A. S. Taylor place one mile from here, was last night called out from his bed and taken away in his night clothes, and it is supposed drowned. No trace of him can be found. His wife, the only witness in the darkness, says her husband hearing a noise went out to see if the stock had broken into his garden. Soon she saw a form pass the door, and another; then voices were heard sounding like those of over a dozen men, and she saw her husband forced to mount an animal from a stump near by and hurried off. The alarm was given, and as soon as daylight came the horse tracks were traceable to the river.

There is no doubt but Spencer was murdered by men of his own color for political reasons. He bears the best character and has been a practical farmer for a number of years. The fact of his declaration on the streets of this place a few days since to support democracy is doubtless the sole cause of his death, and lies at the door of the malcontent office seekers and ignorant negroes. Should the body be found and any evidence of the guilty party, nothing could avert a lynching, and in time perhaps much bloodshed, as the murderers of the negro must have many abettors from recent demonstrations.

A KU KLUX OUTRAGE PERPETRATED IN TEXAS— HANGED, SHOT AND MUTILATED. Longview, Tex., Aug. 31 (Special). About 2 o'clock
A KU KLUX OUTRAGE PERMITTED IN TEXTS HANGED, SHOT AND MUTILATED.

Longview, Tex., Aug. 31 (Special).—About 2 o'clock this afternoon Deputy sheriff Walter Reynolds returned from his search for the body of Harrison Spencer, the colored politician who was forebly taken from his home a few nights ago by a masked band of Ku Klux. Spencer had deserted the Union Labor party and announced his intention of supporting the Republican ticket. Reynolds reported that he had found Spencer's body about three and a half miles from this place, on the west bank of Harris Creek. No sooner had the new spread than over 100 citizens, white and black, started to the scene. The dead man was found hanging from a limb about fifteen feet from the ground with a rope around his neck. His hands were tied behind him and the cords were drawn so tightly that they cut deeply into his flesh. He was evidently shot before the rope was placed around his neck. There is a bullet hole just behind the left ear and one in his left side, and he had been brutally mutilated. A movement is on foot to investigate thoroughly this crime. The following circular was issued this afternoon and 225 citizens responded to the call contained therein:

To all law-abiding citizens: A crime of the most foul nature has just been perpetrated in our midst. Therefore let us come together at 4 o'clock this evening at the court-house and take proper steps that our citizens and officers may act in unity, that the perpetrators of this crime may be discovered and the law of our land vindicated.

J. T. SMITH, County Judge.

A. A. KILLINGSWORTH, Sheriff.

Killed by Klu Klux.

LONGVIEW, Tex., Aug. 31.—About 2 o'clock this afternoon Depty Sheriff Walter Reynolds returned from his search for the body of Harrison Spencer, the local colored politician, who was forcibly taken from his home a few nights ago by a masked band of Klu Klux, supposed to be composed mainly of members of his own race, because he had deserted the Union Labor party, which is very strong among the negroes of east Texas, and announced his intention to support the republican presidential ticket and the democratic state and local tickets. Reynolds reported that he had found Spencer's body about three miles from thii place, on the west bank of Harris creek. No sooner had the news spread than over 100 citizens, white and black, started to the scene. The dead man was found hanging from a limb about fifteen feet from the ground with a three-eights-inch cotton rope around his neck. His hands were tied so tightly that they cut deep into his flesh. He was evidently shot before the rope was placed around his neck. There is a bullet hole just behind the left ear, and one in his left side, and his person has been brutally and horribly mutilated. His shirt is torn from his back, and scars where he had been severely whipped are plainly visible. The body presents a horrible sight, having been feasted upon by flies and worms, the eyes eaten out, and general decomposition having reached an adancee state.

A more secluded spot for the carrying out of such a crime could not have been found in the country. There is no public road near the spot, and the woods are lined with thick undergrowth.

on Thursday, upon the resolution offered by Senator Chandler, instructing the committee on privileges and elections to inquire into the Lousiana election of April 17, 1888, made prominent the facts that political murders and outrages are being committed in Louisiana and Texas for the purpose of influencing the presidential vote. Senator Chandler, in the course of the debate, said:

"I stated when this resolution was before the Senate on a former occasion that these methods of politics which were resorted to in order to secure a return of 136,746 votes and a majority of 84,753 for Nicholls in Louisiana on the 7th of April were a continuing system; that the same species of intimidation, violence, and murder was being continued in the state of Louisiana as a preparation for the election which is to give the electoral votes of the state of Louisiana to Grover Cleveland. Recent facts justify the assertion which I then made, and, disagreeable as I know it is, painful as I know it is, harshly as I know it grates upon the sensitive and patriotic nerves of the senator from Louisiana to contemplate the fact that in his state to-day black men, Republicans, are being butchered in order that the presidential electoral vote of that state may be cast for Grover Cleveland, yet I conceive it to be my privilege and my duty to bring these facts to the attention of the American Senate, to the attention of the people of New Hampshire, if the senator will have it so, and to the attention of the American people, in order that possibly they may be aroused to the enormity of the wrongs that are being perpetrated upon the humble colored voters in this state of Louisiana upon which the senator has passed such a eulogy."

Mr. Chandler quoted from the New Orleans Picayune of Sept. 17 a despatch from Breaux Bridge, La., stating that on the previous Friday evening a gang of unknown men had murdered one black woman, outraged another, and then whipped a black man; also, a despatch to the same paper from St. Martinsville, La., dated Sept. 17, which stated that an affidavit had been made against Sam Polk, as one of the party who had committed the outrages and that he had fled, and which concluded as follows: "The whipping and bulldozing of negroes is getting to be too frequent, especially by irresponsible parties, who, when banded, are criminally inclined. These outrages will be stopped and at once." A New Orleans despatch to the Washington Post, dated Sept. 16, was also quoted. It gave the particulars of the Breaux Bridge outrages and said: "A mass meeting of three hundred white men was held Saturday night to express indignation at the outrages. Resolutions were adopted pledging protection to the colored people and punishment to the perpetrators
With reference to the latter despatch Mr. Chandler said: "I make the prediction, as I did on a previous occasion, that the indignation will end in resolutions. There will be no indictment and no punishment of the perpetrators of these outrages upon these negroes, the object of which is to affect the approaching presidential election, when the parish of St. Martin is to be converted from a Republican parish into a Democratic parish. In the parish in 1874 there were 1,631 white votes and 1,771 colored votes. The vote returned in 1888 was for Nicholls, 1,107; for Warmoth, 1,624. This is one of the few parishes in which at the last election the Republicans managed to obtain a majority. The decree, however, has gone forth from the Democrats of Louisiana that St. Martin shall not be in the presidential election a Republican parish, but shall cast a majority for Grover Cleveland. The Louisiana Standard of September 22 gives the following account of this Breaux Bridge atrocity.

Democratic Murder—An Epidemic of Assassination—Organized Gangs of Democratic Murderers Making the Killing of Negroes a Pastime—How Louisiana Negroes are Being Reduced to Mexican Peonage—Assassination Items as Told in Democratic Specials—No Politics in It, But the Murderers All Good Democrats.

St. MARTINSVILLE, LA., Sept. 17, 1888.

News reached here this morning of one of the most cowardly crimes that ever was committed in this parish. Friday night, at about 11 o'clock, in the vicinity of Breaux Bridge, a gang of four or five parties, some of them so far unknown, whipped a black man, criminally assaulted one black woman, and killed another.

The particulars gathered from the mother of the dead woman are about as follows: On Friday night the gang called at the door of the woman's house and knocked, saying it was the sheriff. She opened the door and recognized one of the parties. Sam Polk. She shut the door on them. They then fired through the door several shots, one of them taking effect in the woman's abdomen and she died next morning. The coroner's inquest revealed the fact that she bore seven months' twins, one of them having the ball through the head. The man Polk was recognized as having engaged in the three crimes. His hat was also found at the door of the cabin. He was not found when search was made for him."

Extarcts from the Picayune, Times-Democrat, and other Louisiana newspapers were submitted in proof of the charges, that these murders and other crimes were committed in August and September. Later in the debate, Mr. Chandler said in reply to Senator Reagan of Texas:

"The senator from Texas complains there was no averment in the case of the

killing of colored people in Louisiana, which I submitted to the Senate, that they were murdered on account of their politics. If the senator had listened to my remarks he would have understood distinctly that I took the ground that these murders were part of a deliberate system; that whether admitted to be political or not they were in fact such; that these disarmings and assassinations of the Louisiana colored people were for the purpose of creating a state of terror as a preparation for the election in November. The same state of things exists in the state of Texas, and I now submit to the senator from Texas the account which I send to the desk of a recent murder, since the late debate, in the state of Texas, which clearly appears to have been the killing of a Republican because he was a Republican.

DIXIE DOTS
Events of a Week in the Sunny Southland.
GEORGIA.

About the biggest farce on record is the manner in which the public roads are worked in this county. There is scarcely a decent road within our borders. The ove. seers get a few hands together, place a pine top in a hole, cover it with a teaspoonful of dirt, and call that working the road. Some places are made perfectly flat when they should be shoveled to the center and made oval. An exchange appropriately remarks: "A little discretion at the proper time might be made to accomplish much, and as good roads not only speak well for a community, but are a public necessity, it is to be hoped the matter will receive the attention of the proper authorities."—Yes, gentlemen, let us have the best public roads possible.

That the people of the north are turning their faces southward is becoming more and more evident. The LaGrange Reporter says:

A gentleman resident in Wisconsin writes us a private letter, from which we make the following extract: "Our people are-reading and talking about the south, and want to know more about it. You know they have been going west for a long time. Dakota is full of Wisconsin people, but they have got enough of it, and think they will not get many more to go. I am sure if you could get a few farmers from here down there, there would be lots of them in a few years. We call 160 acres quite a large farm up here. I know I should like Georgia. Would like to go there to live, but cannot for a year or so, anyway. My father (who visited Georgia once) liked your people very much, and, judging from your paper, they must be nice people." The writer then invites one of the proprietors of the Reporter to visit that section, in the interest of the landowners of Troup, offering to quit work a week to show him around. He is sure it would be of benefit to our people. All this is a pretty big straw, indicating the trend of northern feeling and thought at present.

From the LaGrange, Ga., Reporter.

Last week Callie Swain and Walter McCormick, while out hunting, noticed a robin flying about which seemed to be having a hard time in swallowing a very long worm. Securing a favorable shot one of the boys killed the robin, and was surprised on picking it up to see the tail of a small green snake sticking out of its mouth. The boys brought the bird to town, when the snake was pulled out of its throat and found to be about a foot long. The snake had doubtless come out of its winter quarters to enjoy the spring sun when the robin discovered and tried to eat him. But the southern snake was too much for the northern robin, and would not down, though the robin had swallowed all but about three inches of his tail.

Hogansville Special to The Constitution.

While the majority of our farmers are investing largely in commercial fertilizers, a very respectable minority are depending almost solely upon home-made manures to stimulate and produce their next crops. More compost is to be seen piled out in the fields preparatory to its application than for a long time heretofore. In fact the effort being made by our farmers demonstrates improved methods and increased energy and judgment. Every farm is streaked from center to circumference with terraces, hill-side ditches, and scientifically arranged conveniences for the increase of crops and view to economy. As a whole, to the observer, nothing heretofore equals the prospect of successful operations when the visible signs of practicable management is taken into consideration. The majority of our farmers are Alliance men, which order seemed to answer the purpose intended, that is, to interest and unite them more than all the organizations previously introduced. The great necessity of organization and co-operation among farmers is felt by all, but so often failure has attended all efforts in that direction had almost destroyed all hope of success until by the Farmers' Alliance, upon its simple declaration of principles, embodying no policy but such as is harmonious, refusing admittance of every element conflicting therewith, is proving to be at last an organization suited to the purpose desired. Thousands of dollars have already been saved to the farmers, and in so short a time, as the order is yet only in its infancy. Nothing but encouragement has as yet been experienced, which is causing much enthusiasm among the members, while active preparations are being made for still greater benefits.

The day is not far distant when every farmer under good character is expected to be numbered among the alliance.

Next day is 10th inst., "there is expected to have a large crowd of representative farmers of the Alliance to meet in Hogansville for the purpose of forming among themselves a co-operative association with headquarters at Hogansville. Its purposes will be to raise a sum sufficient to open a mercantile storage and manufacturing business, the success of which will prove of greatest importance to our farmers. Through their general agent all supplies will be obtained at first cost with only freight added. Handle and dispose of their own cotton in lots of from one to five hundred bales, and ginning their own cotton, manufacturing cotton seed oil, and from the meal make their own guano, and grind their own corn and wheat. We have now two extensive ginneries and one oil mill, but in a few months I doubt not that the third ginnery and second oil mill will be erected and operated in Hogansville. The arrangements for the formation of the corporation is being substantially made and will be supported by one of the best farming sections in western Georgia. Let the good work go on.

A sensation was occasioned at Summerville by the report that a mob was organized to lynch Henry Pope, the rapist, who is upon trial for the outrage committed upon the person of Miss Kendrick, last year. It was reported that a large body of armed men were coming in from various parts of the county and would make the attack during the night. Judge Maddox made speedy preparation to give them a warm reception, throwing a strong guard around the jail, and giving notice that every one who should be found to be engaged in the plot should be indicted. The night was looked forward to with some degree of foreboding, but nothing transpired to disturb the citizens.

The prisoner, Pope, learned of the threatened attack, and it is said by some of the guard whose slumbers were interrupted by his supplications, that he prayed with a fervency and eloquence that would have been worthy of a victim of the inquisition.

The evidence of Miss Kendrick, the victim of the outrage, was positive and unequivocal that Pope was her assailant. Her testimony was corroborated by that of other testimony and circumstances, showing Pope in the neighborhood of Miss Kendrick's house about the time the crime was committed. The defendant introduced evidence of witnesses from Alabama for the purpose of showing an alibi. The crime was committed February 3d, 1887. The Alabama witnesses showed that Pope was in Cherokee county, Alabama, from about January 25th up to the middle of March, which, if true, would render it almost impossible for him to have been in this county February 3d. Upon the contrary the state introduced evidence which showed, almost to a moral certainty, that Pope was in this county Sunday, January 30th. The trial has been conducted throughout with that wisdom and impartiality which has always characterized the presiding judge. It is believed by some that should Pope be acquitted he will meet with a summary execution by order of Judge Lynch.

Wm. Smith Dimsdale, a prosperous farmer of Ball Ground, has found, much to his embarrassment, that he is the possessor of two living wives. A few months ago wife number one, who was a handsome woman, of 25 years, met Andrew Harper, a man of stylish appearance, who came to Ball Ground from South Carolina. Harper soon became enamored of Mrs. Dimsdale, who returned his affection.

henry-pope-summerville-1888-03.A6:
A LYNCHING IN GEORGIA
GOV. GORDON'S THIRD RESPITE LEADS TO MOB LAW.
Night to Find Himself Surrounded by Masked Men With Guns—The Negro Swung From the Court-House Banister.

Rome, Ga., May 1.—Henry Pope, the negro who was convicted of assault with attempt to commit rape, at the last term of court in Chattooga county, was taken from the jail at Summerville last night by an armed mob and hanged. Gov. Gordon had issued a respite for sixty days and given it to the Principal Keeper of the Penitentiary, Col. J. R. Towers. He came to Rome yesterday and gave it to Sheriff J. C. Moore, of Floyd county, with instructions from the Governor to proceed to Summerville and bring the prisoner to Rome, for the purpose of having him taken to the Fulton county jail in Atlanta. Sheriff J. C. Moore, with an assistant, Charles Randall, left at 2 o'clock this afternoon, and arrived at Summerville at 8:30 o'clock to-night. The night was rainy and very dark. On their arrival they proceeded to Judge Maddox's house. After a consultation with the Judge, he said he was satisfied that they could not take him away that night, and he said he would meet them at sunrise in the morning at the jail with two guards, and that he would himself accompany them across the mountain. The Judge then sent for Sheriff Worsham, of Chattooga county. Upon his arrival he also advised waiting until morning before taking any action.

THE LYNCHING.

Sheriff Moore and his assistant then went to the hotel and retired at 11 o'clock, and about 2 o'clock Sheriff Worsham came and awoke them, stating that he had been awakened by a crowd and found the door of his room, which is in the jail, fastened and guarded by about fifteen armed men. He stated that a mob of about fifty masked men went to the jail and demanded the keys and the rope that was purchased at Rome a few days ago. They then secured Pope, and, putting the rope around his neck and putting out the lights, led him to the court house, about 150 yards distant, and hung him from the banisters at the top of the stairs. The Sheriff stated that crowds of armed men stood at the corners of each street. Judge Maddox went to the court house, and sent for a doctor. They cut the rope and took the body of Pope down and carried it into the court house. A doctor arrived and found life extinct. The news of the respite published yesterday was carried to Summerville by parties who arrived about two hours before the Sheriff.

HAD BEEN CONVICTED TWICE.

Henry Pope had been twice convicted of an assault upon Miss Minnie Kendrick, in Chattooga county, on February 3, 1887, and was respited by Gov. Gordon Saturday night upon the affldavits of five repectable men that Pope was fifty miles from the scene of the crime on the day it was committed. It was known to Gov. Gordon that there was intense feeling against Pope in Chattooga County and he endeavored to keep the respite secret until Col. Towers would have had time to get to Summerville and bring the prisoner out of the County. Summerville is in the country, 25 miles from Rome, but there is a telephone line from Rome to Tryon factory. The latter place is only 5 miles from Summerville and people are passing from one place to the other often. It is very probable that in this way the news of the respite reached Summerville early in the afternoon.

HOW HE WAS SWUNG.

Sheriff Moore says it looks as though the rope was put on Pope's neck and he was then thrown off the balcony. His neck was not broken. The Sheriff was sleeping in the jail and was awakened by a demand for his keys, backed by about fifteen shotguns. There was nothing for him to do but to give them up. The crowd then took a rope and hung Pope. Miss Minnie Kendricks was going through some woods between her home and the home of a neighbor in Chattooga county Thursday, Feb. 3, 1887. In the woods she met a negro who assaulted her. When she escaped from him she gave an alarm, and the country was scoured for miles around. Several negroes were arrested and brought to Miss Kendrick, who promptly declared as each one was brought that he was not the man.

HIS CAPTURE.

On May 4, 1887, Henry Pope was arrested in Cherokee county, Alabama, and was brought to Summerville May 7. The popular indignation was so great against him that a special guard was organized for the prisoner's protection. A special term was called and held May 9, 1887, and Henry Pope was convicted and sentenced to be hanged July 1. In the court room, as in the jail, the prisoner was guarded by armed men to protect him from the people, who were infuriated against him because of the crime, which they thought he had committed. After the announcement of the verdict the Judge advised the counsel for the defendant not to make a motion for a new trial, because he was apprehensive that in that event a mob would attempt to hang Pope, and good men would be killed in an effort to defend him. The Governor, on June 28, issued an order respiting Pope till Sept. 2, 1887. On Aug. 29 a further respite was granted until Nov. 4. Pending his second respite Judge Maddox granted a new trial on an extraordinary motion. The trial took place during the first week in March, 1888. Pope was again convicted and sentenced to be hanged on May 2 (to-morrow). Gov. Gordon was again petitioned to respite Pope, and the petition was accompanied by such strong evidence to prove an alibi that a respite was granted for sixty days.

INNOCENT MAN HANGED.
Masked Georgia Lynchers Commit a Gross Outrage on Justice.
Outrage on Justice.

ATLANTA, GA., May2.—In Georgia the simple word of a sixteen-year old girl convicts a man of attempting an outrage, against the sworn testimony of numbers of Alabama's best citizens, who swear to have seen the man in Alabama on the day the crime was committed. Henry Pope, colored, was lynched by a mob of fifty masked men at Summerville, in Chattooga county, this morning, at half-past two o'clock. Pope was lynched for a crime of which there is every reason to believe him innocent. In February,1887, Miss Minnie Kendrick, a sixteen-year old girl, while going through some woods between her home and the house of a neighbor in Chattooga county, was assaulted by a colored man. Upon escaping

SHE GAVE THE ALARM.

The woods were scoured and several persons were arrested, but upon being brought face to face with each man Miss Kendrick promptly exonorated him and the search continued.

In May of the same year Henry Pope was arrested in Cherokee county, Alabama, fifty miles from the scene of the outrage. He was placed in company with twenty others, and Miss Kendrick was then asked to see if the man who assaulted her was there. She immediately singled out Henry Pope and said: "He is the man who did the deed. I remember him by his wicked and cruel eyes." Upon this testimony alone Pope was convicted and sentenced to be hanged. Against the testimony of this weak girl were the affidavits of nine men who swore that they were residents of Cherokee county, Alabama, and that Pope was at work there on the day the crime was committed. Among these were his employer, who swore that he worked for him on that day, a merchant who sold him goods on the day of the crime and numerous citizens who saw him, and who swore that he could not have got to Chattooga county if he had tried.

THE AFFIDAVITS OF THESE MEN,
Together with certificates from every county official in Cherokee county as to the high character and disinterestedness of the men who made the affidavits, were sent to Governor Gordon, who respited the prisoner three times, until further proof of his innocence could be had.

He was to be hanged to-day, but was again respited at the earnest request of every leading man in Cherokee county. Fearing trouble when the respite was known, Governor Gordon determined to move the prisoner from Chattooga county to Atlanta, Ga., and sent the Superintendent of the Penitentiary for him. He was to have been removed today. Last night fifty masked men, carrying shotguns, forced the janitor to give up the keys of the jail, secured the prisoner and hung him from the Court House banisters in Summerville, the county seat of Chattooga county. The deed is greatly deplored all over the State, as it is feared a great mistake has been made. The prisoner declared his innocence to the last.

SAVED BY A SHERIFF.

Indignant Citizens of Jackson, Mich., Prevented From Lynching a Man.

His Crime That of Brutally Maltreating an Eight-Year-Old Boy.

LANSING, Mich., Jan. 7.—A painter named Henry Wyman, who live at Jackson, was arrested here last night on a charge of committing a cruel assault on the eight-year-old son of Levi Cothington, a prominent merchant. It is charged that he coaxed the boy to take a ride with him, and when he got the lad into his sleigh, tied his feet together, covered him with a blanket and drove rapidly out into the country. He then dragged the lad into a piece of woods and compelled him to submit to an act of the most beastly nature. He then drove back. The boy told his story and Wyman was arrested. The matter became quickly noised about and threats of lynching were soon made. Deputy Sheriff Van Buren decided to have the prisoner moved to the county jail at Mason. He was taken to the North Lansing depot and put into the baggage car of the southward bound train. At the Union depot a big crowd of excited men had gathered and several forced their way into the car. Wyman was dragged into the smoking car. The indignant citizens made a charge on it, but Officer Seers, who was in the car, took in the situation at a glance and sprang to the door of the car with a revolver in his hand, while Bates guarded the other door, also with a cocked revolver, and they kept the crowd at bay until the crowd moved off. Several windows of the car were smashed. At Mason the excitement was no less intense, and when the sheriff learned that a crowd was coming from Lansing, Company F of the state troops were called on and guarded the jail all last night. There are still mutterings of trouble. Wyman asserts his innocence, and his young wife who came down today believes in him, but the Cothington boy, on his appearance in the police court, positively identified him as his assailant, and four other boys claim to have been similarly treated by him.
henry-wyman-lansing-1888-01-07.A2:
ALMOST A LYNCHING
A MOB AFTER A LANSING BRUTE.
Charged With an Indecent Crime-The Crowd Held Back at the Muzzle of a Revolver-The Prisoner in Jail at Mason.
LANSING, Mich., Jan 7.—A painter, giving his name as Henry Wyman, of Jackson, was arrested here last evening by a Deputy Sheriff on a charge of cruelly treating an 8-year-old son of Levi Cottington, of the firm of Devis & Cottington. Wyman, it is alleged, coaxed the boy to take a ride with him, and when he got the lad into his sleigh, tied his feet together, covered him with a blanket and drove rapidly out into the country, to what is known as the "Forty-acre tract," on the extension of Ottawa st. There he stopped, the boy says, tied his horse, and dragging the terribly frightened lad into the woods, and there by force compelled the boy to submit to a most brutish assault. Then he brought him home, and the boy told his horrible story.

William VanBuren, now a deputy sheriff but widely known as for many years the manager of the State printing office, arrested the man—the right one it is believed, though he protests his innocence—and as the citizens were getting terribly excited, and threatened to lynch him, it was deemed best to remove the prisoner to the county jail at Mason.

It was given out that he would be taken there by wagon, and Officer Bates started with him, but alter a round-about drive he brought up at the North Lausing depot of the Michigan Central railroad, where, in the presence of quite a crowd of excited men who had "caught on" to the ruse, he was hustled into the baggage car of the Michigan Central railroad.

The train proceeded to the Union Depot, where a large crowd of excited men were gathered, and four or five forced their way into the baggage car. The baggageman compelled Bates to take his prisoner out of that car, as he did not want a row there, and Bates dragged Wyman into the smoker. The crowd of indignant citizens made a charge upon the smoker, but Officer Seers, of Jackson, who happened to be in the car, took in the situation at a glance and sprang to the door of the car with a revolver in his hand, while Bates guarded the other door, also with a cocked revolver, and they kept the crowd at bay until the train moved off. Several windows of the car were smashed.

On arriving at Mason the prisoner was lodged in jail. Owing, however, to the state of feeling there, and an apparently well founded idea that a crowd was coming from Lausing, the Sheriff deemed it prudent to call on the State militia for assistance, and Company F, First Michigan State troops, of Mason was called out, and guarded the jail all night.

At the Police Court, in this city, where Wyman was arraigned yesterday afternoon, the Cottington boy positively identified the man as the one who committed the assault on him, and four other boys, who had been similarly treated, were equally positive. An alibi will be attempted to break down their testimony, and his young wife declares her belief in his innocence.

HOME AND FOREIGN BUDGET.
Important Facts Recorded in Concise Style.
Mexico had a sharp shock of earthquake Monday morning which was felt perceptibly through the southern portion of the State. Many walls were cracked, but no loss of life is reported.

The Law and Order League at Sioux City, Iowa, is very active, especially in prosecuting wholesale liquor houses and druggists for selling liquor to minors. Gambling houses have been closed.

A man who gives his name as John Amburger has been arrested near Wellsville, O., suspected of being the one who has stolen many horses in that vicinity.

Charles Naser, of Wall's station, on the P. R. R., aged 22, while coupling cars at Huff's station, was caught in a frog, run over by a train and instantly killed.

The extensive coal works of the Osborne Coal Company. at Salineville, O., which have been idle since June, will resume work in a few days and the indebtedness of $6,000 due employees will be paid in a short time.

Employees of Fisher's foundry, at Allentown, Pa., have a reduction of 20 per cent. in their wages.

The Etna rolling mill and nail factory at New Castle are idle, and may not start this winter.

The Baldwin & Graham stove works, at New Castle, are still idle, with no apparent prospect of resuming.

A row occurred at a christening party, at Rolander Hill, near Wilkesbarre, Pa., in which Anthony Shinisky was fatally stabbed.

The forty threshing machine manufacturers of Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin and Indiana, met at Chicago and formed a "trust." Farmers who may want threshing machines will be the victims of this trust.

The severest winter known in Austria is now prevailing and deaths from exposure are reported daily. The water supply of Vienna is failing, the ice in the Danube having reached there. The Platten Sea is frozen over for the first time in many years.

A National Congress of law and order workers is called to meet at Philadelphia, February 21 and 22 next.
Mary Kelly, aged 70 years, fell into the fire at her home near Rochester, Pa., and before assistance came she was burned to death.

Richard Darnell, a rural bully, entered the Episcopal Church at Cable, O., the other night and created a disturbance. After the pastor. Rev. J. F. Frederick, had thrice knocked him down, he retired.

The gas well drilling for the Normal School in Clarion, Pa., struck sand at 1,300 feet, with a little gas and a show of oil. The second bit in the sand started the well flowing at 20 barrels an hour, with the tools in the well. The strike was unexpected and nothing was at hand to control it.

Two more of the recently indicted Chicago boodlers—John Hogan, School Board member, and John H. Price, ex-Deputy Sheriff—have been arrested. The former gave bail, and the latter in default was committed to jail.

The mysterious death of John Parrott, a farmer, of New Holland, Ind., is causing a sensation. He was a widower, lived alone, and was known to have money about the house. He was found dead in his bed, and his head was a mass of bruises.

Asa W. Wickes, Cashier of the Central National Bank, of Troy, N, Y., is a defaulter to the amount of over $3,000. He has resigned, and the loss will be made good. Wickes was fond of poker playing, and lost heavily. He is now thought to be dying of paralysis.

At Belgrade, Mont., Saturday, the spirit thermometer registered 52° below zero.

A large deposit of bituminous coal is reported to have been discovered in Texas, a short distance northwest of San Antonio.

At Lima, Ohio, Samuel Bowman, touched a match to a can of oil which was being heated. An explosion followed, setting fire to his clothing and burning him to a crisp. His wife in attempting to put out the flames was also fatally burned. Bowman previous to lighting the match said he wanted to see the gas burn.
A novel phase of the Reading strike was developed at Ashland, Pa., where the girls employed in the several hotels and boarding houses struck against the entertainment of the new non-union men, and the proprietors had to get rid of the objectionable guests.

At Cleveland, the Rev. George Hasenpflug, a clergyman of the Evangelical Church of 28 years' standing, was deposed from the ministry for conduct unbecoming a minister and for disrespectful language regarding his bishop.

It was developed in New York that the banking firm of Swenzor & Co., have been importing Swedes under contract to work on a plantation in Louisiana.

Henry Wyman was arrested at Jackson, Mich., for a nameless crime. He was about being removed to Mason when a mob of indignant citizens stormed the train and attempted to lynch him. to W. E. Johnson.

A commissioner was selling the property of Herman Luther under an order of the court to sell and divide it with his divorced wife. The property was bid in by Luther, but he was unable to make the required deposit, and his wife succeeded in bidding in goods. Exciting Scene in Court.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., December 15.—A special to the Americana, from Jackson, Tenn., says: During the trial before Esquire Eaxm, in the tenth district of this county, yesterday, over a settlement between Tom Brown and a colored family named Hicks, Will Hicks cross-questioned Miss Fannie Brown in rather an abrupt manner, and he was told by her brother Tom to be more careful. The negro replied with an oath and knocked Brown down. Other negroes and Peter Brown, brother of Tom, joined in a general fight. Tom Brown cut one or two negroes with his knife and stabbed the mother of Will Hicks in the throat. Tom Brown and his brother were also badly hurt. At last accounts the negroes were armed. There was much excitement and danger of further trouble.

NEW ORLEANS, December 16.—A Grand Coteau special says: As near as can be ascertained, the shooting affair of yesterday was the result of a fend which had existed between members of the Higginbotham family for the last three or four years. The parties were attending the horse races when the difficulty arose. It is said thirty or more shots were fired. A young man named Beard, who acted as peacemaker, was shot and instantly killed. Two of Munroe Higginbotham's sons were shot. One died during the night, and the other is seriously wounded. Two other persons were wounded; one of them was the mother of young Beard; her wound is not serious.

Verdict of Guilty.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., December 16.—The coroner's jury to-day held an inquest on the body of Irene Hawes, found in the lake, yesterday, and returned the verdict that deceased came to her death at the hands of her father, R. R. Hawes.

National Bank Closed.

SAN FRANCISCO, December 17.—The California National Bank of San Francisco suspended payment to-day. R. P. Thomas, president, stated that the suspension was due to the irregularities of the cashier, C. H. Ramsden. The extent of the irregularities are not known but the bank has sufficient funds to insure all depositors against loss. Cashier Ramsden was suspected last week and an investigation of his books has been in progress which so far has not been sufficiently thorough for any definite statement. The bank was incorporated two years ago as a joint organization, the shares being taken by investors in this city and East. Authorized capital, $1,000,000, of which $200,000 was subscribed in coin. It is stated the irregularities are not of a criminal character, but consist principally of bad loans.

DETROIT, Mich., Dec. 19.—An uproar which speedily set all Griswold street aflame with excitement arose on the city hall steps at 12:30 Tuesday afternoon. A sale of property was in progress, being the closing deal between Herman Luther, a Prussian 58 years old, and his divorced wife, Amelia Luther. The woman had the best of the legal proceedings and Luther was wild with rage. As the wife, Paul a son, and Martha and Minnie Luther, two daughters, who sided with their mother, started to leave the steps the old Prussian drew a revolver and opened fire on the party. The first shot struck Paul in the right cheek and passed through, coming out at the neck. Martha and Minnie ran up the street after the mother, followed hotly by Luther, firing as he came.

The street was full of people, and instantly a great and excited crowd had collected. Martha crossed the street in safety and turned to enter a bank, but fell. In a second her father was almost upon her, and leveled his revolver with deliberate aim at the prostrate girl. It took him a moment to do so, and that moment saved her life.

Just as Luther pulled the trigger Henry P. Spencer, a business man, jumped upon him, threw his arm to one side, and the bullet intended for the girl found lodgment in the leg of William Bluff, another spectator.

The crowd, losing fear and caution at the same time, rushed upon Luther and strove to rend him. A pile of bricks had before been seized upon by the people, and a few well-directed ones struck the would-be murderer on the head and body.

With a cry of "String him up!" the mob fought to get to the man, and had it not been for the arrival of the sheriff, two deputies, and a wagon load of policemen the man might have ornamented a telegraph pole.

Luther was terribly pounded and kicked, and was half dead from fright when he was taken in the patrol wagon. His face was covered with blood and his gray hair and mustache matted with it.

james-w-edloe-williamsburg-1888-10-13.A4:
THE WILLIAMSBURG MOMICIDE.
Particulars of the Shooting of Edlee by Policeman Clowes.
[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]
WILLIAMSBURG, VA., October 15, 1888.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]
WILLIAMSEURG, VA., October 15, 1888.

After the shooting Saturday night about 8 o'clock of James W. Edloe by policeman A. T. Clowes the news spread like wildfire and crowds of men, women, and children could be seen hurrying to the spot. The body laid on the platform of the store for fully two hours waiting for the coroner's jury to act before it could be turned over to his family. During the time the crowd, which was almost entirely colored, continued to increase, and to prevent any violence being attempted Rev. John M. Dawson, pastor of the colored baptist church here, addressed the crowd from the platform, advising his people to refrain from all disorderly and violent acts. This in a great measure allayed the excitement. After the body had been turned over to Edloe's friends the gathering dispersed, and the coroner's jury, which was composed as follows—W. H. Braithwaite (foreman), John H. Seymore, W. P. Graves, Samuel Smith (colored), John Cary (colored), Lewis Carr (colored)—assembled at the Mayor's office, and after hearing several witnesses returned the following verdict: That James W. Edloe came to his death from a pistol held and fired by A. T. Clowes, a policeman in the city of Williamsburg. Clowes fired as Edloe assembled the store platform, falling face foremost, and was dead in three minutes, the ball entering on the right side of the head about an inch above the ear and lodging in the brain. The preliminary trial takes place to-morrow (Tuesday) before Mayor T. M. Southal. The prisoner is confined in the city jail and will be represented by Robert T. Armistead, Esq., and the Commonwealth by O. C. Peachy and two others, whose names are not known. The funeral of Edloe came off at 2 o'clock to-day and was attended by an immense number of colored people, many being from the counties of York and James City.

Edloe was a man of about thirty-eight years of age, a mulatto, and of fair education. He was well known in the political world as a prominent Mahone politician, and at the time of his death was deputy treasurer under Rev. John M. Dawson for Williamsburg and James City county. The shooting is universally regretted. It is generally admitted, and will no doubt be proved at the trial, that it was a case of justifiable homicide.

THE WILLIAMSBURG HOMICIDE.
The Preliminary Examination-A Large Crowd Present. [Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
WILLIAMPORT VA. October 16

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

WILLIAMSBURG, VA., October 16.—At 1:20 o'clock P. M. to day a large crowd gathered at the court-house to witness the preliminary examination in the case of the killing of Edloe Saturday night by Policeman Clowes, the colored population predominating, but a good many whites were on hand. Justice R. T. Casey conducted the examination. It seems that on the night of the killing and a short time before a difficulty took place between Clowes and Edloe; the following being the circumstance as given the writer:

Edloe was engaged in a quarrel with one Eli Parker (colored), during which Clowes, as policeman, interfered, telling Edloe that if he did not behave he would arrest him, when Edloe turned on Clowes with the remark that he did not have the nerve, and if he attempted it he would blow his d—d brains out. Edloe asked him why he did not stop a difficulty that occurred a few nights before in his presence, which Clowes denied knowing anything of at the time of the occurrence. Edloe told Clowes he was a d—d liar and had made no arrest because the party was a Democrat. Clowes again denying this Edloe called him a renegade and a d—d lying —, and told him he did not have courage to take it up, Clowes knocked him down with a stick. A bystander remarked "Kill him!" and Clowes replied, "I am too much of a man to hit a man on the ground." He then assisted Edloe to rise. Edloe then left the store, saying "I will kill you before morning." He then passed up the street remarking, as testified to by J. C. Maupin, a Commonwealth's witness: "D—n him, he drew my blood and I will have his." In a short time a crowd of colored people came down the street asking, "Where is Clowes? He hit Edloe." Maupin stopped them and advised them to return home, as they might get into trouble. Soon after Edloe came down the street with a pistol in each hand, saying: "I will kill him before morning." Maupin stopped him, and soon after Southal, the mayor, came up and said: "Edloe, give me those pistols." Edloe replied: "I'll be d—d if I give them to any one. I mean to kill the ____." The Mayor then said: "I demand those pistols or I will have you arrested." Edloe then gave them up and went in the direction of Casey's store, and as he ascended the platform on which Clowes was standing he was shot. Clowes had been told that Edloe had a pistol in each hand and was coming down the street after him, and he knew nothing about his being disarmed by the Mayor up the street. At 7 o'clock the examination was still going on, with a large crowd present. At present the prisoner is represented by R. T. Armistead; Sydney Smith, of this place, and J. F. Hubbard, of Yorktown; the Commonwealth by A. C. Peachy and Cyrus A. Branch. All the evidence is taken down in writing.

At 9:40 o'clock the examination was continued until 10 o'clock to-morrow morning. Edgar Allan has been employed to assist in the prosecution.

LONDON, October 27.—The Sackville letter incident has caused considerable stir in diplomatic circles. Mr. Phelps, the United States Minister, has gone to Hatfield House, Lord Salisbury's country residence in Hertfordshire, to see Lord Salisbury. WASHINGTON, D. C., October 27.—In reply to an inquiry as to what steps have been taken by this Government in regard to the letter of the British Minister. Secretary

[By Anglo-American cable to the Dispatch.]

London, October 27.—The officials at the United States Legation are extremely reticent on the subject of the Saekville affair. Mr. White, first secretary of the legation, when questioned about the affair declined to talk.

SACKVILLE REGRETS.

London, October 27.—Lord Salisbury today received several cable dispatches from Lord Saekville, British Minister at Washington, admitting the facts in connection with the Murchison letter and saying that he regretted them. A number of dispatches from Secretary-of-State Bayard were forwarded to Lord Salisbury, in which the Secretary of State urged that in view of the coming national election in the United States it was imperatively necessary that there should be a change in the British representative at Washington in order to calm popular excitement.

Minister Phelps and Lord Salisbury have had a long consultation. Phelps enlisted upon the necessity of prompt action on the part of the British Government in order to repair the evil. Brutal Murder of a Colored Woman. COLUMBIA, S. C., Nov. 22.—While Jeff Davis and his wife (colored) were returning from church in Lake City, Williamsburg county, they were met by Merritt Ferrett, Belle Gray, and Alex Smiley, all white, who were under the influence of whiskey. The three white men had a grudge against Jeff Davis's son, whom they began to beat, and drew knives on him. To protect her son, Jeff's wife took up a piece of fence rail and started toward the white men. Then they turned on her and stabbed her in the breast and heart eight or ten times, causing instant death. The murderers are at large, and no offorts are being made to bring them to justice. The negroes are wild with excitement in that neighborhood, and unless something is done to bring the murderers to justice serious results may follow. Pleuro-pneumonia in Orange County.
MIDDLETOWN, Nov. 22.—Pleuro-pneumonia of a malignant and contagious form made its appearance a few days ago in a herd of cows belonging to Farmer Joseph Earl of Monroe, this county. The Bureau of Animal Industry at Washington was immediately notified, and Inspector Walworth was detailed to come on here, and by his orders the entire herd of fourteen cows was killed. The stables and pastures occupied by the cattle were disinfected, and a strict quarantine of the premises for four months has been established. None of the neighboring cattle has as yet shown symptoms of infection. How it originated on Mr. Earl's farm is a mystery, for he has brought no strange cattle on his premises during the last four years. It is suggested that the contagion might have been communicated to his herd by diseased cattle passing by on Erie Railroad stock trains. Mr. Earl's place is surrounded by milk-producing farms heavily stocked with cattle.

And a Mob Pursued, Killing the Negro and Returning the Girl to Her Home.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., July 13.—[Special.]—A special from Pell City tonight says that Maude Broyles, the sixteen-year-old daughter of John Broyles, a well-to-do farmer, eloped yesterday with Jim Torney, a negro laborer, employed on her father's farm. As soon as the affair was made public, a crowd of white men started in search of the eloping pair. They were overtaken on Trout creek mountain, near Greenport, and the girl turned and fought her captors with the fury of a tigress. In the excitement the negro was allowed to escape, but several of the party followed on after him, and it is believed he was captured and killed, and his body thrown into the Coosa river. The girl was returned to her parents.

No Fourth of July Celebration.

This year Lancaster has made little

No Fourth of July Celebration.

This year Lancaster has made little or no preparations to celebrate the Fourth of July, and it is likely that the day will be dull enough to drive many of our citizens away. It seems rather strange that Lancaster cannot get up any kind of a celebration when Columbia and other smaller towns do so well. Last year a fine display of fireworks was given in McGrann's park and thousands of people were delighted. The money for this purpose was raised by private subscription, and there is no reason why a sufficient sum for a similar purpose could not again be raised. A gentleman of this city tried his hand at collecting a few days ago, but he gave it up in disgust in a short time.

Queer Doings at the Prison.

Isaac Lorah, who was elected a watchman at the prison in the spring, was asked to resign about two months ago because he slept while on duty. Benj. Brubaker, of Florin, was elected to take his place, but he failed to report at the prison for duty. Today a special meeting was held to fill the place. Brubaker was present and asked to be given until Monday when he would be ready for duty. This they would not agree to, and they said they would rather elect another man. Finally Brubaker agreed to go on to-night. Lorah, who is a son-in-law of Inspector Eshleman, has been on duty since Brubaker was first elected. The latter is Eshleman's brother-in-law.
john-bower-bowen.A2:
Escape from Lynchers.
UNION BRIDGE, Md., June 15.—John Bowans, colored, was taken from the jail here a little after one o'clock this morning by a band of 12 or 15 colored men, all masked, and carried to the outskirts of the town, where he was strung up by the neck to the limb of a large oak tree. He motioned to be let down, and the rope was slackened so that he could speak. He made good use of the opportunity, and slipping through the rope jumped away like a shot. The lynchers gave chase and fired several shots after him, but without effect. He has not yet been captured. Bowans was arrested yesterday for assaulting another colored man named Othia and a colored girl named Hollenberry. The motive was jealousy. The girl and Othia, who is blind, were on their way home night before last from this place, when they were overtaken by Bowans, who asked the girl to go with him. She refused and he then struck her in the face, breaking her jaw-bone. Othia then tried to defend her, but being blind could do but little. Bowans slashed him terribly all over his face and body with a razor. He also assaulted the girl, almost severing her ears. Both are very low, and Othia is not expected to live. Bowans is the colored man who made an assault upon Miss Taylor, of this place, about sixteen months ago, and served a year in the penitentiary for the offense.
john-bower-bowen.A5:
But a Close Call—Arrest of a Colored Desperado—Taken from the Lock-Up by Colored Men Who Attempt to Lynch Him—He Escapes After the Rope is Around His Neck.

On Wednesday night last, John Bowens, colored, made an assault upon a blind man named Otho Jones and Ida Milbury, both colored, who were on their way home from Union Bridge to Muttontown. Bowens wanted the woman to go with him, but she refused. Bowens then assaulted her with a razor, nearly severing both cars. Jones interfered, but being blind could not see what he was doing, and Bowens gashed him in numerous places with the razor. The woman's jaw was broken, and Jones received nine cuts on the face and body. Both are reported to be in a critical condition.

On Thursday Bowens came to this city and returned to Union Bridge by the 8.20 p. m. train. Upon its arrival he was arrested and placed in the lockup.

About one o'clock on yesterday (Friday) morning a crowd of colored men broke into the lockup, took Bowens and started out of Union Bridge for the purpose of lynching him. They had everything in readiness and upon reaching a tree the noose was placed around his neck and they attempted to draw him up when the rope was found to be too short. Bowens was released, though closely guarded, and his captors were engaged in lengthening the rope, when he made a sudden leap and escaped.

Bowens has the reputation of being a desperate character, and has served one term in the penitentiary and has also been in the House of Correction.

A rumor prevailed that Bowens was hung and that after the deed the men became frightened, cut the body down and buried it.

Another rumor says that Bowens took to the woods, is thoroughly armed, and will not be taken without a desperate resistance.
