john-bower-bowen.A12:
JUDGE LYNCH FOOLED.
A Masked Party Let a Coon Slip Through Their Fingers
After Stringing Him Up to the Limb of a Tree.
A Twelve-Year Old Boy Murders a Younger Playmate.
A Jealous Husband Kills His Wife and the Hired Man.
UNION BRIDGE, Md., June 15.—John Bowans, colored, was taken from the jail here a little after 1 o'clock this morning by a band of twelve or fifteen colored men, all masked, and carried up to the outskirts of the town, where he was strung up by the neck to the limb of a large oak tree. He motioned to be let down and the rope was slackened so that he could speak. He made good use of the opportunity, and, slipping through the rope jumped away like a shot. The lynchers gave chase and fired several shots after him, but without effect. He has not yet been recaptured. Bowans was arrested yesterday for assaulting another colored man named Othea and a colored girl named Hollenberry. The motive was jealousy. The girl and Othea, who is blind, were on their way home night before last from this place when they were overtaken by Bowans who asked the girl to go with him. She refused and he then struck her in the face, breaking her jaw bone. Othea tried to defend her but being blind could do but little. Bowans slashed him terribly all over his face and body with a razor. He assaulted the girl almost severing her ears. Both are very low and Othea is not expected to live. Bowans is the colored man who made an assault upon Miss Tyler of this place about sixteen months ago.
john-bower-bowen.A19: Bowen, the colored desperado that made a savage attack on a colored man and woman in the vicinity of Union Bridge and narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of colored citizens, has been captured and placed in jail at Westminster,
john-bower-bowen.A21:
JOHN BOWEN CAPTURED.
A Long and Tiresome Chase-An Interview With Him-What He Says of the Attempted Lynching.
A Long and Tiresome Chase—An Interview With Him—What He Says of the Attempted Lynching.

The Westminster correspondent of the Baltimore Sun, under date of June 24, says:

Deputy sheriff Tyler arrived on the 5 p. m. train yesterday, having in custody John Bowen, colored, who escaped from a lynching party at Union Bridge, Carroll county, on June 15. He was met in Union Bridge by Israel Zeiber, a former deputy sheriff, of this place, who returned with them to Westminster. The news of Bowen's capture spread rapidly, and quite a crowd gathered at the depot here. There was no excitement and no demonstration of any kind. Bowen was taken to the jail in a closed carriage and placed in charge of the sheriff. Deputy Tyler has been in search of him since Thursday, and followed him from Emmitsburg to Greencastle, Pa., and captured him yesterday morning sitting on a fence near that place. Bowen offered no resistance, but asked protection. While passing through Union Bridge very few persons knew of the arrest, and there were not many at the depot. Everything is quiet and no excitement whatever. Bowen is charged with brutally assaulting a colored woman and blind colored man.

He is about five feet eight inches in height, medium dark, with high receding forehead, prominent lower jaw and thick lips, and wears a constant smile on his countenance. He is said to be a man of considerable courage, but had some dread of passing through Union Bridge, where he thought a crowd might attack him while he was handcuffed and defenseless. He appears to be greatly relieved now that he is in the custody of the sheriff and has the thick walls of the jail around him. His counsel, Mr. I. E. Pearson, found it hard to convince him that there was danger to him in his giving bail and going at large. "Why," said he, "they cannot hang me after I give bail, can they? There is no law for that." "Yes," replied his counsel, "they might hang you without any law." "Oh, no," said Bowen, "they can't hang me without law." He evidently thought that the hanging at Union Bridge was by authority of the law.

In an interview held with Bowen to-day he made the following statement: "I was in Westminster on Thursday, the 14th, to consult Mr. I. E. Pearson who, advised me to go back to Union Bridge and give bail. I did so, and went back on the 8.20 p. m., train and went direct to Mr. Calvin Wentz's saloon to get him to go my bail. While there Constable Repp with a crowd came down and with drawn pistols arrested me. I never resisted an officer, and would never do so. I was always anxious to give myself up if I would be protected, but after my first arrest the officers took so little pains to save me from the mob that I considered my life would be endangered if I surrendered to the officers. Constable Repp put me in the lock-up. About one o'clock that night I heard the mob at the door, and was terribly frightened. Old man Milbury, father of the girl, had a rope. There were two or three 'coons' and a large crowd of whites. I recognized all, and can give their names. They said they were going to hang me. I said: 'Men, this is cowardly—give me a chance; I am an innocent man,' but they would not listen. They put a rope around my neck and choked me so I could hardly breathe. Milbury called out to the crowd, 'Are you all ready out there?' and a voice I recognized replied, 'Yes, bring him out.' None of the crowd at first wore masks, but afterwards some of them put handkerchiefs over their faces, so the people of the town could not recognize them. I resisted all I could, but they had the rope around my neck and were too many for me. They put me in a wagon and took me out to the tree. I struggled and begged all the time, but to no avail. All the way I could hear the men swearing at me and urging those in charge of me to hurry up. When they reached the tree, which stands in a field belonging to Mr. Granville Haines, near the town, most of the crowd drew back a few steps and stood on one side. Two or three others threw the rope over a limb. While they were getting ready they forgot in their hurry to tie my hands, and as they prepared to draw me up I slipped my thumbs under the hoose, and quick as a flash darted away from them, taking the crowd entirely by surprise. They never had me off my feet at all, and the story that I asked time to pray was not true. I could tell from the manner and conversation of the men that they were in dead earnest, and would not give me time for anything, and would never have let me down after once drawing me up. They were all greatly excited. There is a great feeling of spite against me in Union Bridge by some people, and they urged the men who had me in charge to hurry up the job. They made a mistake in not tying my hands, but I suppose they were so much excited they forgot to do it. It is all a lie about my talking to people and making threats of burning the town and killing people. I am not revengeful, and don't want to be revenged; only if I am to be punished for breaking the law, the Union Bridge people ought to be treated the same way. They tried to kill me, and I did not hurt any of them, and they are guiltier than I would be even if I had done what they accuse me of doing."

Bowen gave his counsel the names of the people who, he says, tried to lynch him, but refuses to make them public and says he does not want them punished. He says they were excited and he does not believe they would harm him after their anger cools off a little. He persistently denies having assaulted Ida Milbury and her blind companion, Jones, both of whom have recovered.
john-bower-bowen.A22:
Escaped the Lynchers-Not a Jury Baltimore Sun Special. WESTMINSTER MR. DEC. 4. The cause
WESTMINSTER, M.D., Dec. 4.—The case of the state against John Bowen, colored, for assault with intent to kill Charles Jones, and Ida Milberry, both colored, was finished to-day. The jury, after being out five hours, returned a verdict of guilty on both charges. Bowen, it will be remembered, assaulted a colored girl, Ida Milberry, and her companion, Jones, a blind man, at Union Bridge, and severely beat them both. The attack was of such a character that much indignation was excited against Bowen, who was taken from the lockup and an attempt made to lynch him. He escaped from his captors and wandered about the country for some days before he was apprehended and lodged in Westminstsr jail.

mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A1:
EXCITEMENT IN SAVANNAH.
A NEGRO RIOT QUELLED AFTER SOME SERIOUS FIGHTING.
Three White Men Dying and Several Negroes Killed and Hurt-Frantic Colored Women in the Mob-Whislakey Caused It
Three White Men Dying and Several Negroes Killed and Hurt—Frantic Colored Women in the Mob—Whiskey Caused It.

SAVANNAH, Nov. 29.—Two policemen and a white man at the point of death, one negro dead, one negro dying, and other negroes wounded, are the casualties resulting from a riot in a negro quarter of Savannah at noon today. Whiskey was the cause of the uprising. A crowd of drunken negro men and women were getting into a free fight among themselves when Policeman McMurray ordered them to disperse. A negro jerked the officer's club out of his hand and began raining blows on his head with it. The bluecoat thereupon shot his assailant, and when the latter ran pursued him down the street, firing the other bullets in his revolver at him. The negro fell mortally wounded.

The shooting brought several hundred negroes to the scene, and, when the policeman's last cartridge had been fired, they attacked him in a body with clubs, brickbats, and every other implement and missile at hand. He was knocked down three times, but finally ran into a house and barred the doors and windows. With the ferocity of savages, the negroes now cried for the life of every white man in sight.

They tore off the blinds of the house in which McMurray had sought safety, smashed in the windows, battered down the doors, and swarming into the interior, reduced him to insensibility, and then threw him into the middle of the street, where frenzied men and women wreaked additional vengeance on his inanimate body, and finally left him for dead. His skull is fractured, and he is supposed to have suffered internal injuries.

Policeman Cronan heard the shooting and started to learn the cause, but was stopped by the mob before he got within two blocks of the scene of the McMurray tragedy. He suffered a fate similar to that of his brother policeman. It is believed that his jaw is fractured in addition to his other injuries. His life is also hanging in the balance.

A laborer named Crimmins pluckily rushed to Cronan's rescue, but he, too, was soon lying insensible, covered with bruises and blood, in the street. About this time a squad of police rushed to the scene in answer to a general alarm from headquarters and the mob, 2,000 to 3,000 strong, scattered like sheep.

The negro shot by McMurray died at 5 o'clock this afternoon. The negro who is dying has a bullet in his head. All the wounded negroes were hustled away by their friends before the police squad arrived. Eight arrests have already been made, and more are to follow. Four of the prisoners are women, one of whom smashed in McMurray's face with a stone as he lay insensible after the crowd had left him.

The reserve police are on duty to-night, and a further attempt at rioting could not succeed. At 10 o'clock to-night a murder in which a negress was killed by her paramour occurred near the scene of the riot. The negroes are drunk and in an ugly mood, and that part of the city is dangerous.
mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A3:
A RIOT IN SAVANNAH. One Negro Killed and Several Police-men Severely Injured. SAVANNAH, Ga., Nov. 29.—An attempt by the police to quell a disturbance among a crowd of disorderly negroes in the western part of the city this afternoon resulted in a riot, during which one negro was killed, two policemen and a white man, who went to their aid, seriously injured, and several negroes wounded. Patrolman McMurray, in dispersing the crowd, was set upon and knocked down. The crowd closed in upon him, but he got up, and, finding his club useless, drew a revolver and began firing. Other officers heard the shooting and hastened to the place. Patrolman Cronin was knocked down and his skull broken. McMurray was driven three or four blocks down the street and escaped into a house, but the crowd broke through the windows and threw him into the street, where the negro women beat him with bricks until insensible. The police were notified at headquarters, and a squad of mounted officers soon arrived. By this time 1,000 negroes were in the street, yelling and crying, "Kill them, Kill them." The police held the crowd back, and eight of the ring leaders were arrested. The crowd was finally dispersed. To-night a negro with seven bullet wounds in his body was found dead in the part of the city where the shooting occurred. FOUND AT LAST. A Man Arrested For a Murder Committed Years Ago. LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Nov. 28—Ten years ago A. J. Simmons became involved in a controversy with one Higdon, in Jefferson county, Alabama. They made up, however, and separated. Two days afterwards, at church, Simmons, it is alleged, called Higdon out into the dark, and without provocation or warning, stabbed him to death. He fed to Baxter county, this state, took the name of A. J. Morrow, married an estimable girl and settled down to the life of an exemplary citizen. Several children came into the household. The neighbors held him in high esteem and no shadow of the old crime ever fell across the threshold. The family of the murdered man, however, never abandoned their search for him, and a few days ago an Albany sheeuft arrived here with a requisition for Simmons, alias Morrow. It was duly honored by Governor Hughes, and news reached the city to-day that the criminal had been arrested and carried back to the scene of the murder. He claims that he can prove his innocence on a plea of self-defence and cheered his wife and family with a statement that he would be home again within three weeks. Leprosy Among the Indians.
Leprosy Among the Indians.

Ottawa, Nov. 29.—Word has been received that the Chinese lepers in British Columbia have communicated their terrible malady to the Indians, who, in that province, number 50,000. Senator McInnes, M. D., from British Columbia, states that out of the total Indian population of the province, which he placed at 40,000, he believes that there will not be 5,000 living in a quarter of a century as a result of the leprosy. The Columbia authorities have for several years been officially informed of the presence of the Chinese lepers, but took little or no action against them, fearing that the agitation of the subject would turn away the tide of emigration coming from Europe.

A Mysterious Shooting.

New Haven, Conn., Nov. 29.—Shortly after 5 o'clock this afternoon, people passing along Orchard street, near Henry Donovan's saloon, heard two pistol shots in quick succession, and they rushed to the spot just in time to see John B. King, a young law student in Prentice Chase's office, fall to the sidewalk dead. A man was seen to run up the street, but he disappeared before anyone could stop him. The saloon proprietor denies all knowledge of the affair, and states that there was no row in his place. The affair is very mysterious, and up to 11 o'clock no very satisfactory explanation of the shooting had been obtained, nor a clue to the identity of the murderer.

He Fooled With Dynamite.

He Fooled With Dynamite.

CLEVELAND, O., Nov. 29.—At Sandusky, O., to-day Albert Walker attempted to throw out some dynamite, when the compound exploded, tearing off his arms and inflicting other injuries, from the effects of which he died in a short time.

An Elevator Burned.

CASSELTON, Dak., Nov. 29.—The elevator at Greene's siding, on the Northern Pacific railroad, was destroyed by fire to-day, entailing a loss of $50,000.

Death of a Well Known Horseman.

TORONTO, Ont., Nov. 29.—W. E. Owens, the well known horse trainer, died to-day of inflammation of the lungs, after two days' illness. His name was a familiar one on every race course in America.

The New York Graphic Sold.

NEW YORK, Nov. 29.—The Graphic was purchased by Henry Stoddard yesterday on behalf of a syndicate. He will make it republican. Stoddard is supposed to represent the national committee.

Chiefs Arthur and Sargent.

NEW YORK, Nov. 29.—Chief P. M. Artnur, of the Locomotive brotherhood, left this morning for the west. Grand Chief Sargent, of the locomotive firemen, followed this afternoon. Their destination is unknown.

A Pickpocket.

C. H. Pease is charged with stealing a watch from Mr. Martane, while the latter was sitting in a saloon on Tenth street. He was arrested by Officer Bloom yesterday.
mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A5:
BEATEN BY A MAD MOB.
ONE THOUSAND NEGROES RUN RIOT IN YAMACRAW.
Policemen McMurray and Cronin Beaten into Insensibility—One of the Rioters Shot and Dies from His Wounds—Others Supposed to be Wounded—How the Trouble Started—Policeman Quinn's Wife Holds the Mob at Bay with a Pistol—Eight of the Rioters Arrested.

"Kill the —— —— when he ain't thinking." That was the fate intended for Patrolman Pat McMurray in yesterday's riot in Yamacraw.

Patrolman Daniel J. Cronin and John Crimmens, an employee of the Southern Vulcanite Pavement Company, it was thought, were mortally wounded. Mike Tillman, one of the negro rioters, died last night with eight bullet wounds in his body. Several other rioters were wounded, but they escaped.

The riot started a few minutes before noon on Farm street in the vicinity of Orange.

THE START OF THE RIOT.

Policeman McMurray had arrested a negro, and was starting with him to the barracks when he was set upon by a crowd of the negro's friends. His club was wrenched from him and he was knocked down. The negro whom he had arrested stood over him and was about to strike the officer over the head with his own club, when McMurray drew his revolver and fired.

The negro turned at the shot and ran, and McMurray broke through the crowd and pursued him, firing. At Orange street the negro attempted to escape into a house, but the door was shut against him, and he was captured on the steps. He was badly wounded, exclaiming, "I'm dying!" and dropped to the sidewalk.

IN THE MOB'S HANDS.

McMurray left him and started back down Farm street, where he met a mob of several hundred negroes, armed with clubs and rocks, hooting and yelling "Kill him, kill him!" Before he had time to defend himself he was knocked down. Struggling to his feet he fought his way through the mob and took refuge in a house between Bay street and Cooper Shop lane, kept by Pearl Prendergast.

By this time Farm and the adjoining streets were filled with an excited mob shouting, "drag him out," "kill him." McMurray was unarmed. Nothing but empty cartridges were in his revolver. His club had been wrenched from him and bleeding from his wounds he was unable to fight.

DRAGGED INTO THE STREET.

The mob broke in the windows and half a dozen infuriated negro women seized the wounded officer by the throat and dragged him into the street. Joe Cotton, one of the leaders of the mob, grabbed a rock and yelling, "Kill the —— —— when he aint thinking," and struck the already unconscious man a murderous blow on the head.

Patrolman Tom F. Quinn, of the Ocean Steamship police, who lives on Bay street, near Farm, was awakened by the shouts of the rioters, and, seizing his pistol, he hurried into the street. The mob soon saw him coming and shouted "Kill him," but the officer kept them back with his pistol. "We want justice!" "He killed the man for nothing!" "Kill him! Kill him!" the crowd kept shouting.

DROVE BACK THE CROWD.

Quinn drove the mob back from the house where McMurray was. Hearing the noise inside, he hurried to a gate leading to a lane back of the house, where he was met by one of the inmates, who said that McMurray was safe. Turning back, he went to the front of the house again. McMurray was lying on the ground insensible. By his side Mrs. Quinn stood with a revolver in her hand holding the mob at bay. While she kept them back, her husband and Joseph Mack carried the unconscious officer to Quinn's house. Mrs. Quinn stood guard over the wounded man until the ambulance arrived, and he was taken to the hospital.

PATROLMAN CRONIN SURROUNDED.

While McMurray was fighting the mob on Farm street, Patrolman Cronin, who was hurrying to his assistance, was surrounded on Orange street. He was patroiling Bryan street when the riot began. In crossing Montgomery street he heard the shots. Hurrying to West Broad, he ran down Orange street, and it was there, lying in the middle of the street, that he was afterward found. John Kline, a tailor for Charles Gassman, and his daughter were standing on the stoop at Kline's house, No. 21 Orange street, when Cronin came down the street. Kline's story is that the officer ran down Orange street and met a negro boy who was running away from the riot. Somebody told the officer to arrest the boy, and he did so. Later a negro passed and told the officer that he had the wrong man, and Cronin released him, but afterward rearrested him and started to the barracks, when a crowd of negroes surrounded him. The crowd pressed on the officer, and tried to take the boy from him.

HIS PISTOL TAKEN FROM HIM.

Cronin drew his revolver, but it was wrenched from him and fell to the ground. As soon as the mob saw that he was unable to defend himself they closed in upon him, and beat him until he was unconscious. When they had left him a negro woman rushed to the middle of the street where the officer was lying, and struck him several blows on the head with a brick.

During the excitement John Crimmens, employed by the Vulcanite Paving Company, ran up to assist the officer. He made his way through the crowd to where Cronin was, and seizing the officer's club succeeded by well-directed blows in driving some of the infuriated negroes back, not, however, until he had been severely beaten and cut. Crimmens was afterward picked up by the ambulance and taken, with McMurray, to St. Joseph's Infirmary.

CRIMMENS' WOUNDS.

He had a ghastly wound over one eye, and three long deep gashes on his head. He was stabbed in the back, one of the fingers of his right hand was broken, and it is thought that his chin is fractured. Crimmens seemed to rest easy after his wounds had been dressed. He said that as he was passing Orange street on his way to a barber shop he heard the patrolman's cries for help, and ran to where the difficulty was going on. Just as he reached there the mob knocked the pistol out of Cronin's hands and would have shot him had he not beat them back with a club. He drove the crowd back, so that they were unable to get the pistol which he thought had dropped to the ground, until he was knocked down from behind.
mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A6:
five minutes after the information reached the barracks, the ambulance and mounted officers were at the scene of the trouble. Chief Green and Sergt. Linng arrived shortly after with a mounted squad and the rioters were dispersed. They hung about the lanes, and in the dives all the afternoon, but the streets were kept clear. A squad of officers was kept in readiness in case of an outbreak, but by 10 o'clock last night everything was quiet, and the police do not fear any further trouble.

M'MURRAY'S STATEMENT.

As soon as the ambulance arrived, 'McMurray was taken to St. Joseph's Infirmary, where Drs. Dunn and Brunner dressed his wounds. The wounded officer was seen by a MORNING NEWS reporter last night. He said that he was on Farm street a few minutes before 12 o'clock. As he passed Pine street he met a large crowd of negroes, and ordered them to get off the sidewalk and they did so. He went on farther toward New street, and had gone but a short distance when he met a couple of negroes. One of them remarked that he was going to have the other arrested, and called to the officer. The other replied: "—— the officer." McMurray turned and arrested him. He was quickly surrounded. One of the crowd shouted: "—— you, I will kill you." The negro caught hold of the officer's club, and, wrenching it from him, struck him over the head with it twice. McMurray drew his revolver and the negro caught it and tried to strike him again with his club. McMurray succeeded in wrenching the pistol from him and began shooting. The negro ran down Farm toward Orange, and the officer pursued him, firing as he ran. Running up on a stoop near the corner of Farm and Orange streets, the negro tried to push open the door of the house, but it was closed against him.

RUN DOWN AND CAPTURED.

McMurray followed him up the steps and arrested him. In going down the steps to the sidewalk the negro fell and said: "I am dying." McMurray left him there and went back up the street, where the fracas began, to get his helmet. Before he had gone far he was attacked by a mob of 300 or 400 men and women, armed with sticks, rocks and clubs. The men were cursing and the women were screaming at the top of their voices: "Kill the —— rascal." Before he had time to defend himself he was set upon by the mob and was knocked down. Regaining his feet he ran into a house kept by Pearl Prendergast. The mob followed him, and, being refused admittance, they broke in the windows and doors, and entering began clubbing him again. He was thrown into the street, where he was beaten until he was insensible.

Policeman Lysaught, of the Ocean Steamship force, was in a barber shop on Bay street being shaved when he heard the shooting. Picking up his coat, belt and pistol, he hurried to Farm street. As he passed Quinn's house he saw McMurray lying on the floor. The street was filled with an excited crowd, shouting "Go for him, "kill him."

Patrolman Sweeny of the Ocean steamship force arrived soon afterward and arrested William Hamilton, one of the leaders of the mob.

M'MURRAY'S PROTECTOR.

The Prendergast woman, into whose house McMurray ran, said tnat she heard the firing, but she thought it was firecrackers. She opened the front door to look out, and had hardly got the door open before McMurray came running up on the stoop all covered with blood, crying: "Save me, save me," and rushed into the house in a stooping posture. She shut and locked the door, but by this time the mob had got to the house and had broken in the door. They swarmed over the fence into the back yard. She stood in front of the door with her dress covering McMurray and confronted the mob when the door was burst in. Seizing hold of her they hurled her through a window sash at the side of the room, at the same time beating her over the head. McMurray attempted to get out the back door, but he was stopped by a crowd of women who had scaled the fence. One of them seized an axe in the yard, and struck him with the flat side, felling him to the floor. He was then dragged into the street.

BRINGING IN THE RIOTERS.

Chief Fernandez of the fire department was among the first to reach the scene of the riot and succeeded in arresting one of the ringleaders. The negro was crouched in a chimney corner under a hut. The chief crawled under the house and pulled him out. Officer Stegins, while hunting for some of the instigators of the affray, met a young negro who told him that he knew one of the parties implicated in it. The officer started with the negro to an out of the way place where, in all probability, he would have suffered as the other officers had when a white boy whispered to him that the negro was one of the rioters himself, and that he saw him when he struck Officer Cronin. Stegins arrested the negro and carried both the prisoner and the white boy to the barracks. The name of the boy was taken and he was summoned as a witness against the negro this morning.

DIED FROM HIS WOUNDS.

Mike Tillman, the negro whom McMurray is supposed to have shot, was carried out to the home of his mother, on Lumber street, near Little Jones street, and Dr. B. F. Sheftall was summoned. The physician found eight bullet holes in the lower part of his abdomen and thighs. It is likely that the balls passed through the body. The wounds were dressed, but Tillman died in a short time. Coroner Dixon was notified, but owing to his inability to secure witnesses last night tha inquest was postponed until this morning.

EIGHT OF THE RIOTERS ARRESTED.

The police had arrested eight of the rioters up to last night, and are on the track of others. It is believed that several of the leaders are wounded, but that they are kept in hiding. At midnight Farm street was as quiet as the Bay. Officer McMurray was resting quietly at the infirmary. The last report from Cronin was favorable. McMurrey was considered a brave officer. He is about 25 years old. and was transferred from the Ocean Steamship force a short time ago. He was formerly a member of the Savannah, Florida &
mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A7:
RIOT IN SAVANNAH.
An Attempt to Arrest a Drunken Negro is Resisted by a Vigorous Attack.

SAVANNAH, Ga. Nov. 30.—[Special.]—A riot started at noon in Yamacraw. Policeman McMurray attempted to arrest a Drunken negro, when a crowd resisted the officer and attacked him.

He drew his revolver and shot into the mob, and is said to have killed one and wounded another.

The officer called Policeman Crohan to his assistance.

The negroes surrounded the policemen with knives, rocks and pistols and wounded them terribly.

A longshoreman, named Maher, was also brutally hammered and cut.

McMurray sought refuge in a neighboring house, which was broken open by the rioters, and McMurray was dragged out and beaten and cut about the head and back.

The wounded men were taken off in an ambulance, and may recover.

It is not known yet how far their injuries extend.

Only one arrest was made, that of an old negro who gave his name as Joe Carter.

Crohan killed a negro in arresting him four months ago, and the negroes had him marked for slaughter.
mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A8:
TWENTY-SIX IN JAIL.
NINETEEN YAMACRAW RIOTERS DISPOSED OF.
Two Held for Assault with Intent to Murder—Seven Arrests Yesterday and Half a Dozen More Last Night—The Coroner's Investigation of Mike Tillman's Death—The Jury's Verdict—Condition of the Wounded—McMurray and Cronin Improving—Crimmins Getting Better—A Fund for Officer Quinn's Wife.

Twenty-six of the Yamacraw rioters had been arrested up to last night. Nineteen were before the police court yesterday morning.

Joe Cotton, who was one of the first arrested, and Robert Berrien, Dan Henderson and Henry Campbell were held to await the result of Patrolman McMurray's injuries. Henry Williams and Robert Lewis were remanded for trial for assault with intent to murder. Edward Fraser, William Phillips, Esta Watts Samuel Johnson and Simpson Gordon were held for a further hearing. The four negro woman—Lizzie Gibbons, Maggie Ross, Lucy Palett and the woman known as "Texas Blue" were fined $100 each. Thomas Maxwell was remanded for trial for assault and battery, and James Hamlet was fined $25.
SEVEN MORE ARRESTED.

The seven who were arrested yesterday, and half a dozen more, who were picked up last night will be given a hearing this morning.

The evidence against Lewis and Williams, who were held for assault with intent to murder, was strong. Not one of the prisoners admitted having been concerned in the riot. Pearl Prendergast, the woman in whose house Patrolman McMurray took shelter from the mob, was the principal witness. She identified several of the prisoners who were in the mob when it broke into her house. Williams was one of the leaders, and he was one of the first who struck McMurray when he was dragged into the street. Johnson was also in the mob, and urged the negroes on. He was one of the ringleaders. Cotton, Berrien, Henderson and Campbell, all had a hand in the assault upon McMurray, and they will be kept in jail until he is able to appear against them.

YESTERDAY'S ARRESTS.

A number of the rioters arrested yesterday are women. Officer Farr arrested a negro named G. A. Robinson, on Bryan street, near the Harnett house yesterday afternoon. He is supposed to be one of the number that beat Patrolman McMurray with a bed slat as he lay on the street. Detectives spotted the negro and had him arrested. They say that they will be able to prove that Robinson was one of the leaders of the riot.

William Williams, a young negro, was also arrested, and Assistant Chief Lee ordered him taken to the house of Policeman Cronin for identification. Cronin suffered intense pain all day, and his physician forbade any communication with him, but when the wounded man was informed that a negro man, supposed to have been in the riot, was outside waiting to be identified, Cronin raised up in his bed and said: "Bring the man in."

IDENTIFIED BY CRONIN.

Officer Prindible marched the negro into the room. When Cronin saw Williams he said: "That is one of my assailant." Cronin identified Williams as being one of the first who attacked him. He said that Williams knocked his pistol out of his hands, and endeavored to take his club away from him. Williams was taken to jail and will be given a preliminary hearing this morning. Isam Brown, who shot and killed Nancy Johnson Thursday night, is said to be one of the instigators of the riot. The officers are scouring the city and country for him.

HIDDEN BY FRIENDS.

A brick mason named Schultz, living out near Battery park, was informed late in the afternoon by one of his employees that a negro with a wound in his neck was being secretly treated by a physician out near the extension of the West Broad street car line. He said the name of the wounded negro was William Green, and Mr. Schultz said that it was understood that he was implicated in the riot. The matter was reported at the police barracks, and officers were sent out to look after the man, but they were unable to find him. Schultz's informant, who is himself a colored man, got out of the way, and just where the wounded negro is, if there is one, is a conundrum to the officers.

Crimmins, the employee of the Vulcanite Paving Company, who was wounded while trying to assist Officer Croniu, was removed to the city ward at St. Joseph's infirmary yesterday. Although his wounds are as serious as those of either of the policemen, he seems to be resting better and is in better spirits than either of them.

COTTON ONE OF THE RINGLEADERS.

He said yesterday afternoon that Joe Cotton, the negro who was among the first that the police arrested after the riot, was one of the ringleaders. Crimmins recognized Cotton as the man who sawed wood for J. J. Barrett, with whom Crimmins boards. When he first saw Cotton in the riot the negro had an ax and was running toward the policeman and himself. Crimmins tried to get to him, but was knocked down from behind. His endeavors to rescue the officer from the mob are applauded by everybody. He is a fearless man, and would have done some good work if he had been equipped as an officer. McMurray slept the greater part of the day, and his physicians say that he is getting along as well as he can be expected to under the circumstances. Policeman Cronin was under chloral when a MORNING NEWS reporter saw him, and was not in a condition to talk. His face is considerably swollen and his features are hardly recognizable.

THE CORONER'S INVESTIGATION.

The coroner began his investigation yesterday morning. It was with a good deal of difficulty that witnesses were obtained. None of the prisoners in the police jail were available. It was almost impossible to secure witnesses from among the negroes in the neighborhood where the riot occurred. Detectives were sent out, but very little information could be obtained that would prove of service in the investigation. A jury of 12 men—nine of whom were white and three colored—was summoned. The white men were: L. W. Brickman, J. Strauss, James T. Fitzgerald, John Cullum, Bernhard Ungar, F. G. Jaugstetter, Lee Platshek and G. Ebberwein. The colored jurors were: Abram H. Mordecai, A. Ashton and Sam Jefferson.
mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A9:
PELTED WITH ROCKS.
When the officer started back for his hat the rocks began to fly so thick that he had to run. The crowd cried "Kill him," and began hurling rocks at him. Mikel saw no interference by any of the crowd while the officer and the negro were fighting for the club.

William Vollers, who keeps a grocery at the corner of Farm and Pine streets, and H. F. Heemsoth, who keeps opposite Vollers' place, were both witnesses of the affray. Their testimony was substantially the same as that of Mikel's.

Dr. Sheftall, who examined Tillman's wounds, testified that he had eight bullet holes in his body. They were made by four shots, the bullets going clean through his body.

The jury was out half an hour and rendered the following verdict: "We, the jury, find that Mike Tillman came to his death by wounds from a pistol held in the hands of party or parties unknown while engaged in riotous conduct." The three colored jurors disagreed with the verdict and so signed their names.

A FUND FOR OFFICER QUINN'S WIFE.

A 25-cent subscription was started last night for the purpose of raising a testimonial fund for Policeman Quinn's wife, who stood guard over McMurray as he lay in the street in front of Pearl Pendergast's and held the mob at bay with her revolver. The subscription was started just before noon, and before 10 o'clock the fund had reached $30. It was first started for the purpose of getting a gold medal, but it has been decided to make the testimonial in the shape of a purse.
mike-tillman-savannah-1888-11-29.A12:
RAIDING THE RIOTERS.
One Found Guilty, One on Trial an Seventeen Indicted.
One Found Guilty, One on Trial and Seventeen Indicted.

It was a rough day in the Superior Court yesterday for the Yamacraw rioters. Dan Henderson was tried and convicted of assault with intent to murder Officer Patrick McMurray on Thanksgiving day.

The trial of Joe Cotton for assault with intent to murder Officer McMurray was begun and was in progress at the hour of recess last night. It will be concluded today. A feature of the trial was the heavy rock, with the blood stains on it, which was used by the rioters on the day of the bloody fray, and figured in the trials yesterday, being on Solicitor General Frazer's desk during the day.

The grand jury yesterday indicted sixteen colored men and one colored woman, alleged Yamacraw rioters, for assault with intent to murder Officer D. J. Cronin. The following are the parties indicted: Virgil Stephens, Robert Lewis, Bob Berrien, William Williams, Joe Cotton, Tom Washington, Edward Frazier, George H. Robinson, Hiram Sterling, Lucius Capers, Frank Johnson, William Doyle, Tom Maxwell, William Cunningham, Dan Henderson, Arthur Patterson and Rosa Jones, alias Rosa Slater.

CAIRO, ILL., January 9.—Marshal Brizendine, of Ciinton, Ky., yesterday morning succeeded in capturing the man Price at Dresden, Tenn., who a few days ago foully murdered Sheriff Henry Winter, of Clinton, while resisting arrest. The prisoner is held in jail at Dresden by the sheriff of that city, who claims a part of the reward of $2,000 offered for Price's arrest. The facts appear to be that Brizendine succeeded in tracing and locating his man, and called upon the sheriff at Dresden to assist. The latter declined to have anything to do with the matter until Brizendine swore out a warrant, after which the arrest was effected. The Ogle brothers were also captured, one charged with assisting in the murder, the other in the escape of both parties. When the train on the Illinois Central passed Clinton this morning a large and excited crowd surrounded the depot for the avowed purpose of lynching Price should he be on board.

The bodies were permitted to hang until after daylight, when they were taken down by the authorities and buried. The mob is said to have been composed of men residing in Hickman County, many of them not even wearing masks of any description. Many of the avengers, however, wore handkerchiefs over their faces. The doors of the jail were broken as assender with but little confusion, and the nooses were slipped under the ears of the doomed men without a word. A signal from the leader was sufficient to have them drawn suddenly into the air, where their struggles soon ceased.

About three months ago Sam Price was arrested near his home in Clinton by Sheriff Henry Winter for some violation of the law. Asking for permission to enter his mother's house for a change of clothing, he suddenly reappeared at the door with a rifle and shot the sheriff in his tracks. The deed was applauded by the mother, who was on the spot, and who was undoubtedly largely instrumental in causing the murder. After a long chase and a reward of $1,200 had been offered, the fugitive was captured at Dresden, Tenn., and brought to Kentucky a few weeks ago, being kept in Dresden jail some time on account of the danger of lynching if he was confined at Clinton. Two brothers-in-law of Price and his mother, all more or less implicated in the murder, were in the jail, but were unmolested. Reems on Saturday night was detected stealing chickens from the yard of J. P. Jackson, in Clinton, and when ordered out of the yard by Jackson he drew a revolver and fired two shots, both taking effect in the breast, causing Jackson's death a few hours later.

INDIANA AND ILLINOIS NEWS
The Daily Chronicle of Happenings of Various Kinds in the Two States.
Death of Miss Downey, Young Grubb's Victim—A Sensational Lawsuit—Reunions of Veteran Soldiers—Notes and Gleanings.
INDIANA.
The Death of Grubb's Victim Rouses a Fear of Mob Violence.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

PRINCETON, Sept. 19.—Miss Gertrude Downey, who was shot by Sylvester Grubb, at the fair grounds, last Thursday, died this morning from the effects of her wounds. Grubb has been taken to Evansville to prevent any attempt at mob violence. It is reported that a crowd started into town on two different nights from the neighborhood where the girl resided, but returned when they learned that the prisoner was not here.

EVANSVILLE, Sept. 19.—The death at Princeton, to-day, of Miss Gertrude Downey, the young lady who was so brutally shot last Thursday by Sylvester Grubb, her rejected lover, has caused considerable uneasiness here, from the fact that the fiend is in the Evansville jail and that there is great danger of his being lynched to-night, the jail officers having been notified that there is a movement on foot in Gibson county to lynch him if possible. Sheriff Schaum, who is in Indianapolis, was summoned home and will arrive during the night.

Sensational Lawsuit at Greensburg.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

GREENSBURG, Sept. 19.—A suit that will attract much attention was filed in the Circuit Court to-day. The title is Mary J. Vornholt vs. Sarah R. Roberts and Wm. R. Roberts. The facts connected with it are these: Jeremiah K. Tullis and wife lived near Sardinia, this county, many years ago, and became quite wealthy. Their only child was the plaintiff in this action, now Mary J. Vornholt, her husband being a merchant at Westport. About five years ago the mother died, and soon after the father threw off the habiliments of mourning, and became gay and festive for one of his age—about sixty-five years. He went to Indianapolis to live with the defendants, Mrs. Roberts being quite attractive, and much younger than Mr. Tullis. Oct. 22, 1866, Tullis made a deed to Mrs. Roberts for 160 acres of fine farming land, on which he and his wife formerly lived, retaining, however, to himself a life estate. The consideration, as expressed in the deed, was "For the sum and consideration of my support heretofore and hereafter, and of natural love and affection, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged." Mr. Tullis died a few days ago, and Mrs. Roberts now has possession of the land. This suit by the daughter is for the recovery of the farm and damages. There will probably be another action in Marion county, as he also gave her a deed for a house and lot in Indianapolis which he owned. Mrs. Roberts is not a relative in any way of Mr. Tullis, but formerly lived at Lebanon, Ind.

That Dynamite Conspiracy. CHICAGO, Oct. 13 — What was thought at first to be the work of one crank, has turned out to be a well organized dynamite conspiracy to blow up the street cars and other property of the North Side street car company. Three arrests have already been made, and two more of the alleged conspirators, the police say, will shortly be taken into custody. Jules Katsberger, who was caught in the act of placing four small bombs on the tracks on Sedgwick street by Detectives Cudmore and Mercier, Thomas Nicholson and Peter Thompson were arraigned before Justice Kersten to day. As Capt. Schaack was not ready for trial, the case was continued for ten days. The conspirators were released on furnishing $10,000 bonds each. "It was a murderous conspiracy," said Attorney Furthmann. "The conspirators intended to destroy both property and life, but their scheme was nipped in the bud." Congressmen Not in Their Seats. WASHINGTON, Oct. 13 — The capital was
Congressmen Not in Their Seats.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 13.—The capitol was almost deserted to-day. Neither House of Congress was in session and none of the committees assembled. It was stated with some show of authority on the Senate side that the date of adjournment would be Saturday next, and that an adjournment resolution would be brought in by some member of the ways and means committee early next week. Senator Allison said this morning that no understanding had been reached, and in fact no conference on the subject had been had. He added: "At the rate at which senators have been leaving the city we will not have a quorum here Monday."

Gen. Clark, the clerk of the House, said to-day that no meeting of the ways and means committee had been held to consider the matter of adjournment, and that no day could be fixed.

Either Conly or McAuliffe.

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 13.—Letters received here by sporting men from Jack Dempsey and other well known pugilists say the winner of the Conly-McAuliffe fight in the California Athletic club on the 26th instant will be the unknown who is to meet Jake Kilrain. Conly is regarded by experts here as a sure loser, though he is training hard and in fine condition. McAuliffe has thickened since his fight with Glover so that he cannot reduce his weight below 220 pounds. He stands six feet four inches, five inches above Conly and is as confident of winning as if he had the purse in his pocket.

CHICAGO, Oct. 13.—A tall, blonde woman

A Woman Dynamiter.

CHICAGO, Oct. 13.—A tail, blonde woman evidently a foreigner, made some small purchases last night at Whiteford's drug store, corner of Harrison street and Marshall avenue. After she had left the store Mr. Whitford discovered a parcel under the counter from which smoke was issuing. Unwrapping the parcel, he found the hub of a pulley wheel, plugged at both ends, from one of which projected a smoking fuse. He put out the fire of the fuse and turned the bumb over to the police, who found it filled with dynamite.

Hotel Guests Poisoned.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 13.—At Johnson City, 100 miles east of this city, on the East Tennessee railroad, fourteen guests of Smith's hotel are reported to be poisoned by something eaten at supper. Three have died and several others, it is feared, cannot recover. It is believed that the poison was administered intentionally by some malicious person unfriendly to the hotel proprietor.

Lynchers Outwitted.

Lynchers Outwitted.

PRINCETON, Ind., Oct. 13.—A lynching affair was narrowly averted near here last night. It was expected that Sheriff McGarry would pass through Francisco on the evening train with Sylvester Grubb, the slayer of Miss Gertrude Downey, and a hundred men, armed and masked, boarded the train at that point and went through it, searching for the murderer. Fortunately the sheriff had taken another train and the mob was cheated of its victim.

A Big Lumber Firm Fails.

ASHLAND, Wis., Oct. 13—J. M. Lane & Co., lumbermen at Washburne, made an assignment yesterday to T. S. Clark, of Grand Rapids, Mich. Lane & Co. took one of the Rood & Maxwell mills and other property a year ago when that firm failed for $500,000. The affairs of the company are unknown to anyone outside, and the assets and liabilities cannot be ascertained.

They Fleaded Guilty.

They Pleaded Guilty.

ADRIAN, Mich., Oct. 13.—At the session of the circuit court yesterday morning, five girls from the industrial home were arraigned, charged with arson, the offense consisting of an attempt to burn Creswell cottage on the 20th of September. The court gave the culprits a week in which to get their parents and friends here to speak for them, and will pass sentence Friday next.

Ali Recovering.

QUINCY, Ilir., Oct. 13.—All of the victims of Wednesday night's amphitheatre disaster are reported doing nicely and it is now thought that no fatalities will result, though several of the most seriously injured will be confined to their beds for several months to come. The Hon. A. W. Welis and Dr. Bowman, reported dying Thursday night, will recover.

Women and Whisky Killed Him.

MASON CITY, Is., Oct. 13.—Perry, Welish, agent of John Paul's lumber yard at Britt, has disappeared after defrauding the company out of quite a sum of money. A number of citizens hold notes against him, each having John Paul's name forged to it. Women and whisky prompted him to crime. He leaves behind a wife and family.

A Business Block Burned.

A Business Block Burned.

VALENTINE, Neb., Oct. 13.—Fire started in the rear of a hardware store shortly after 10 o'clock yesterday morning and destroyed the finest business block in town. The United States signal office was among the buildings consumed. The loss is $60,000; insurance small.

Railroad Yardman Strike.

BRAINERD, Minn., Oct. 13.—All Northern Pacific yardmen went out on a strike this morning for an advance in wages. This is the first labor trouble the company has ever had. All trains are blocked.

To Be Hanged For Arson.

DANVILLE, Va., Oct. 13.—Gov. Scales, of North Carolina, yesterday respired for thirty days Mollie Poteat (colored) who was to have been hanged at Yanceyville for burning a dwelling.

Three Children Lose Their Lives.

MEXICO, Mo., Oct. 13.—Minnie Boyd, aged 7, was burned to death Thursday night at her home, her dress catching fire and the smoke suffocated her two baby sisters.

WEATHER INDICATIONS.

WASHINGTON, D. C., Oct. 13.—For Eastern Pennsylvania and New Jersey: Light local rains, followed Saturday night by fair, warmer, westerly winds.
sylvester-grubb-francisco-1888-10-12.A3:
INDIANA AND ILLINOIS NEWS Masked Men Search an Air-Line Train for a Murderer, but Do Not Find Him. Fear of Burying a Woman Alive Delays a Funeral—Two Politicians Meet Accidental Deaths—Piatt County Sons of Veterans. INDIANA.
A Mob of Would-Be Lynchers Boards the Wrong Train in Quest of a Murderer. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

VINCENNES, Oct. 12.—Sylvester Grubb was brought to this city, yesterday, from Jeffersonville, for trial for the murder of his sweetheart, Gertie Downey. This fact developed a mob of masked men. They supposed Grubb would be brought over the Ohio & Mississippi road. Two men boarded the Air-line train at Oakland City, to prospect for Grubb. They were to signal at Francisco, eight miles east of Princeton, where Miss Downey lived, if Grubb was on the train, but he was not there. The leader of the Princeton band was at Francisco, and wanted to take that train home. Francisco is merely a flag station, so he flagged the train, innocent of the mob's plan, and the train stopped. Eight men at once entered each coach, inspected every face, and, without a word, quietly left the train. There were sixty of the mobbers. Once before a mob collected a mile east of Princeton, but Grubb was in the Evansville jail at the time, and thus they were baffled.

A Supposed Case of Suspended Animation. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MARION, Oct. 12.—Last Tuesday Mrs. Charles Oman, of Jonesboro, died, was arrayed for burial and arrangements for the funeral were made. Later, friends of the deceased detected what they considered signs of life, and the body was disrobed, put to bed and stimulants applied, but without success. The funeral services were held yesterday afternoon, but the remains were still so strikingly life-like that it was decided to postpone the burial. It was announced from the pulpit of the Methodist Church, after the ceremonies were over, creating a decided sensation. To-day an examination was held, which satisfied beyond a doubt that Mrs. Omar was dead. The remains were interred this evening.

Singular Coincidence in Deaths of Politicians. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

BRAZIL, Oct. 12—Harrison township, by a remarkable coincidence, has lost by accidental death the chairman of both the Democratic and the Republican committees. Casper Rader, Democrat, in returning from a rally at Coal City, was thrown by the upsetting of his buggy under the wheels of a parade wagon loaded with young ladies, and his skull was crushed. This was three weeks since. In returning from the Porter rally here, Friday night, J. C. Wilbur, Republican, fell from a platform while the train was running at full speed. One coach passed over him. He was picked up insensible, much bruised, but, strangely, not dead. He died yesterday and was buried here to-day. Both were good citizens and are a loss to the community.
sylvester-grubb-francisco-1888-10-12.A8:
GERTRUDE DOWNEY'S MURDERER.
A Knox County Jurr Says Sylvester Grubb Must Suffer the Extreme Penalty.
VINCENNES, Ind., Oct. 19.—The trial of Sylvester Grubb for the murder of Miss Gertrude Downey was begun in the Knox Circuit Court Oct. 12. The defense was a plea of insanity, and a strong pull was made to save his neck from the rope. The case was a romance-tragedy in real life, and excited great interest in this community, the court-room being crowded day after day to hear the shocking details of the story.

Grubb is a young man, twenty-four years of age, and two years ago met Miss Gertie Downey. It was a case of love at first sight. Both these young people lived in Gibson county. Letters passed between them, and then Grubb proposed marriage. The young lady did not wish to marry him, and refused longer to see him. Then he wrote her a letter, vowing revenge, if she cast him off forever. He proposed to go away for a year, and see how that would do. He told her he would disgrace her forever if she cast him off. This letter was introduced in the trial. A day or two before the tragedy he called at her home at Francisco, eight miles east of Princeton, and when the young lady refused to see him he sat for three hours on a pile of lumber near the house, hoping still to have the privilege of seeing her, but all in vain. On the morning of the fatal 13th of September he went to the Princeton fair, hoping to see her there. On the way he remarked to a friend that she was there with another young man, and he wanted to see her but once more. They met on the fair ground, and he asked her to walk with him. Unwillingly she went with him, telling her lady friend to remain at that spot, as she would be back in a few minutes. As they went toward an unfrequented part of the ground, it was observed that they were quarreling. Suddenly, and without notice, he shoved his revolver in her face and fired, the ball striking just below the right eye, and the powder burning her face. She turned and ran away screaming, the blood saturating her white dress. He fired two other shots at her, one hitting her in the arm, the other missing its mark. Then he pointed the pistol at his own head, and snapped it twice, but it failed to go off. When parties rushed in to interfere, he flourished his revolver around and told them to stand back. After a moment, however, he surrendered to the officers, and was at once lodged in jail.

The young lady died in great agony, after lingering six days, and the indignation of Miss Downey's friends was so great that an attempt was made to lynch the murderer. His neck was saved by spiriting him away to Evansville. Then he was taken to Jeffersonville for safe keeping, and was brought here for trial.

The jury took the case last evening. On the first ballot the jury decided that Grubb was guilty of murder in the first degree. The second ballot was to decide whether it should be the death penalty or imprisonment for life, and nine were for inflicting the extreme penalty of the law. The insanity dodge was not considered in the jury-room at all. After deliberating eight hours a verdict of death was reached.

The prisoner was brought into court this morning and the sentence read to him. He seemed to take it as a matter of course, and there was scarcely a perceptible blanch on his cheek. Many encomiums have been passed upon the jury for its moral courage in affixing the death penalty as a matter of justice to the slain girl.
sylvester-grubb-francisco-1888-10-12.A10:
To Pay the Death Penalty.
VINCENNES, Ind., Oct. 27.—Sylvester Grubb, the young man who shot and killed his sweetheart on the Princeton fair grounds last September, has been sentenced to be hanged April 19. He received the sentence without betraying any emotion, and when asked how he now looked upon his crime, replied that he felt that he had done nothing wrong.

thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A2:
MURDER IN NORTH CAROLINA.
The Perpetrator Captured and Shot to Death.
WASHINGTON, N. C., May 6.—On Saturday afternoon this community was shocked by the reported murder of Mr. Joshua H. Cox, a lumber man of Blount's Creek, sixteen mil s from this city, by Thomas Frazier, an employee of Cox's brother. There had been bad blood between the parties for some time past, and on Saturday afternoon Frazier, accompanied by some friends, entered Cox's store and demanded liquor, which Cox refused, and, turning, left for his mill a few yards distant from the store. Frazier immediately seized a gun loaded with buck-shot from the hands of one of his friends standing near and shot Cox, killing him instantly. Frazier immediately fled, swimming a creek in his flight, but he was intercepted by the brother of the murdered man, who bound him and placed him in the house of a neighbor, under a strong guard, preparatory to bringing him to this city on the following morning for incarceration in the county jail. A magistrate, fearing attempted release by Frazier's friends, posted sentinels at different points in and around the premises, securing Frazier with heavy chains to a post in the building. During the night a company of masked men, adroitly evading the sentinels, gained admission to the temporary prison, took possession of the murderer, knocked off his irons, gagged and bound him, and dragged him to the scene of the tragedy, and with guns and pistols shot him to death, mutilating his body almost beyond recognition. Frazier has always been considered a desperate character, having confessed to several, other murders. The community is greatly excited, and fears are entertained for the safety of Frazier's friends, who have fled. Mr. Cox leaves a wife and five small children.
thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A3:
A Murderer Killed by a Mob. NASHINGTON N. C. MAY 7. The
A Murderer Killed by a Mob.
WASHINGTON, N. C., May 7.—Thomas Frazier, a saloon keeper, shot and instantly killed Joshua H. Cox, a prominent lumber dealer, at Blount's Creek, near here, and then fled from the town. He was captured in the evening and put under guard in a farm house, preparatory to being placed in the county jail the next morning. During the night a number of masked men seized Frazier, and, taking him to the spot where he had murdered Cox, killed him with guns and pistols. His body was mutilated almost beyond recognition. Frazier was considered a desperate character. Cox leaves a widow and five small children.
thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A5:
MEDICINE-MEN.
ANNUAL MEETING OF THE NORTH CAROLINA ASSOCIATION.
A Brutal Murder—Struck by Lightning— Searching for Miss Foe's Assailant— Other Notes.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
annual session of the North Carolina Medical Society began this morning at Williams's Hall, Fayetteville—Dr. T. D. Haigh, of Fayetteville, presiding, and Dr. Julian E. Baker, of Tarboro', secretary. The attendance is up to the secretary. This afternoon President Haligh delivered the annual address. To-morrow evening the people of the town will give a banquet and ball to the society. On Thursday the society will participate in the memorial-day exercises, and on the evening of that day the annual oration before the society will be delivered.

Near Davidson College lightning struck the warehouse of John Caldwell and burned it with its contents, causing a loss of $1,200.

The municipal election at Durham yesterday was quite exciting. There were three tickets in the field, headed by John F. Freeland, W. J. Christian, and Thomas C. Oakley respectively for mayor. Oakley was the labor candidate, but many of his pledged friends deserted him and voted for Christian, who was elected.

The people of Monroe are greatly excited by the brutal murder of Policeman John Pearce by a negro named Bill Weddington. There was a row at a negro festival, and Pearce arrested the leader in the disturbance and started to the guard-house with him. A mob of negroes gathered and decided that they would rescue the negro who was under arrest. Weddington with a heavy iron bar in his hand was in the rear of Pearce. Frank Thomas, another negro, armed with a bludgeon, cried out, "Kill him!" Whereupon Weddington with one stroke crushed the skull of Pearce, who soon died, never having regained consciousness. Weddington was arrested at once, and Thomas, who had fled to Charlotte, was also captured. Both are in jail at Monroe. Thomas was tried for murder two years ago and got off. Pearce leaves a wife and four children.

The French corvette Brisson has arrived at Wilmington, whose people are showing her officers many courtesies.

It has been found that there are not enough legal signatures to the petition for the local-option election at Charlotte, and the county commissioners have withdrawn the order for the election.

The Federal Court began to-day at Asheville—Judge Dick presiding.

Reports to the Department of Agriculture from Durham and Orange counties state that the wheat and oats crops are being ruined by the prolonged and unusual drought. The same report says the tobacco-plants look well, and that large crops will be planted.

Mr. Hasten Poe, whose sister, Miss Ida Poe, was shot at Carthage by Robert L. McNeill, returned here to-day. He reports that her wound is not at present regarded as dangerous. No tidings of McNeill can be heard. This morning before daylight the town of Carthage, and particularly the house of McNeill's father, was strongly guarded, if having been rumored that McNeill was back in town in hiding. Search for him continued all last night, with the avowed intention of lynching. There is a belief this afternoon that he has after all gone safely away, and is now in Texas or on his way there for refuge.

North Carolina is rather coming towards the front in the matter of lynching. There has not been a legal execution this year, yet there have been five persons lynched. On the 27th of January Matthew Blouat, John Blount, and Patterson Spruill (all colored) were disposed of at Plymouth by his Honor Judge Lynch, and the same judge had another victim at Washington March 12th in the person of a white man, who boasted that he was the assassin of General Bryan Grimes. The last victim at this date is Frazier, who was disposed of at Washington last Saturday night for the murder of Cox. Of the persons sentenced legally to be hanged there have been the following, the commutations being in every case save one to life imprisonment: Charles F. Jones, Newberne; Lucien Rowe, Durham; James Thomas, Hendersonville; Allen McCarter, Statesville, and Daniel Biggs, Wilmington.

The Wake county Grape-Growers' Association met to-day and beard reports. It is discovered that vineyards west of the city and in this township were not hurt by the frosts of late April, while vineyards east of the city have suffered much damage.

Rev. Dr. C. H. Strickland, of Nashville, Tenn., was this evening called to the pastorate of the First Baptist church of this city. He is a very able man and will receive a $3,000 salary.

Captain E. R. Stamps, president of the Board of Directors of the penitentiary, and Mr. W. J. Hieks, warden of that institution, are now in the Blue-Ridge country inspecting the convict quarters in that section. The penitentiary is greatly cramped for funds and may have to remove from railways some of the convicts whose labor has been furnished free.

Major John Gatling, once so prominent as a lawyer, and who died yesterday morning, was buried this afternoon from Christ church, Rev. Dr. M. M. Marshall conducting the services.

The unfortunate white woman who drowned herself some days ago in Robeson county was a native of Robeson county. She ran away from her husband some months ago, and the greater part of the time wandered here and there.

There has been some dispute as to whether the names of the signers of the petition for a local-option election in Barton's-Creek township, Wake county, were or were not those of bona-fide voters, and so the county commissioners have been considering the matter.

The pea crop in the Goldsboro' section is about all picked. It has been quite remunerative. Next week the land now in peas will be planted in corn or cotton.

The Cape-Fear and Yadkin-Valley railroad make a fine showing in the matter of net earnings for the year ended April 30th. They were $31,188 in excess of those during the previous year.

A great revival is in progress in the Baptist church at Fayetteville. There have been many converts.

It is rather noticeable that the Democratic Convention of Cumberland county did not instruct its delegates as to the man they should support for Governor.

Mrs. Rebecca Long's house, in Richmond county, was burned a night or two ago, causing a loss of $1,500, with no insurance. Raleigh is well represented at the session of the Grand Lodge of Independent Order Odd-Fellows, which met at Greensboro' this morning in the hall of Buena Vista lodge. Grand Representatives Charles M. Busbee and C. B. Edwards are present. Captain W. A. Bobbitt, of Oxford, is grand master.

There were elections yesterday at several towns. At Shelby the Democrats were successful and W. L. Damson was reelected mayor. At Newberne the "Coalition party" carried the day. This is the "Reform party," composed of Democrats and the better class of Republicans which figured so extensively in the campaign of 1886. At Goldsboro' the Democrats were again winners, electing eight of the nine aldermen. At Greensboro' John A. Barringer was elected mayor.

Great fires have raged through the forests in Caldwell and Watauga counties, in a district covering some fifty or sixty square miles. The damage is immense. A great deal of the timber burned is chestnut.

ALEXANDRIA.
thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A8:
A DOUBLE TRAGEDY.
TERRIBLE MURDER SPEEDILY AVENGED.
A DESPERATE CHARACTER RIDDLED BY LYNCHERS' BULLETS—CRIME MAKES WIDOWS ANN ORPHANS.
[From Washington Gazette-Extra.]
Again has our community been shocked by another terrible tragedy. Like a thunder clap the startling announcement came that Mr. Joshua A. Cox, a peaceable and useful citizen and successful lumberman of Blount's Creek, 16 miles from Washington, had been murdered by Thomas Frazier, an employee of Mr. H. Mac Cox, deceased's brother. Bad blood for Cox had boiled in the veins of Frazier for some time past, and on Saturday afternoon, accompanied by two friends, Newton and Adams, he entered Cox's store and demanded liquor, which Cox refused, and then walked off towards his mill, a few yards distant. Frazier, who had been drinking, now boiling with rage, thought it "d——d strange others could buy when he could not," and seizing a gun which was in the hands of one of his friends standing near, emptied the contents of both barrels, which literally riddled Mr. Cox with buck shot, producing almost instant death. Frazier fled through the swamp near by to the house of Mr. H. Mac Cox, where his clothes were thinking to secure them and escape, believing his employer absent. Mr. Cox, however, had heard of the murder, but not having left the house, arrested Frazier, and with the aid of others, who came up, bound him and carried him to a small dwelling near the mill, where he was placed under a strong guard, preparatory to bringing him to this city, the following morning, for incarcecration in the county jail. A magistrate, fearing attempted release by Frazier's friends, posted sentinels at different points around the premises, securing the murderer with heavy chains fastened to a post within the building. Toward morning a company of masked men, adroitly eluded the sentinels and gained admission to the temporary prison, and overpowering the guard, took possession of Frazier, knocked off the irons, and gagged and bound, dragged him near to the exact spot where he stood when he fired the first shot at his innocent victim. Here a volley of gun and pistol shots was emptied into his body, instantly killing him and mutilating him almost beyond recognition, and then the lynchers dispersed, having done their work in much less time than it takes to tell the story.

Frazier was considered a desperate character, having confessed to several other murders, among them the killing of Mac Waters, several years ago, while night watch at Kugler's mill, in this town. The community around the scene of the tragedy is mutch excited, and fears are entertained for the safety of Frazier's friends, who had not been seen since Saturday night, and is supposed to have got an inkling of danger and fled to parts unknown. Frazier was the son of a prominent lawyer in Pender county, but had lived in this county for a number of years.

Mr. Cox was a very highly respected citizen. a hard worker, and a useful man. Many will morn his death, but none will feel it so keenly as his widow with her five small children, whom we all pity in their sore affliction.

LATER.—At the Coroner's inquest held Sunday over the body of Frazier a verdict of "death at the hands of parties unknown to the jury" was I rendered.
thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A10:
Murder and Lynching. Another horrible affair has happened in our State. It was a double tragedy. Mr. Joshua Cox, living at Blount Creek about 16 miles from Washington, was shot and killed by Thomas Frazier last Saturday night. Frazier attempted to escape but was captured and lodged in jail. That night, a crowd of masked men, took the law into their own hands, went to the jail, brought Frazier out, and riddled him with bullets. There were two other men, Wm. B. Adams and John M. Newton, implicated with Frazier in the murder, but they made their escape. They have been declared outlaws and it is thought that they are hiding around in the swamps near Washington. Disgraceful.
Moore county comes to the front with a most unpleasant affair. Bob McNeill, a young man of a family of good standing in the county, called, last Saturday night, at Shaw's Hotel in Carthage. He asked to see Miss Ida Poe, a young lady stopping there, but she refused to see him. He then went to the parlor, and knocked. Miss Poe, who was in the parlor, not thinking it was McNeill, opened the door; when she did, McNeill caught and closed the door behind her. He then asked, "Why have you gone back on me?" "I have not," she replied. McNeill then drew a pistol, pointed it towards her and fired, the ball penetrating her thigh. He immediately ran out, got into a buggy and made his escape.

Miss Poe is a young lady of pleasing manners and belongs to a family of the highest standing. She is a sister of Mr. Hastings Poe, of Raleigh. The wound though very painful is not very serious.

Every effort is being made to capture the jealous rascal. The CHRONICLE hopes that the attempts will be successful and that the law will punish him to its fullest extent.
thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A11:
IN AMBUSH.
AUTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE A BEGRO IN
NORTH CAROLINA.
Two Bullets Take Effect-An Arrest-Negroes Going to Southern California- Personal Notes.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
M E F I C H, N, C, May 12 — The State

RALLEIGH, N. C., May 12 — The State Medical Society, which has held its annual session at Favetteville, has adjourned. Dr. W. T. Ennett, of Burgaw, was elected president, and Dr. J. M. Baker, of Tarboro', secretary. Elizabeth City was chosen as the place at which the next meeting will be held on the third Tuesday in April. The society adopted appropriate resolutions relative to the death of Dr. O. F. Manson, a former member, who recently died at Richmond, Va.

A desperate attempt was made in Craven county, near Dover, to assis-sinate Caesar Beeton (colored) as he was riding along the public highway. Men in ambush shot him, one bullet wounding him in the breast and another cutting off one of his fingers. S. B. Humphrey was arrested, and was tried yesterday, charged with the commission of this crime. He was held to appear.

Many negroes are leaving the section between Salisbury and Asheville, and are going to live in Southern California. It appears probable that this emigration will become much more extensive.

This year a wheat fair is to be held at Statesville, and from the energy the people of Redell county are showing in arranging for it, it will be a success and on a large scale.

Wilkes county has issued bonds for the extension to Wilksboro', its county-seat, of a railway. A large force is now engaged in grading, and the people are mightily cheered at the prospect of railway communication at a very early day.

Winston will seek to make her tobacco fair, to be held the coming autumn, a representative display not only of the resources and chief industry of that lively town, but of the Piedmont section and of the tobacco interest generally.

It is by no means improbable that electricity may be used as a motive power on the Asheville street-railway. Parties from that city are now examining the Richmond system.

It is learned that many citizens in parts of Beaufort county say that by the aid of corrupt jurors so many murderers have escaped the law that Judge Lynch is a necessity, or, in other words, that they feel obliged to take the law in their own hands. Hence the Parker lynching in March and the Frazier lynching last week. The coroner's jury, by the way, has never been able to discover the men who so quickly and so terribly avenged Frazier's brutal murder of Cox.

The rains, which are general and copious, came in time to do the cotton crop an incalculable amount of good. Farmers ran quite near to a serious drought, and were just beginning to fully realize the danger. Cottonseed had in some cases laid in the ground for weeks without sprouting, all for lack of the necessary moisture.

The returns secured from all parts of the state by the Department of Agriculture leave no doubt as to the fact that the people are in a better condition than at this time last year. This applies particularly to the farmers. They are using less commercial fertilizer and more home-made manures, and they are raising more pork. They last year began more careful farm work and this year are carrying that plan still further. With moderate seasons good crops may be expected and a healthy state of business in the autumn.

Cherry Jordan and Marinda Jordan are in jail at Winton, Hertford county, charged with murdering the infant child of the latter by drowning it in a well. The first-named woman is the child's grandmother.

Dr. T. G. Jones, pastor of the First Baptist church of Norfolk, will deliver the annual address—June 19th—before the graduating class at Chowan Baptist Female Institute, Murfreesboro'.

Farmers in the Blue Ridge section report the wheat crop as in fine condition.

The present fishing season in the northeastern section of the State is said to be the dullest, with one or two exceptions, in many years.

Reidsville, one of the most progressive places in the State, has voted in favor of a proposition to issue bonds to the amount of £20,000 for public improvements. Only twelve votes were cast against it. Reidsville will soon have the electric light.

Dr. J. F. Miller, superintendent of the colored insane asylum at Goldsboro', is at Norfolk attending the National Convention of Insane-Asylum Superintendents.

Goldsboro's memorial-day exercises will be held next Monday. The heavy rains prevented them on Thursday last.

Colonet T. W. Goodrich has been elected mayor of Henderson.

Gifford Lewis, for many years a deputy sheriff of Nash county, was found dead in the woods a day or two ago.

News has been received of a severe storm which swept through Nash county. Its path was a mile in width. It tore the roof from Haywood Goodman's house, and gave his people a dreadful fright. Oaks and other trees a foot in diameter were torn to pieces. There was considerable hail.

Pneumonia is reported to be quite prevalent in the southern section of Person county.
thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A14:
The Economist, in comment upon the Beaufort County Tragedy, which was reported in the last issue of this paper, says as follows:

"Beaufort county has recently had some reputation for lawlessness, but we do not suppose it is a safe retreat for bad men for they are generally visited by the vengeance of the law, which tho not swift seems to be sure. But a tragedy, occurred on the 5th inst., at Blount's Creek, some 16 miles from Washington, which shows not only a diabolical purpose of murder but a defiance of law and the constituted tribunals of justice."

thomas-fraser-blount-s-creek-1888-05-06.A17:
Joshua Cox's Murderers.
RALEIGH, N. C., June 5.—[Special.]—Interest in the murder of Joshua Cox, in Beaufort county, and the lynching of Frazier, his murderer, is revived today. Two men, one named Newton, and Thomas Adams, were concerned in this crime as accessories. Both fled. John M. Newton was captured. Several attempts to lynch him have been made, but failed. Friday the grand jury found a true bill against him for murder, and his trial is to begin tomorrow. Adams is yet in hiding in the great swamps, which are in that section.
