TREASUREK HILL'S MURDERER.
The Son of the Sheriff of Panola County
Confesses, Giving all the Details.
Special to the Gazette.

BECKVILLE, TEX., Feb. 28.—About noon yesterday Tom Forsyth, son of the Sheriff of Panola county, was arrested for the murder of County Treasurer Hill on February 10. Young Forsyth has been under suspicion since his finding the sack of silver near the yard of the negro barber, Tippett, and has been under close surveillance since. When arrested he is said to have endeavored to throw the crime on Tippett, but immediately afterwards weakened, saying: "No, he is innocent. No one had anything to do with it but myself."

He is said to have confessed that he committed the murder while court was adjourned for dinner. The details of the confession are said to be horrible in the last degree. The widow of the murdered treasurer is said to have lost her mind, and the mother of young Forsyth fell in the street upon hearing the crowd crying out that her son was arrested and was making a confession. Two of the best women in the county are thus plunged into a living death, and numerous relatives throughout the county are worse than horror-stricken. Forsyth is but twenty-two, and does not look like a villain.

All but $700 of the money has been recovered. Being so far from telegraphic facilities makes it impossible to get particulars.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

Special to the Gazette.

LONGVIEW, TEX., Feb. 28 —For several days officers and citizens have been secretly hard at work on the Panola county murder case, Thomas Forsyth being the suspected murderer of County Treasurer Hill on the 10 h inst. He was known to have gambled very freely with the construction crews on the new railway nearly completed to Carthage, losing as high as $200 in one night, and this money all bore the stain of blood on its face. Several of these blood-stained bills were proved beyond a doubt to have been in the treasury at the time of the murder and robbery, but on account of this young man's social standing his arrest was deferred till the last possible moment, or till the evidence had piled up so high that nothing else could be done. The arrest was made as quietly as possible, but the fact flew like lightning and it was shouted so loud through the streets of the quiet little town that Forsyth's mother heard that her son was arrested and had made a full confession, the details of which are said to be horrible in the extreme. Mrs. Forsyt fell swooning on the streets apparently losing her mind, while at the home of the murdered County Treasurer, it is said, his widow has become a hopeless maniac. Young Forsyth is scarcely twenty-one years of age, and has acted as deputy sheriff for his father for seven or eight years, having the esteem and confidence of all who knew him. The only part of his confession known here is that he killed Treasurer Hill at noon Friday while the court had adjourned for dinner. It will be remembered that young Forsyth was the man who found the money buried near the residence of the negro barber Tippett who, he now says, had nothing to do with the murder or robbery. Great apprehension is felt for the safety of young Forsyth against mob law, but as his father is sheriff, it is likely with the assistance of 100 sworn deputies, he may be saved till he is moved to a place of safety, which is the plan suggested. Nearly all the stolen money was recovered. Owing to the absence of wire, and only one mail each day, but few particulars are obtainable.

Panola County's Hideous Mystery

Panola County's Hideous Mystery Cleared Up.

LONG VIEW, TEX., Feb. 28.—Information has been received here from Carthage, the county seat of Panola county, that Thomas Forsyth, son of the Sheriff of Panola county, was arrested yesterday for the murder, about two weeks ago, of County Treasurer D. C. Hill. It is said that Forsyth has confessed the crime and has restored stolen money amounting to more than $6,000. The excitement over the confession is intense and Forsyth may be lynched. FORSYTHE'S CONFESSION.
Incidents of the Lynching--He Entered the Treasurer's Office With No Thought of Murder.
His Detection Due to Poker Playing. He Lost and Resorted to the Buried Money to Pay His Debts.
His Only Begret that He Did Not Kill Par- ker when He Found He was Spotted. The Murderer's Funeral.
FORSYTHE'S FUNERAL.
Special to the Gazette.

BECKVILLE, TEX., March 1.—As the particulars of the hanging of Tom Forsythe at Carthage yesterday came in the terrible details show both the murder and death of the murderer to have been surrounded with scenes almost unparalleled in the annals of crime. With his arms pinioned behind him, young Forsythe was led to the foot of a ladder placed against the tree whereon he was to hang, by unmasked men, friends and neighbors, who with sorrowful faces meted out justice. One of the two sons of the murdered treasurer adjusted the rope around the doomed boy's neck. Nearly all the details of the hanging were known to the lynched boy's friends, who are reported to have said, as death was deserved and must inevitably come the sooner the end was reached the better. Clasped in each others arms the loving mother and sister of the doomed son and brother prayed with streaming eyes and moans of anguish to the God of mercy for their loved one, while he with stoical non-chalance climbed the ladder, received a drink of water from the hand of the son of his victim and leaped into eternity. Those who saw the leap say it seemed as if the neck was stretched the distance of a foot. Death came rapidly and then the body was cut down, taken into the late treasurer's office and laid in the blood of his victim. It was then taken to an hotel and prepared for burial by the same men who had just seen justice meted out to him, whose body they as gently and carefully prepared for the grave as though he had died a peaceful death at home. He was buried in the afternoon. Business houses closed and every one attended the funeral. The case has been worked up by United States Deputy Marshal Howell Parker of Longview, assisted by Detective H. Miller and the local authorities.

FORSYTHE'S CONFESSION.

Special to the Gazette.

LONGVIEW, TEX, March 1.—The following is the confession of Tom Forsythe, the murderer of D. C. Hill, treasurer of Panola county, at Carthage, Feb. 10. He said the way he killed old man Hill was as follows: At noon on Friday, he went into Hill's office to get a $20 bill changed. Hill went to the safe to get the change, threw off the combination, and as he leaned forward to unlock the inner door of the safe with a key he always wore attached to his vest by a string, he picked up the axe and struck the blow that floored Hill, striking another blow after he had fallen. He then opened the safe and crammed some of the money into his pocket. Hill began to struggle and then, with his penknife, which the day before he had honed to a razor-like sharpness, he cut the old man's throat, catching him by his long gray beard, and thus

HOLDING THE HEAD BACK.

He then secured his booty, looked cautiously out, saw the coast clear and left, locking the door behind him. He then went to an old blacksmith shop, kicked some of the boards aside, threw the money in and covered it up. A man passed just at the time and he thought the clinking sound of the falling money must have been heard. He watched that man all the afternoon, but he at last became convinced his fears were groundless. He went out to see his girl, came back about 11 p. m, returned the horse he had hired at a livery stable, got the money and hid it where it was found. He had no thought of killing old man Hill until he went to get the $20 bill changed, for Hill was a good friend of his. He had merely sharpened his knife the day before

BECAUSE IT WAS DULL.

Saturday afternoon Eugene Wyley was arrested on suspicion and Tom Forsythe was sent to get some witnesses whom Wylie said were at Beckville, who could prove an alibi for him. When the boy got to Grigsby's camp he hired a messenger for $2.50 to go on after the witnesses and sat down to a poker game in which he lost $113. After he returned to Carthage he made up his mind he would use no more of the money, but would marry his girl and go to Georgia, but when he got up here and got broke in Longview he went back to Carthage. He had to use the money. Had it not been for that poker, would never have trapped him for he never intended to use any more

tom-forsythe-carthage-1888-02-29.A9:
THE LAST ACT. The Murder of County Treasurer of Panola County Avenged by the Death of Tom Forsythe. He is Taken from Jail by Unmasked Men and with a Rope Round His Neck Leaps into Eternity. His Neck is Broken—The Body is Cut Down and Placed in the Spot where Hill was Killed. HOW IT WAS DONE.
Special to the Gazette.

BECKVILLE, TEX., Feb. 29.—The last act of the terrible drama is over and the murderer of County Treasurer Hill has gone to meet his victim. In the court-house yesterday the confession of the terrible crime was listened to by an excited crowd. With his hat tipped back on his head, a cigar in his mouth and legs crossed over the corner of a table, Tom Forsythe told the story of his crime, and while the cheeks of brave men blanched at his recital he himself was calm, cool and collected. His confession condensed, is that having a $20 gold piece to change, he went to Mr. Hill to get it changed. While the old gentleman was stooped at the safe the sight of the money overcame and tempted him to the deed, and an ax lying handy and the courthouse being deserted for dinner, gave him an excellent opportunity. He felled him with the ax, striking a number of times. He afterward cut his throat with his knife. After locking the door upon going out, he put the keys in his overcoat pocket.

At 10 o'clock last night a large number of men got possession of him and told him, "You must die to night."

It is said his mother so far recovered as to send word to please

NOT BURN HER SON, which it is reported was not the intention. At that hour he was talking beneath a tree, when he said: "Don't haul me up. I want to die and that quickly, and if you will let me go on to the limb I will jump off when you tell me you are ready."

He was allowed to do this, and after seating himself on the limb he asked for a drink of water, which was given him. Immediately afterward he was told all was ready, and he leaped into eternity. His body was taken down, and by midnight was lying in one of the offices of the courthouse.

A feeling of intense sadness pervades the entire county over the many tragedies which have been the outcome of a wild and reckless life, and great is the sympathy existing for both the victim's widow and the heart-broken mother of the murderer.

FURTHER PARTICULARS.
Special to the Gazette.

LONGVIEW, Tex., Feb. 29.—Last night while the news of the arrest of Tom Forsythe and his confession of the murder and robbery of D. C. Hill, treasurer of Panola county, was being flashed over the wires from this place, quite another scene was being enacted at Carthage which has no telegraphic communications. About 400 men were taking out of jail by force young Forsythe who offered no resistance, but begged only to be spared death by fire. He climbed up a ladder while both of his hands were pinioned behind him, and at the word jumped off, breaking his neck and dying at the end of the lynchers' AVENGING ROPE.

All this was done quicker than it takes to record it. No masks were used and the bright moonlight at 10 p. m. shone as bright as day, disclosing the familiar features of about 400 of Panola county's best citizens. The scene was in the court yard right in plain view of the hotel verandah. After life was extinct he was cut down and carried by the lynchers to the very spot still stained with the blood of County Treasurer D. C. Hill and laid down in a similar position and the mob quietly dispersed and friends took the young man's remains and prepared them for the coffin. His body was taken to Beckville for interment.

THE CONFESSION.

Below we submit in a few facts and parts of his confession made to Mr. H. E. Parker, who worked up the case and who deserves great credit for his shrewdness. Mr. Parker's first suspicion was aroused when he took young Forsythe to the spot where Treasurer Hill was murdered and from that time on he left nothing undone to find out where the money was concealed. He first succeeded in getting young Forsythe to believe he was after the negro barber, Tippett, thereby turning all suspicion. He brought young Forsythe up to this place ostensibly to shadow Tippet, whose father lives here. While here young Forsythe gambled, and being broken borrowed money from Mr. Parker which he paid back at Carthage when he returned. The young man continued to lose and repenish from the stolen money, each visit to which was closely watched until

THE WHEREABOUTS OF THE MONEY was located. Mr Parker wishing to locate the silver, which Forsythe seemed never to resort to, asked him if he could not get him some silver as he could not raise any in town, to which Forsythe assented and soon was shadowed to a thicket in the woods near Carthage. After some search a broken pine limb was found, under which fresh dirt was discovered. Upon digging the silver was found and guarded. Then further developments were waited till Monday, when the arrest was made and the lynching was deferred by the promise of young Forsythe to confess in open court and be protected, which was promised but which mortal could not have done. The money was found in young Forsythe's trunk in his room at his father's. Young Forsythe, in his confession, said he killed Treasurer Hill at noon while no one else was at the court, and buried the money in an old out-house near by and rode out in the country to see a young lady that evening. Returning late at night he took the bills to his room and buried the silver as stated above.

A full statement is promised by Mr. Parker, who lives here, which may disclose interesting facts which have never been published.

A RINGING DENUNCIATION.
Governor Ross Discusses and Denounces Mob Violence.
lowing letter to Judge J. H. Long of Carthage, Panola county:

EXECUTIVE OFFICE
AUSTIN, March 5, 1888.

Hon. J. H. Long, Carthage, Texas.

My dear Judge:—Upon the statement of facts presented, I feel that the reward has been justly earned, and it will be paid to the parties entitled to it. At the same time, without discourse or any unkindness, it is with immesurable regret that I cannot let the occasion pass without uttering my opinion that this instance of mob violence in a community of people presenting all the physical evidences that go to make up a peaceful, industrious population, hitherto observant of law and order, and supplied with local and convenient tribunals, was an unwise proceeding; made without sufficient cause.

Indifference on my part would be endorsement and patronage of guilt. The executive, though obligated to see the laws faithfully executed, is nevertheless powerless to reach by law the grand jury which refused to indict, or the petit jury refusing to convict and even the officers who fail to do their duty are beyond his reach, still the probable consequences to society at large are too grave for silence.

Whenever there is a refusal to obey the laws made by the people in due form and whenever popular opinion in any community can override them, or on any excuse, however plausible, take the administration of justice from the proper tribunal into their own hands, government in a proper sense ceases to exist and society lapses into a state of barbarism.

I am aware that it is sometimes urged in justification of lynch law, so called, that our laws are imperfect and not properly executed, and because of mal-administration in the exercise of the power belonging to the state and counties to secure obedience, bad men, under certain conditions may be relieved from punishment. This is unquestionably true; and it would be strange if it were not, since our laws are made by fallible legislators, expounded by fallible judges, and executed by fallible officers. But this is no excuse for violating them, such as they are.

The way to gain relief for the violators of law is not by inaugurating lawlessness. It so, we might as well tear down our temples of justice. The very worst law is better than no law, and those who have an interest in the country or the prosperity of the state; those who have property to be preserved; those who have liberties to be protected; those that have rights that they cherish, are the last men in any community who should give sanction to acts of violence. Let every man take the vindication of his rights, the redress of his grievances or the punishment of offences into his own hands, regardless of the laws of the land, which are at once the standard to define the limit of his liberties, and the guardian to defend them, and the result will be that each man will be arrayed in deadly strife against the others, to the possible extent of extermination, it may be.

The first thing to do in this world is to be right, and to plant ourselves in a positeon on which we can stand in sunshine and in storm, and while Forsy was certainly guilty of an act stamped by Deity with the worst seal and signet, I cannot see by what method of reasoning the good people of Panola county, while earnestly protesting obedience to law and order, could pursuade themselves into an attempt to measure out retaliation as a recompense of his crime in due proportion to its extent. This was not only futile, but a usurpation of the powers belonging only to an allwise and allpowerful being.

Punishment is not to be administered by way of vengeance. If their action is claimed to have been in the interest of just punishment for a crime which otherwise would have gone unwhipt of justice, there is some measure of excuse. But all right-minded men, when passion has calmed, must see that this is anarchy, pure and simple, and that the desrest rights of their community and society would be sacrificed by its prevalence.

Having been "sculptured into precedent" it is liable also to be renewed upon much slighter provocation, and lead to the possible detriment of some of those who could hereafter with poor grace plead exemption from its usurping force by an an appeal for the protection of that law which they were willing to see meted out to another, however guilty. Such things have happened within my own observation in time past.

Anarchy in Texas---Two of its Late Exhibitions.
Governor Ross has done himself himself credit by publishing a strong protest against mob law in Texas, which he justly brands as anarchy. We copy from the Huntsville Item a summary of the case which called forth the Governor's manifesto:

Tom Forsyth, the confessed murderer of county treasurer Hill of Panola county, was hanged by the indignant citizens of Carthage shortly after his capture. The particulars of the lynching are revolting. With his arms pinioned behind him, young Forsyth was led to the foot of a ladder placed against a tree whereon he was to be hanged by unmasked men, friends and neighbors. One of the two sons of the murdered treasurer adjusted the rope on the boy's neck. Nearly all the details of the hanging were known to the lynched boys friends, who said as death was deserved and must inevitably come, the sooner the end was reached the better. Clasped in each others arms the mother and sister of the doomed son and brother prayed with streaming eyes and moans of anguish to the God of Mercy for their loved, while he, with stoical nonchalance, climbed the ladder, received a drink of water from the hand of the son of his victim and leaped into eternity. Those who saw the leap say it seemed as if the neck was stretched to the distance of a foot. Death came rapidly and then the body was cut down, taken to the late treasurer's office and laid in the blood of his victim. Far better than that had been the trial of the culprit by law and his execution in a legal manner.

We copy from an exchange a summary of the facts in the other case which transpired about the same time as the above:

In Wharton county is a village called Spanish Camp. It is a retired and isolated spot in the edge of a dense forest. Here some negroes had gained possession of some land which they were quietly tilling and from which they had raised a crop. Some white men coveted the ground and ordered the negroes to vacate. This they refused to do. The matter came to a trial in a court of justice and the negroes won the suit, the court sustaining their legal claim to the property. This was about one month ago. Finding that threats could not intimidate, nor law dispossess these colored men, their white antagonists, in the dead of night, gathered a posse of their own diabolical breed, who armed themselves with winchesters and shotguns, surrounded the house while eight negroes were asleep inside, saturated the outside of the building with kerosene, while the inmates to whom the law had given possession were within, fired it, and as the roasting victims attempted to escape shot them down in cold blood, killing seven out of the eight and wounding the sole survivor.

The Governor scarcely alluded to this latter outrage, which he ought to have denounced quite as strongly as the other. He however justly adds:

The people of the world will seize hold of these casual or incidental acts of violence occurring in Madison, Wharton and Panola counties to blacken whole communities, and to misrepresent the entire state as well as baptize our people anew in a perfect stream of calumny. Hence, as the executive charged with the care for these public interests, and jealous of the honor and fair name of the state, I record my utter condemnation of mob violence of every character, and urge the people to a prompt and fearless vindication of the supremacy of the laws wherever and by whomsoever they may be assailed.

Frances B. Willard, pres., and Caroline B. Buel, sec., of the National W. C. T. U. have appointed a week of prayer from the 18th to the 25th inst. for the National, state and local organizations of the Union, and earnestly urge its observance. We make the following extract:

Seek God. Seek Him alone for a great awakening of the church and nation. The liquor traffic is here with its abominations legalized because of spiritual death. We need conscience aroused and made true. Sisters of the W. C. T. U., set the week apart, hold at least one meeting a day for the quiet, unostentations seeking of God herein suggested. Two public evening meetings, with sermons, gospel talks or conferences would be of great value. The evening of March 25 might be made effective by union services where these can be secured. When churches cannot give way for this, hold such a meeting in the afternoon of that day.

No topics are suggested lest they lead from the one central thought of all the days. Many things you will remember: our own work, our country's needs and perils, the workers who must go out into the coming contest, the pleaders at the fireside, the voters at the ballot box, but this one thing seek and find—God's touch of power upon our own spiritual life, and the spiritual life of the nation.

San Antonio, Tex., March 12.—At an early hour this morning the residence of Dr. J. B. Johnson caught fire and was almost wholly destroyed before the department reached the scene. NOT QUITE AS STRONGLY.

The San Marcos Free Press commenting upon the outrages committed in Panola county and in Wharton county calls attention to the manner in which the governor of the state denounces the Panola defiance of law while he coos mildly as a sucking dove over the seven-fold more damnable outrage committed in Wharton county. The Free Press says that the governor has scarcely alluded to the latter outrage which he ought to have denounced quite as strongly as the other. "Quite as strongly" is good. In Panola county young Tom Forsyth was lynched for the murder of Treasurer Hill. The lynching was not only a most lawless act but it was most barbarously done, without attempt at concealment and the culprit, alter death, was dragged to the office of his victim and rolled in his blood, this in the presence of the criminal's mother and sister who stood by sobbing and praying for God's mercy on their wayward and erring son and brother. This is the Panola county outrage of which Governor Ross complains so loudly and complains so justly—the lynching of a confessed murderer. The other case, the Wharton county outrage, against which he did not protest very audibly and which the Free Press thinks should have been denounced quite as strongly, was the murder of seven colored citizens in cold blood. because they accepted the decisions of the district court in a land case and retained possession of the property which the court had decided was theirs in law and equity. For refusing to surrender their legal rights and vacate their home, they were murdered in cold blood, their murderers having first fired the house while their innocent victims were asleep, that they might shoot them down by the light of their own burning home. This is the outrage which the San Marcos Free Press thinks that Governor Ross should have denounced "quite as strongly" as the lynching of the murderer of county treasurer Hill. This is the outrage for denouncing which the Light has been branded as the instigator of sectional feeling and the engenderer of sectional hate. This is the outrage for which the Light condemned the democratic press of this state for having the lock-jock, so far as any denunciation of the black hearted deed was concerned, and for which denunciation it has been charged with trying to revive race prejudices. The Light remarks with great pleasure that one democratic journal has so far opened its moral optics as to see that the murder of seven colored citizens in cold blood should be quite as strongly denounced as the lynching of one white murdered whose cold blooded crime was confessed. The Light will look hopefully and anxiously for some farther signs of returning sensibility on the part of the democratic press of this state over the matter of the Wharton outrage. When found, the Light will be most happy to chronicle the fact and give publicity to the protest.

MARYLAND.

At an early hour last Tuesday morning, fire broke out in the toy warehouse of Prior, Hilgenberg & Co., 107 South Sharp street, Baltimore, and before the firemen could get to work an explosion of fireworks wrecked the building and caused the flames to spread with alarming rapidity to the drug house of J. H. Winkilman & Co. and the hat house of M. S. Levy & Co., on the north. Scarcely had the firemen entered the edifice occupied by the drug house when the inside of the building seemed to suddenly drop in. A terrific explosion followed and the immense building collapsed.

The entire fire department had by this time reached the scene, and as the attention of the men was concentrated on the building under which their comrades were buried, the flames had a chance to spread, and spread they did with frightful rapidity. In an incredibly short space of time the entire block, running from Lombard to Plat streets, was a seething mass of flame. At the drug house the firemen worked bravely. Holes were cut through the pavement and every effort made to reach the imprisoned men, but they were buried under a great mass of brick and iron and the fierce flames were roaring around the spot.

Awful groans came from the pile which had the effect to make the working firemen put forth superhuman efforts and after more than an hour's work it became evident that some of the men were alive and that they were being roasted to death. John Kelly, of truck number 2, managed to crawl out from the rubbish and of the men who entered the building he was the only one to escape with his life. He was horribly cut and bruised, but his injuries are not serious.

The intense heat several times drove the firemen from the building where the bodies of their unfortunate comrades were lying under tons of brick and iron, but they persisted in the search and shortly after noon the first body, that of Mr. Wagner, was brought to the light. No spot was on the body of Harry Walker, standing erect, as if packed in. Near him was found what was left of George Bowers, but no other bodies were found until nearly 6 o'clock, when that of George Kerins was uncovered. The bodies were terribly disfigured, the flesh being burned off in many places. The search is being pursued tonight with the aid of electric lights.

John Pollard, a negro switchman of Montgomery, was run over and killed by an engine last Tuesday night.

A special from Rome, Covington county, Alabama, says that the negro man, William Martin, who recently committed a brutal assault on Mrs. McClellan, a respectable white lady, met with a horrible fate. He was captured by a posse of citizens, but had to be shot down before he would surrender. He partially recovered from his wounds, and was turned over to a deputy sheriff to be taken to Florida. Before he got across the Alabama line, the negro was taken from the officer and his body was riddled with bullets and thrown into an old well. He had made a full confession of his crime, and said he meant to kill the entire McClellan family.

Pauline McCoy, the young negro woman who was recently convicted in the circuit court of Bullock county, of the murder of Miss Annie Jordan, a demented young white woman who wandered from her home in Montgomery last spring, has made a full confession of the crime to the jail physician at Union springs.

The murder was committed near Three Notch. Pauline says she and Annie Jordan had a quarrel, and that she choked the young woman to death and concealed the dead body in the bushes. The murderess is sentenced to death on the scaffold on the 18th of October.

KENTUCKY.

Sam Scanlan, an ex-fireman of Louisville, shot his wife three times and himself once last Thursday. It is thought both will die.

Scanlan had been on a continuous spree since his brother, Jim Scanlan, the race course sport, was killed at St. Paul, about a month ago. He was almost wild with liquor when he returned home about 11 o'clock today.

As soon as he saw his wife he rushed into the house, seized her, and without a word of warning shot her. She broke away and ran. Scanlan fired again, shattering her right arm and, as she tried to clamber over the fence, shot her a third time bringing her to the ground. He then placed the pistol just below his jaw and fired, tearing a hole through his mouth and throat and imbedding the ball in his brain. Scanlan was taken to the city hospital and his wife was left at their home. She is shot twice in the body and once in the arm.

TEXAS.

Passengers and crew on the Texas Pacific train from the east were considerably excited Friday morning over an attempt to wreck the train near Woodlawn, this side of Marshall.

Three miles this side of Woodlawn station the train was brought to a very abrupt stop, which bumped several heads and shook the passengers up considerably, but caused little interest until it became known that an attempt had been made to wreck the train. From the means employed by the wreckers its was generally agreed to be the work of robbers and they were expected every moment to swoop down upon the train from the surrounding jungles. Two ties were securely spiked in the center of the track and one fastened across these so as to rest upon either rail.

The work was done by persons who understand spiking, and they must have been numerous and strong enough to handle very heavy green ties. The place selected for the wreck is a high bridge, from which the train would have plunged into a deep, rugged ravine, carrying many of its passengers to destruction.

The front wheels of the engine ran upon the obstruction before a complete halt could be made. But the engineer had seen the trouble in time to "slow up." The timbers were removed as quickly as possible and the train pulled out to avoid robbery. Most of the passengers having received the alarm, were up and in arms, however, when the conductor returned to the train and were ready for the robbers. This is the third attempt to wreck this very train at the same place. This leads to the belief that an enemy of the road or of some member of this particular crew is the guilty one. Every effort is being made to find him out. The lists of acquaintances of the conductor, engineer and others have been carefully checked off to find from these, if possible, some person who harbors a grudge against any member of the crew. The cattle agent of that division of the roads thinks perhaps he has the criminal on his list among the roll of claimants for cattle killed near Woodlawn. Another theory is that there is a crazy wrecker of large in the thickets whose grievances are all imaginary, and who has undertaken destructive schemes of various kinds recently, one being an effort to blow up a neighboring aw-mill with dynamite.

wallace-mitchell-syracuse-1888-06-26.A3: SYRACUSE, Kan., June 26.—Sheriff Huff man arrived here today from Trinidad, Col., having in charge Wallace Mitchell, who murdered the boy Johnson and wounded his father, in this city on the night of June 9. In an interview he said: "I was born in Denton county, Texas, December 6, 1869, and have in Kansas six years. My father was killed in the big Horn masacre. My step-father, W. W. Fane, has a farm and horse ranch near Hazleton, Harper county, Kansas. Was in Coolidge about May 25, and met Oscar Johnson there. I engaged to work for him for my board. Went to Syracuse with a bunch of ponies and met his brother August there with his boy. From there all went to Hartland, Kansas. I slept with Oscar in Syracuse; he proposed to murder his brother in Hartland. He told me his plan, said his brother had about $2,000 in his left vest pocket and left pants pocket, I should go back to Syracuse with August and his son, during the night kill the old man, and he (Oscar) would come in during the night and divide the money. He would go back to camp. I to Coolidge and south from there to the Texas Panhandle. The old man, the boy and myself reached Syracuse, got there Tuesday night. I went to bed in the wagon, Johnson and his boy slept on the ground. I slept about an hour, then awoke, waiting for Johnson to come. He did not appear, and at 1 o'clock I got up, took the ax, and going to the bed, struck the old man on the head. The boy rose partly up and I struck him. I thought them both dead. I searched the two pockets, found in one four dollars in currency and the other checks and drafts for nine hundred and sixty dollars. Then I took the train to Coolidge. I went south on the cattle trail next day; got into a cow camp in the night; took a horse, went to Minneapolis, Col., then to Stonington, where I was captured by one of the cowboys, given over to the sheriff and taken to Trinidad." No one believes Mitchell's story about young Johnson being connected with the murder. Joe Mitchell, a brother to Wallace, was lynched in Ashland, Clark county, for killing two men and wounding a girl. Wallace is a tough looking customer, and talks of his bloody deed with the utmost composure. Public feeling is strong against him, and the people may forestall the courts.
wallace-mitchell-syracuse-1888-06-26.A7:
Wallace Mitchell, Murderer, Lynched at Midnight by a Mob.
He Is Strung Up on the Spot Where His Victim Was Slaughtered.
Redskins Loaded With Fire Water Go Gunning for Herders.
A Kentucky Woman's Love Prompts Her to Kill Her Rival.
SYRACUSE, Kan., June 27.—Wallace Mitchell had his preliminary trial before Justice Waggoner yesterday. He pleaded guilty to the murder of Oscar Johnson and the attempted murder of August Johnson. He repeated the story of his crime with the utmost sang froid and as if it was an everyday occurrence. At the conclusion of the testimony he was remanded to jail until the September term of court. The cold-blooded recital of his fiendish deed by the prisoner had an exciting effect on the people, and everywhere on the streets knots of men were gathered, with him as the theme of conversation. It was easy to see that a storm was brewing and that

SUMMARY JUSTICE
was to be visited on the man. After dark matters came more to a focus, and about midnight a body of men numbering a hundred or more gathered around the water tank, and under the lead of a captain proceeded to the vicinity of the jail and demanded admittance of the sheriff. This he refused, and declared his intention to protect his prisoner at all hazards. The citizens seemed loth to make any assault on the sheriff, but were none the less determined to have their man. Two men were again sent to demand the keys, but the sheriff was gone. A number of the assailants started in hot pursuit while others went for railroad iron to batter in the doors. The sheriff, however, was soon overhauled, but another delay occurred. He had thrown the keys away. After a short delay they were found, the doors unlocked and the culprit brought out. He was taken directly to the place where the murder was committed and given all the time he desired for

PRAYER AND CONFESSION.

He entirely exonerated Oscar Johnson from complicity in the murder and said the sheriff of Las Animas county, Colorado, helped him to make up the story. He then made his last prayer, and at about the hour he killed the boy—1:30 a. m.—hung a lifeless corpse from the cross piece of a telegraph pole. Mitchell's crime was the murder of a little boy twelve years old and the attempted murder of his father for money and the endeavor to implicate another man in the hideous crime. The verdict of the people sustains the lynching.
wallace-mitchell-syracuse-1888-06-26.A11:
Four Lynchings in Kansas.
KANSAS CITY, June 28.—A mob at Minneapolis, Kansas, took Chubb McCarthy, murderer of Mike Dorsey, from jail early this morning and hanged him. This was the last of four lynchings in the state within twenty four hours. According to Kansas law a person convicted of murder in the first degree is sent to the penitentiary for one year and then is liable to be hanged at any time the governor has ever signed a warrant under such circumstances and as a result there are fifty-four murderers under sentence of death in the State Prison. To day's record is the outcome of the situation.

Two weeks ago Wallace Mitchell assassinated a man and a boy at Syraouse. He escaped to Colorado, but was captured and brought back Tuesday. He confessed his crime with coolness and deliberation. This so enraged the citizens that they took Mitchell from the officers, and, dragging him half dead to the scene of his crime, hanged him to the crossbeam of a telegraph pole and riddled his body with bullets. The news spread through out the state, and the settlement seemed to be that lynch law was the only remedy on hand. At Minneapolis Chubb McCarthy was in jail awaiting the action of the grand jury. His crime had been most flendish, and he had been caught in the very act. At 12 o'clock an armed band, numbering 200, silently rode into the streets of the town. Guards were posted at the residences of all officials and the streets leading to the jail were thoroughly patrolled. A squad broke the doors of the prison and the jailor was compelled to give up the keys to the culprit's cell. The murderer was taken to the bridge crossing the Soloma River and suspended high in the air.

At Chetopa a different scene was wit nessed John Risbee and Wylie Lee had been arrested by the Marshal and his deputy. In making a desperate attempt to escape they had shot both officers. The Sheriff captured them and held them in the City Hall until the arrival of the train which was to carry them to the county seat. A turbulent crowd gathered about the hall. At 12 30 last night word was brought that the deputy was dead and the marshal dying. A special guard had been placed about the building Suddenly the electric light went out. The officers were speedily overpowered by 300 men. The prisoners were dragged from under a table where they had crawled, in a vain hope of saving their lives. They were dragged into an adjoining room, the windows kicked out, and the doomed men placed on the sill. Ropes were fastened to heavy timbers and around their necks and against the muzzles of Winchester rifles they were ordered to jump into the street. The strong ropes were slack, and as they tumbled from the window they fell a distance of thirty feet almost to the ground. Risbee's neck was broken and Lee strangled to death.
wallace-mitchell-syracuse-1888-06-26.A13:
ALLOWED TIME TO PRAY.
Lynchers Kneel an Hour with Their Victim and Then Mang Him.
A Garden City (Kan.) telegram says: This morning at half-past 1'clock J. W. Mitchell, the murderer of Oscar Johnson and would-be murderer of August Johnson on June 9th, was taken from the jail at Syracuse by a mob of one hundred and fifty men and hanged to a telegraph-pole. Yesterday afternoon Mitchell had a preliminary examination, at which he confessed the crime, implicating a younger brother of August Johnson as an accessory to the deed. In the coolest manner possible, and in the presence of the murdered boy's mother, he narrated every detail of the act.

Fearing a lynching Sheriff Hoffman called on the citizens to help him defend the jail against any attack which might be made, but none responded and he was compelled to stand guard over the small one-story structure alone with his Winchester.

READY FOR VENGEANCE.

About midnight the crowd made their appearance and two of their number were sent forward to parley. The sheriff was requested to surrender the jail and give up the keys, which he refused to do. A number of the crowd then went to the railroad and carried over a bar of railroad iron to use as a ram against the walls. The demand upon the sheriff was renewed, but fearing he would lose the keys against such odds he left. The mob gave chase and the sheriff threw the keys away. After a short time the keys were found and the crowd returned to the jail.

IN THE HANDS OF A MOB.

Opening the doors the crowd brought out the prisoner, who piteously inquired, "Are you going to hang me here?" He was taken to the spot where he committed the murder, where he again made his confession, but this time he stated that he was alone responsible for the murder, and young Johnson had nothing whatever to do with it. He was given time to pray, and kneeling, the mob following his example, he prayed aloud for nearly an hour, calling for forgiveness.

HANGED TO A TELEGRAPH-POLE.

He was then taken across the railroad track, where the rope was placed around his neck, the knot being tied in the most approved hangman style. The rope was swung to a telegraph-pole twenty feet in the air, without resistance on his part. He died without a struggle.

The coroner arrived at 8 o'clock. The body was cut down, and an inquest held, but no one could be found who knew anything about it.

Mitchell's home was at Hazelton, Bourbon county, and his relatives have been telegraphed to. He was a worthless fellow, and the people of Syracuse, while regretting the manner of his taking off, say that he received his deserts.

A Deliberate Lynching Party.
Lynching parties are not always frenzied with passion. Sometimes their proceedings are characterized by all the deliberateness and solemnity of a regular court. The crowd that lynched Murderer Mitchell at Syracuse, Kan., on Wednesday of last week, for instance, quietly led the murderer to the scene of the murder and there compelled him to confess. Then he was told to pray, and for almost an hour the crowd listened reverently while the wretched man made a rambling prayer. When he ceased praying the people, many of whom had been upon their knees while the man prayed, promptly took him in hand and strung him up until life was extinct.

wallace-mitchell-syracuse-1888-06-26.A29:
Insecurity of Human Life.
Four men were lynched in one day in Kansas last week, two in Minneapolis, one in Syracuse, two at Chetopa and one in Illinois, making five in all, three whites and two negroes. There is no country in the world where human life is so insecure as in several of the United States of America. It is a reproach upon the state and national government. It is a damnable outrage, not possible anywhere but in this boasted civilization of the 19th century in a free country. —The Iowa Citizen.

Nothing in the world makes human life as insecure as war, and nothing is a greater reproach to a State or Nation than to go to war, and nothing is a greater standing disgrace than a standing army, and nothing is more opposed to Christianity than the teaching, the spirit and practice of war.

william-patterson-louisville-1888-06-17.A2:
On the Verge of a Lynching.
LOUISVILLE, June 17.—A strange story was made public to-day in connection with the Governor's action on the application of William Patterson for a pardon. Patterson is a negro who, with another, in broad daylight attacked Jennie Bowman, a servant girl, in a fashionable suburban residence, last year, and beat her in such a horrible manner that she afterwards died. Both were captured, and Patterson denied his guilt, while the other confessed. The latter was hanged, but retracted on the scaffold his statement that Patterson was with him at the time of the murder. A tremendous effort has been made to secure Patterson's pardon, although he was convicted and his sentence affirmed in the highest court in the state. A petition was sent to Governor Buckner, who gave him a respite of one month, as he had not had time to examine the case.

The Legislature was then in session, and the Governor respited him again until June 22. He announced a couple days ago that he could not again interfere with the sentence. To-day it was learned that a well organized plot had been laid for a few men to lynch Patterson in case he had been pardoned. The plan was for one or two to go too the jail at a time and then seize the keys, unlock the door and hang the prisoner. It was thought this could be done so secretly and quietly that the authorities would not have a chance to interfere in time. Less than a dozen prominent citizens who had taken great interest in the case had fully arranged the plans and in fact they came very near taking this action. When the first respite was granted, they actually held a meeting to make the arrangements when some of the cooler heads persuaded them that the Governor would not interfere.
william-patterson-louisville-1888-06-17.A3: William Patterson the accomplice of Albert Turner, in the murder of Jennie Bowman, must die on the scaffold at last. Gov. Buckner has given this case a long and very careful investigation and study, hearing all the evidence and argument of the attorneys for and against, and declined to interfere with the court's judgment. The execution will take place next Friday.
william-patterson-louisville-1888-06-17.A5:
DIED PROTESTING HIS INNOCENCE. A Negro Hanged in Louisville for a Crime He Says He Did Not Commit.
Louisville, June 22.—William Patterson, a negro, was hanged in the jail yard shortly after daybreak this morning. His conduct on the scaffold was the most vigorous protest of innocence possibly ever heard from a man executed by the law. He concluded by saying:

"I have never seen my so-called victim, and either before or after her death could not distinguish her from Queen Victoria herself. I know that no earthly power can now save me from this," glancing at the noose, "but I swear I am as innocent of her death as I am that of Marie Antoinette."

The execution was a most bunglesome affair. The noose had not been properly adjusted, and when the trap was sprung the knot slipped under his chin.

He struggled for four minutes.

On June 21 a year ago Jennie Bowman, a servant-girl, was murdered while protecting her employer's house from robbery. There were evidence that two persons had committed the crime. Albert Turner, a negro, was arrested and confessed, implicating Patterson. Turner was hanged one month after the crime.

Patterson, however, fought his case through all the courts, making a final appeal to the Governor.
william-patterson-louisville-1888-06-17.A6:
PATTERSON STRANGLED.
Shocking Scenes at the Execution of a Murderer.
REMARKABLE OCCURRENCE.
Four Minutes After the Drop Falls the Victim Speaks—Slowly Strangled to Death—Belief in His Innocence by Many.
LOUISVILLE, Ky., June 22.—William Patterson (colored) was hanged this morning at 6:10 o'clock, in the yard of the Jefferson county jail.

He was convicted with another colored man, Albert Turner, for assaulting and fatally beating Miss Jennie Bowman on April 23, 1888. Miss Bowman was a domestic employed by a family who lived in a fashionable suburb, and the crime was committed about 10 o'clock in the morning.

The family were all absent from the house at the time, and no one witnessed the murder. Turner and Patterson were arrested on suspicion, and Turner immediately confessed. Patterson protested his innocence.

On April 27th, a mob surrounded the jail bent on lynching the two negroes. The State militia was called out and guarded the prisoners for three days, keeping the mob at bay, when the excitement subsided, and the crowd dispersed.

Turner pleaded guilty, but on the scaffold said Patterson was innocent. He was hung on July 1. Patterson was tried, convicted, but appealed his case, and the lower court was sustained. The Governor respited him three times, but refused to interfere further.

Patterson protested his innocence on the scaffold. He was slowly strangled to death, and four minutes after the drop fell said: "Curse them!" and then, "Lord save me!" His struggles were frightful. Many people believe firmly in his innocence, and there were strong attempts to secure his pardon. Dr. Garvin, the attending physician, says that talking after the drop is unprecedented in the history of executions
